The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?

BBC News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 00:52:39 GMT

Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.

The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.

But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.

The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.

The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.

It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.

But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.

The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.

That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.

Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.

One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.

Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.

But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.

"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.

"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."

The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.

The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.

Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.

Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.

The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.

Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.

It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".

Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.

He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."

The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.

Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.

Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.

In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.

Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.

"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.

Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.

Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.

Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.

In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.

Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.

Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.

His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.

"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.

"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

Ambika Mod says the 'glass ceiling is always getting higher' for South Asian actors

BBC News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 00:49:00 GMT

An overworked junior doctor, an aspiring writer and now a ruthless assassin.

Ambika Mod's TV credits are becoming as diverse as the roles are complex.

The actress broke through as the overwhelmed Shruti in BBC medical drama This Is Going To Hurt in 2022, and gained wide recognition for her starring role as Emma Morley in Netflix's miniseries adaptation of David Nicholls' bestselling novel One Day.

Mod, who joins the cast of Black Doves for the second season of the streamer's spy thriller, tells BBC Newsbeat she is careful about the roles she takes on.

As the daughter of Indian immigrants the 31-year-old, from Hatfield, says a "central tenet" of her work is to "change how South Asian women are seen on-screen and the characters that we are seen in".

She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege" some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles.

Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.

Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism".

"I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through.

"I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."

A report from the Creative Diversity Network suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.

And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom found people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.

It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".

It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.

Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical.

"I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says.

"And I'm not looking to regress."

And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next."

"I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says.

"And also what's going to be fun, as well."

Her latest role as Laila, a lawless agent of the covert Black Doves, attracted her as it subverted a lot of espionage genre tropes.

The character is introduced in season two to assist Keira Knightley's agent Helen on a mission as the stakes get even higher for those working with the secretive organisation.

Mod says it was "such a good time" working alongside Knightley and getting to do some extreme stunt sequences together.

"Honestly, the main reason I wanted to do it was because of all the stunts," she says.

"Really badass but it was so much fun.

"It was just so fun to take down an absolutely staggering number of men in every single episode."

The thriller also has a dark humour to it, which aligns well with Mod who often brings a dry wit to her characters.

Her comedic career goes back to when she was about 18, and while studying at Durham University she was part of its sketch comedy group.

Despite having not done stand-up for about five years, she says she would "love" to do more comedy in the future.

"I do sometimes think about going back to it," she reveals.

"I have a lot of stories to tell."

Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

BBC News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 00:48:59 GMT

Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.

Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.

Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.

In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.

Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.

Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.

The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.

Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.

"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.

That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."

The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.

But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.

Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.

"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.

Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.

"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.

Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".

Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.

Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".

"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.

Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.

With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.

A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.

In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.

The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.

But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.

As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

The rise of microdramas: The 'snackable' shows made for the scrolling age

BBC News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 00:45:45 GMT

Every evening, Heather Sharrock settles down to watch her favourite show.

But it's not on Netflix or iPlayer, or even on her television - it's on her phone.

And while some of us might get through a handful of episodes of our latest must-watch series every night, Heather can binge on dozens - because the 55-year-old from Scotland is into microdramas.

"There's so much rubbish going on in the world at the moment," Heather says. "It's just nice to switch off and not think for a little while."

Microdramas - already huge in China - are becoming increasingly popular in the UK, and can be found on apps like ReelShort, CandyJar and DramaBox. Last week, producers announced classic Neighbours storylines would be repackaged as super-short vertical episodes, one of the latest signs the format is moving into the mainstream.

Made up of snappy, high-octane episodes, they are usually 60 to 90 seconds long. Many focus on themes like forbidden love, family feuds and secret billionaires, and nearly every instalment ends on a dramatic cliffhanger. Each series tends to have 50 or more episodes, making the total runtime comparable to a feature film.

Diane Aitken, 45, a fan from Scotland, likens the werewolf- and vampire-themed microdramas she enjoys to 1980s US soaps Dallas or Dynasty "on steroids".

The shows emerged in China in the late 2010s as cheap and quick-to-film adaptations from online novels, says China-born filmmaker Samantha Sun, and for many fans they're a form of escapism.

Sarah-Jayne Lunn, 46, from Doncaster, says they helped her cope during a difficult period in her life. "Straight away I was hooked," she says. "I didn't have to overthink."

Jen Cooper, a microdrama viewer who now works as a consultant in the industry, agrees. She says microdramas were originally popular among middle-aged women looking for romance content, with many BookTok and romantasy devotees watching them, but they are are now popular with a much wider audience.

Last year, China's microdrama market was worth more than 100 billion yuan (£11bn) and viewer numbers surpassed 800 million, according to China's National Radio and Television Administration. But they're also big in South Korea, India and the US, with streamers including Prime, Peacock and Disney+ announcing plans to add microdramas to their services.

In the UK, TattleTV, which bills itself as the the country's first dedicated microdrama app, was launched earlier this year, while the Royal Television Society held an industry panel discussion on microdramas this summer.

Companies are also looking to capitalise on the buzz around microdramas, making branded short video ads for social media, with examples including productions from Jamie Oliver, the Co-op, and a Channel 4 and Sol de Janeiro collaboration.

Microdramas have to be fast-paced to keep viewers' attention, says Charlotte Brokenbrow of Welsh production company Spare Arrow, which made its first series this year.

"If you leave too much air in the script and in the video, then someone's going to get bored and will scroll on," she says.

As well as breakneck speed, microdramas have proved popular because people can watch them in bite-sized chunks, leading some analysts to describe them as "snackable".

They also feed into a shift towards "casual, low-commitment viewing that we can dip in and out of," says Dr Tina Kendall, associate professor of film and media at Anglia Ruskin University.

Some people told BBC News they watch them in the car while waiting to pick up their children from school, while others said they have one on in the background while they catch up on housework or admin.

It's so "obvious what's going to happen", Sarah-Jayne says she can even enjoy them while she is working.

Dedicated apps typically hook viewers by letting them watch the first few episodes for free, before then requiring a subscription. CandyJar costs £49 for one year, while DramaBox costs £110, but most microdrama apps allow binge-watchers to buy weekly subscriptions or watch ads in exchange for free episodes.

As you scroll through the apps, themes such as mafia bosses, enemies-to-lovers plotlines and cowboys recur.

Sun says Chinese production companies often replicate successful formulas, with only minor tweaks - and that's something Heather has noticed, too. "A lot of them have been the same story, just set in a different setting," she says, adding that she's now "fed up" seeing billionaire CEO storylines.

More outlandish titles include I Adopted My Stolen Baby, Craving My British Cowboy and Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas.

Some fans say they feel certain plots have been degrading to women, in some cases involving crude depictions of violence and sexual assault. "It became a bit of a sort of joke that the female actress has had a million hideous things happen to her and been crying and screaming 10 million times before she's even got to lunch," says Coco Taylor, an actress who starred in her first microdrama in 2024.

Taylor says she has turned down roles in some series because she felt they were too misogynistic. But she and many other microdrama fans say the storytelling has developed which they credit to more storylines now being written by US and UK teams, and they speak enthusiastically about microdramas branching out into genres such as comedy, thriller and horror.

Haydn Wakeling, founder of production company Black Swan, first heard about microdramas earlier this year through a film industry contact. "Fast-forward to now and it's all anyone's talking about," he says.

Financially, microdramas are very attractive to directors and producers, Wakeling says - it typically takes less than two weeks to film a microdrama of between 60 and 90 minutes, pushing down costs.

Director Dan Löwenstein worked on his first microdrama, Mafia Lover, in February 2024. He's now on his 38th. Initially he worked on shows commissioned by Chinese apps, but says he's now working with US platforms, global streamers and UK companies, after the industry in China pivoted to AI production.

The UK is now Europe's largest audience for microdramas - and while many fans and producers in the industry are excited about the format's future, it's not without its critics.

Some deride microdramas as low-quality content that ruins people's attention spans. In an opinion piece for The Guardian, one writer said the shows were "catastrophically brainless and objectively bad".

But, as microdrama fan-turned-consultant Jen Cooper says: "No one's saying that this is profound, but if you've had that emotional reaction and you've made someone smile or made a hard day easier, then surely that is something wonderful to celebrate."

Can the Zelda remake capture the magic of the original?

BBC News Sun, 08 Nov 2026 00:37:45 GMT

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before, video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying

BBC News Sat, 07 Nov 2026 23:02:35 GMT

For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.

The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.

One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.

Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys. The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.

They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu.

A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find, with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.

Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.

Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.

For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.

"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.

Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.

Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.

As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.

Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.

Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.

"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year. "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."

Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.

That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.

Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.

But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."

There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.

For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.

Free newsletter

Doppler microwave sensors detect movement; others sense body heat or vibration. A new variety is triggered by the approach of any Bluetooth device.

Drones slip far behind the lines to place mines precisely on tracks and paths, or around trenches, giving a greater chance of finding a victim than random scattering. New Scientist November 07, 2026

At a certain point, it becomes impossible to convey the urgency of the climate crisis in words. Calls to “intensify efforts” to cut emissions or countries “expressing alarm” at the pace of climate change start to ring hollow after years of rising emissions. At a certain point, you have to ask, what difference will another carefully worded declaration really make?

This is a live question: next week, countries will gather at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, to progress the global response to climate change. For the seasoned attendee, these gatherings follow a predictable rhythm: some pomp and ceremony at the start when the world leaders are in attendance, followed by a quiet first week of backroom talks, escalating tension and fights over finance in the second week, all rounded off with a late-night showdown as countries argue over the wording of a final agreement.

In the context of ever more dire warnings from scientists and increasingly severe real-world climate disasters, this is an event cycle that is wearing thin. To many of those in attendance – and millions more looking on from afar – it is becoming increasingly clear that COP summits are failing to deliver meaningful progress.

Advertisement

This is a relatively new problem. For decades, the job of a COP negotiator was to forge some kind of global agreement to address climate change. That was no mean feat, and it took years of hard work and dedication to deliver the Paris Agreement in 2015. After the treaty was struck, climate negotiators then spent a few years busily drawing up the rules that would govern how the agreement would work in practice. But with that work largely completed by 2021, since then, COP summits have been left to drift, plagued by arguments over finance and bewildering last-minute disputes over the wording of seemingly uncontentious statements. At last year’s summit, for example, countries couldn’t agree on even mentioning fossil fuels in the final agreement.

COP31 will largely follow the same format. Arguments are already brewing over funding, negotiators are flexing their pens to hammer out details of new bureaucratic mechanisms, and hosts Turkey and Australia are limbering up for fresh disputes over which adverbs to deploy in a final agreement. This is your official warning: COP31 will not be the meeting that saves the world from climate peril.

But there could be one bright spark at the summit. An electrification pledge being touted by the Turkish presidency would see countries promise to increase electricity’s share of their final energy consumption to 35 per cent to 2035.

Focusing the climate effort on electrification is a smart move. In the current landscape, with disinformation rife and a climate denier still in the White House, electrifying stuff is probably our strongest climate weapon. High oil and gas prices and geopolitical instability make the energy security benefits of electrification obvious, while cheap green power could ease cost of living pressures in high-income countries and unlock development in low-income nations.

Electric power is also just so much more efficient than burning fuel. Electricity currently provides about 23 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, but it powers sectors that make up 46 per cent of the global economy, energy analyst Jan Rosenow pointed out recently. If the world’s economy transitioned to a highly electrified state, powered by renewables, total primary energy use – the raw inputs into the energy system – would fall by almost 50 per cent, Rosenow’s analysis shows. Electrifying stuff is a common-sense move, before you even get to the climate benefits.

Plenty of richer countries are not moving fast enough on this stuff. China and Indonesia are ahead of both the US and the UK on electrifying their economies, while India and Brazil are catching up fast. We could learn a lot by looking beyond our borders. Annual climate meetings should become an opportunity for countries to swap notes and share best practice on the energy transition, not fight over the wording of virtue-signalling statements.

For too long, COPs have been generating a lot of words and not much action. But efforts are under way behind the scenes to redesign these meetings as useful events for the clean energy transition. The push for electrification offers a hint of what this could look like. If it delivers, COP summits might yet have a useful future.

Such a move wouldn’t be unprecedented. Earlier this year, a NASA-funded mission carried out by commercial outfit Katalyst Space was launched to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, whose orbit was decaying in a similar fashion to Hubble’s. The mission failed due to a steering problem, but was widely regarded to be possible. Katalyst Space didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Alise Fisher at NASA says the agency is open to ideas from inside or outside the organisation, and isn’t taking anything off the table. “It wouldn’t be appropriate for the agency to speculate about specific potential responses, so we don’t inadvertently limit them, but NASA is looking to explore a range of technologies and approaches, including those the agency may not have considered previously.”

NASA’s call-out explains that a private company would need to supply everything for the mission: the launch vehicle, the spacecraft and, if applicable, the crew. The space agency issued a similar call for ideas in 2022, but did not proceed with any despite reportedly receiving eight submissions. It did investigate a proposal by SpaceX, but the company didn’t respond to New Scientist’s questions on whether it would be submitting a new proposal this time.

Thomas Haworth at Queen Mary University of London is part of a panel of scientists advising NASA on what direction to take with Hubble, which he describes as “the greatest telescope of all time”. He went into discussions with colleagues expecting the focus to be on how NASA could be advised to extract the most science from Hubble before the end of its life, but found that re-boosting its orbit was actually higher on the agenda, he says.

“It’s within the realms of possibility,” says Haworth. “The overall document that we’re coming up with, which still isn’t submitted yet, is going to try and strongly make that recommendation. There is quite a lot of effort to argue for a boost.”

Is an old NASA probe about to redraw the frontier of the solar system?

NASA is likely to make a decision quickly once that recommendation is in, because planning a boost mission will take years, says Haworth. “You need to decide now.”

Stephen Wilkins at the University of Sussex, UK, says Hubble has unique abilities unmatched by any other instrument – including the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope.

Hubble can do high-resolution ultraviolet imaging better than anything currently available. NASA aims to launch the Ultraviolet Explorer in 2030, which will cover the same part of the spectrum but with a tenth of the resolution, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) may launch in the 2040s and match Hubble’s ability. But if Hubble is allowed to burn up in 2032, this could leave a decade or more of lost science, and if the HWO is cancelled, then that could be a virtually permanent setback.

Launching a mission to physically grapple with the telescope, which is 13 metres long and weighs over 12,000 kilograms, will be no easy task. But it could also bring intangible benefits besides lengthening Hubble’s lifespan, says Wilkins.

“While repair is more complex now that we don’t have the space shuttle, attempting to repair Hubble helps maintain key skills that will be essential for future space exploration or exploitation,” he says. “Whether or not repair makes sense ultimately depends on the cost, but maintaining skills should also be considered.”

Why NASA is sending a probe to Europa – and what it’s looking for

Mark Norris at the University of Lancashire, UK, was previously funded by the Hubble budget to scour archived images for ultra-compact dwarf galaxies. “I’d worked out that, in the archive of these galaxies that Hubble had been surveying for other projects, the things I was interested in were must have been in the images by chance,” he says. “It basically built the foundation of my career. I wouldn’t have a permanent job now if it hadn’t been for that insight.”

Hubble was always designed to be serviced, says Norris, so it is fitted with grapple points for robotic arms to grab hold of. But raising its orbit wouldn’t be a permanent solution and it has begun to show its age.

“The instruments are gradually degrading through exposure to the space environment,” he says. “It’s a bit of a miracle it’s still going, but they over-engineer these things and they did service it so many times – they made sure that when the last service was done, everything was left working. It’s still doing really great science.”

NASA administrators will need to make difficult decisions about costs, as ongoing servicing and ground support will be needed on top of any mission to boost Hubble’s orbit.

“If they can save it, it makes sense, but it depends how much [it costs] and what gets axed in order to save it,” says Hayworth. “Say, for example, if they cut LISA [a plan to build a space-based gravitational wave detector]. This is probably personal and biased, but I think the science from that is so exciting that it would be a shame to lose that for the sake of an old instrument.”

A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave for a future moon base

New Scientist November 06, 2026

In video-game terms, the moon is the first level in an unfathomably giant, never-ending realm. It is the place where we, the players, learn the controls and try very hard not to die, in preparation for safely exploring the rest of the solar system. At a convenient 385,000 kilometres from Earth – a stone’s throw in cosmic terms – our planet’s companion is a great testing ground. And the race is on to claim a piece of it for a base.

Unfortunately for us, the moon is also a preposterously dangerous place to be. The volcanic dust there is adhesive, abrasive and corrosive, able to eat through spacesuits and machinery like a swarm of voracious locusts. Its daytime temperature can reach 120°C, while its benighted craters can plunge to -245°C, which is close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature in the universe. There are moonquakes, which (unlike Earth’s own tremors) can last for tens of minutes. And its lack of an atmosphere means that its surface is unprotected from asteroids (which can splatter you) and space radiation (which can give you cancer).

There are so many awful ways to perish on the moon. China knows the risks. So does the US. And yet, these two countries – along with their many friends and enemies – aren’t just keen on sending astronauts to the lunar surface; they are also planning to establish their own nuclear-powered bases, home to rotating astronaut crews.

Advertisement

Asteroid hit the moon and flung rocks 120 kilometres from the crater

I know what you’re thinking: this sounds like the stuff of science fiction, in the sense that you think it will never happen or, if you do, you suspect that it will go horribly, dramatically wrong. But I have been covering these plans for several years now, and I can promise you two things. The first is that, because this new space race is being (partly, perhaps largely) driven by nationalistic zeal, a moon base is much closer to being realised than you might think. The second is that you’re right: if space agencies aren’t exceedingly careful, things could go wrong.

Neither side wants to see a dead astronaut on the lunar surface, which is why these bases must be nothing short of impregnable fortresses. To that end, NASA recently announced that it has selected three new uncrewed scientific missions to the moon, each designed to further the goals of its Artemis programme. The first is a sophisticated seismometer, which will listen out for moonquakes and meteorite impacts. The second will hunt for signs of ice that can be turned into potable water, breathable oxygen and rocket fuel.

So far, so expected. But the third robotic mission really stood out to me, because it is going to investigate a subterranean lava tube.

Yes, you read that right: a tube, burrowed out by actual lava, on the moon.

Lava tubes are extremely cool – and I’m not just saying that because I’m a trained volcanologist. I have walked through several on Earth. They’re serpentine, cavernous things. They often form when a scorching-hot river of molten rock is rushing through a channel. When the river runs out of momentum or magma, the top – exposed to the atmosphere – cools quickly, forming a roof. The rest of the lava drains out elsewhere, leaving an eerie, inky-black hollow behind. Some of them even have nice acoustics, which makes them great alternative gig venues.

The moon is a great big ball of frozen magma. It’s geologically comatose today, but a stegosaurus could have looked up and seen the crimson glow of freshly erupted lava painting the lunar surface. And where there’s an abundance of lava, there are oodles of lava tubes. The problem is that, from the perspective of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter satellite, suspected lava tube sites just look like deep, shadowy pits.

The Marius Hills pit, on the moon’s nearside, is a prime example. It looks like someone punched a hole in the lunar surface, which is why it’s thought to be a natural skylight for a lava tube. Keen to find out for sure, NASA is sending a robotic mission there to scout it out – and not just to settle a few bets between lunar geologists.

Jessica Atkin knows more than anyone else about what it would take to supply food for a moon base. She reveals how to build a lunar farm and what astronauts can expect to dine on

NASA notes that lava tubes offer “natural, ready-made shelters that provide crucial thermal stability and shielding from deadly ionizing radiation and micrometeoroid bombardment”. That’s right: one day, NASA’s astronauts might be living in ancient volcanic vaults to avoid spending too much time on its truly terrible surface.

The mission to the Marius Hills pit – the first plan to explore a lunar lava tube – doesn’t have a launch date just yet. But it does have an excellent name: the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Yes, that one, the warrior dwarf from Middle-earth who loves his axe, despises evil rings of power and frequents all kinds of dangerous caves.

I reached out to Nathaniel Putzig at the Planetary Science Institute, the principal investigator of GIMLI. He swears that the name wasn’t inspired by J. R. R. Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings. He says that he simply wrote down words describing the mission plan and arranged them to make a pleasing sounding acronym.

“At the time, I was only vaguely aware of the Tolkien association, not fully realising that I had happened upon the name for legendary dwarf Gimli, member of the Fellowship of the Ring and the first Lord of the Glittering Caves,” he told me. The name, he said, “won out in the ranked choice voting by team members”. Thank goodness, because it’s literally perfect for this mission.

GIMLI is a joint effort between the Planetary Science Institute, NASA, the Norwegian Space Agency and US tech firm Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. It won’t abseil into the pit itself. Instead, it will land next to it and use its suite of instruments – including a ground-penetrating radar, seismic sensors and a device that measures subtle differences in the moon’s gravitational field – to map out the hidden subsurface, while its cameras take shots of the pit and its walls.

Presuming the skylight does lead to a lava tube, GIMLI won’t just scratch a scientific itch. It will inform NASA’s plans to keep its astronauts from being murdered by the moon.

Car-sized asteroids burn up in Earth’s atmosphere without consequence. But on the moon, they slam, unimpeded, into the ground, and explode like a pile of dynamite. Very rarely – as happened in 2024 – an asteroid the size of a couple of football stadiums crashes into the lunar surface with the force of an atomic bomb. Astronauts are far more likely to be imperilled by pebble-sized asteroids, which sound like less of an issue until you realise that they travel at tens of thousands of kilometres per hour, effectively making them hypersonic space bullets. Fortunately, the roof of a lava tube would handily absorb their impacts.

If the ceiling of frozen lava was thick enough, it would also offer protection from a major solar storm. When the sun is feeling irritable, it can launch a salvo of super-charged particles our way. Earth’s magnetic field and substantial atmosphere deflect and soak up many of them. But the exposed moon takes these bombardments head on. In the event of an especially intense solar outburst, astronauts there could receive a fatal dose and die weeks or even days later of acute radiation sickness. Hiding in a lava tube could save their lives.

Thank goodness, then, that the GIMLI project exists, and can help us answer the many questions we still have. What are the moon’s lava tubes like? Are they roomy? Do they look stable? Could you fit an astronaut habitat in them, or a small nuclear reactor that powers a nearby base? Seeking these havens out is, in NASA’s words, “important groundwork for safe, long‑term living on the moon”.

NASA is targeting the lunar south pole for its upcoming crewed Artemis missions. This is where it wants to establish the first moon base, largely because it is thought to be home to crucial reservoirs of water. Should we expect that base to be at least partly concealed in a lava tube?

“Lava tubes necessarily form in volcanic terrain, and there is little or no evidence of such terrains in the heavily cratered highlands of the south polar region,” says Putzig. So, probably not. But, he adds, “other outposts may well be established elsewhere that lava tubes may be identified”.

Most lava tubes will also require something like rappels, or makeshift elevators, for astronauts to access them. This creates its own hazard: if a clumsy moonwalker trips, falls and gets stuck in a lava tube, or the machinery malfunctions, there’s a chance that they could die down there. Considering all the other ways the moon could take them out, this would be a pretty embarrassing end.

Lava tubes may be a bit of a hard sell: they could be onerous to find, troublesome to access and potentially a bit bleak to live in. I’m willing to bet that, if you’re going to camp on the moon for several months at a time, you would probably prefer to eschew a dark, volcanic labyrinth for a spot on the surface. Even if you’re at risk of being blasted by tiny space rocks, you at least get to see Earth, and the stars cresting the lunar horizon. Even on the moon, the call of the night sky may prove too bewitching a prospect to pass up.

National leader Christopher Luxon now says he will call Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong, after ruling out her party throughout the election campaign.

However Luxon has continued to rule out Act leader David Seymour as Finance Minister, saying the role must go to a National minister.

As new MPs arrive at Parliament, outgoing Finance Minister Nicola Willis says her last caucus meeting tomorrow will be “filled with emotion”.

Former Prime Minister Helen Clark has called for an in-depth election review, after Green Party leader Chlöe Swarbrick claimed the overhang strategy and changes to enrolment laws showed “the system has been gamed”.

Use our interactive to see who’s winning in every electorate.

Find out how the overhang works.

Six big takeaways from election 2026: Who’s winning, what might change and the big surprises

New Green Party MP Rohan O’Neill-Stevens accepts he probably took some votes off Labour’s Rachel Boyack in the race to win the Nelson seat, which has been claimed by National’s Blair Cameron.

Cameron, who lost the Nelson electorate to Boyack by fewer than 30 votes in 2023, holds a 1210-vote lead over Boyack ahead of the special votes being counted.

O’Neill-Stevens, a former Nelson deputy mayor, received 2952 candidate votes. That was slightly more than the 2791 votes Green Nelson candidate Jace Hobbs received in 2023.

Arriving at Parliament today for his induction alongside fellow new Green MP Craig Pauling, O’Neill-Stevens accepted he may have taken some voters away from Labour.

“I’m sure there are some, but I think equally I know people who split their vote between National for their party votes and the candidate vote.

“It’s pretty early to say anything around that until we’ve got those vote-split reports, certainly from my conversations on the ground, people did make that decision despite us running a clear party vote campaign with people who probably weren’t going to vote for Rachel anyway but look, there’s still votes to be counted and that analysis to come.

“It’s too early to really have a clear picture, but also it’s the reality is that we exist as a separate political party, and exist in that seat.”

Act leader David Seymour has replied to Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong's claim this morning on Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast and the Herald’s live blog that his party's board also needed to sign off on negotiations.

“Ms Wong is incorrect. Act’s constitution requires the Leader to consult the board," Seymour said.

"It does not require board approval to begin negotiations, nor does it give the board any power to override the democratically elected caucus. This is significantly different to her own party’s constitution, which gives two unelected people a veto over any arrangement she might try to enter and is less democratic than any other party.

“I would encourage Ms Wong to be more careful to not make incorrect claims about other parties’ constitutions, simply to justify the arrangements of her own party.”

Re-elected National MP Simeon Brown thanks voters in Pakūranga.

David Wilson, a returning NZ First MP, says he isn’t happy with his party’s result. “No, no, we thought we were gonna get around mid-teens,” Wilson said.

He didn't know what contributed to that downturn in NZ First’s polling from earlier this year.

“Reality has bitten and the people have spoken, and that's the way it is.”

Wilson wouldn't say if he believed the comments from his colleague Michael Laws contributed. He wouldn't comment on them, saying that was above his pay grade.

New MP Taine Randell said he was “a wee bit disappointed” in the result, reckoning it could have been higher.

Winston Peters is keeping his counsel on his party’s results until the final votes are counted.

Harete Hipango, a new NZ First MP who previously served in National, said it “feels very different and very invigorating” in the new party.

She said she had received a phone call from her former National colleague Judith Collins, to “say congratulations and to wish me well and it is about service and duty”.

She wouldn't go into detail about the results for NZ first but she was “celebrating the fact that there's 12 of us that have come into this special place here to represent the interests of New Zealanders”.

Told about Wilson’s comments about NZ First’s results, she said those were “David’s thoughts”.

“My thoughts are collectively, with the caucus of New Zealand First, with the leadership, and I'm down here in service and on duty.”

National leader Christopher Luxon has ruled out David Seymour as Finance Minister in a new coalition Government.

Asked on RNZ's Morning Report whether David Seymour could be finance minister in a new Government, Luxon replied with an absolute no.

"I must be very clear. This is not negotiable. The finance role will go with a National person," he said.

"I think New Zealanders understand that this party that's got the largest number of votes could reasonably be expected to control the Treasury benches."

He said the party will work through exactly who gets that role "in due course".

Several factors could have influenced the low voter turnout at this year’s election, says Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne.

An estimated 74% of eligible people handed in their ballots before voting closed on Saturday evening, 4% lower than the 78% who did in 2023.

Le Quesne told Ryan Bridge TODAY that lots of reasons seem to impact turnout.

“We had a pretty good enrolment rate. It really comes down to what happens on the day and people who haven’t made their mind up whether they want to vote or not.

“Weather can have an impact, we did have a bit of rain in some places on election day, but it’s a bit hard to pin it down to any one factor.”

Outgoing National MP Nicola Willis says tomorrow will be her “last hurrah” with her colleagues.

The former Finance Minister lost her seat in Parliament on Saturday after National’s number of electorate wins left no room for list MPs to get any seats.

She told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast that tomorrow will be her last caucus meeting with the National Party.

“We will have the caucus of our new MPs coming in, welcoming them and farewelling the departing ones, of which I am one. So that’ll be my last hurrah with my colleagues and I’m sure [it] will be filled with emotion.”

Willis said she will act as Finance Minister in a caretaker Government, but any major decisions, if needed, would be made in consultation with other parties in a bipartisan way.

She plans to take a break to spend more time with her family, exercise and read a book or two.

She told Hosking she does need to work as there is "a mortgage to pay and four children to look after".

NZ First’s new MP Craig Stobo has arrived at Parliament.

He said he was feeling “fantastic” and “very good”.

“Very grateful for the people that voted for us,” he said.

Stobo wouldn't comment on NZ First’s result, acknowledging that the special votes still need to be counted.

Rakesh Naidoo, elected off Labour's list, acknowledges “there’s a lot of scenarios that’ll play out before the end of the month” in terms of the votes land. But he says Hipkins is “the right person to lead Labour”.

“I have full confidence in Chris Hipkins being a leader.”

He said he was here to “serve our communities”.

“The first thing that I have in mind is actually getting my feet under the desk and then continue to serve New Zealand.”

Harry Mowbray says the National Party needs to return to the principles it used to stand for.

The wealthy businessman and political donor said the vote-splitting campaign he helped push made the difference in getting the right bloc the numbers to form a government.

Asked on Ryan Bridge TODAY what his message to National leader Christopher Luxon was, Mowbray said “try and go back to the very first principles that National stood for”.

“It’s just shocking that National are looking at private property like the supermarkets, like Foodstuffs and trying to divide them up.

“It’s very apparent those guys haven’t got any clue about what happens in that business and the structure of the business and why it works.”

Mowbray said the only party he was confident would take the country in the right direction was Act.

A Rotorua primary school is closed this morning following the “catastrophic destruction” of several classrooms in a weekend break-in.

Six classrooms and two cloak bay areas at Western Heights Primary School were ransacked on Sunday, with paint thrown across carpet, walls and desks and children’s work destroyed.

Principal Brent Griffin told the Rotorua Daily Post he had never seen anything like it, describing the scene as “catastrophic destruction”.

“In the 24 years I’ve been here, we’ve had two events involving vandalism but nothing to this degree.

“To check through the CCTV and see three teenage girls and a young boy causing the damage, it’s horrific.”

He said they were not connected to the school.

Griffin said it had been a “tough 16 hours” since the damage was discovered, but the school’s community had been wonderful and it would reopen tomorrow.

In a message to the school community, he said he was alerted by security to multiple activations at the school on Sunday.

“When we arrived, we were met with total devastation. Eight classrooms had been demolished, ransacked, whatever you want to call it.

“Paint thrown all over the rooms, all over the carpet, walls, children’s desks, furnishings, absolute devastation”

Griffin described the offenders as the lowest form of life.

“Fortunately, we have clear CCTV footage, the police have been informed, and we are very likely to find the offenders.

“Our tamariki’s mahi was destroyed and their rooms demolished. Who could do that to our beautiful tamariki? It’s hard to understand.”

Griffin said four of the rooms destroyed were the rooms of the 5-year-old students.

“The three girls and a boy who did this should be absolutely ashamed of themselves.

“If your tamariki came home covered in paint, you now know how it happened,” Griffin said.

“If they belong to you, I ask you to do the right thing and make them front up and take responsibility for their actions.”

“This is heartbreaking for our kura. An estimated cost to repair the damage will exceed $75,000,″ Griffin said.

The school was due to open at midday on Monday to allow for police investigations and a commercial clean-up.

“To my staff and community members who spent over four hours reshaping the classrooms, trying to save the tamariki’s mahi, removing paint, my heart felt aroha goes out to you,” Griffin said.

“It’s not a great way to spend a Sunday afternoon.”

Griffin described the offenders as a complete embarrassment to their whānau and community as a whole.

Rotorua Police Inspector Ewan Dunsmuir said police were making inquiries after a report of a burglary at the school about 4.50pm on Sunday.

“Police are due to conduct a forensic examination today.”

More to come.

The son of an elderly woman who was scammed into buying $6600 worth of The Warehouse gift cards is calling on the company to do more to protect vulnerable customers.

Earl Patterson said that while his 80-year-old mother intentionally purchased multiple The Warehouse gift cards, including 10 valued at $500, she was tricked into doing so by scammers.

He has since laid a formal complaint with The Warehouse questioning how purchases to the tune of $6600 in a single month weren’t flagged.

“We talk about grooming for young people, but I think there’s grooming for old people too ... talking about trust and friendship when people are alone.”

Patterson told the Herald $5000 of the total was spent across just two days in October, with his mother buying five gift cards on October 15 and another five the following day.

Chief store operations officer Ian Carter acknowledged that while The Warehouse staff spoke to the customer before she bought the gift cards, they’re working harder to recognise warning signs.

“We’re very sorry to hear that our customer has been the victim of a scam, and we’ll do everything we can to help investigate.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

“We do have safeguards around gift card purchases, including conversations with customers about large or frequent purchases over $500, and scam warnings displayed in our stores and around gift card stands.

“Our initial review shows that our team were concerned, spoke to the customer about their purchases and brought over a security guard to help. However, these transactions still went ahead, so we’re working through what more we can do to help our team recognise warning signs and protect our customers.”

Patterson said the scam began when his mother, who lives alone, thought her new online “friends” needed help.

He first noticed last week while helping his mum go through her affairs while visiting her.

“I noticed a whole bunch of transactions from the Glenfield Warehouse. Most of them were $100, $150, and then there were two significant ones, essentially a day apart, of $2500 – so a total of $5000.

“That kind of raised some pretty big alarm bells for me ...

“A vulnerable person at 80 years old doesn’t really know what she’s doing.”

He said he believed the online scammers then asked for photos of the back of the cards to be able to use them on The Warehouse website.

Patterson had now put several contingencies in place, such as getting his mum a new number, and had removed her email address connected to accounts.

“She didn’t want to say anything because I think it became a bit of a shame thing or she was building a relationship or friendship because she’s alone and wanted someone to talk to.”

The national Grey Power president, David Marshall, said it was concerned about how scams were becoming increasingly sophisticated, describing them as a “devastating form of financial abuse”.

“This case highlights how quickly significant sums can be drained when online manipulation intersects with physical retail channels.

“When large-value gift card transactions pass through automated or staffed checkouts on consecutive days, the system should, ideally, trigger an automatic intervention.

“Strengthening these retail safeguards is essential to protecting older members of our community from what could (for some) be financially ruinous fraud.”

Marshall suggested setting up bank account alerts for trusted family members or friends for large or unusual transactions, and regular check-ins for family members who live alone.

“Isolation can be a vulnerability exploited by scammers.”

From 15-minute drones to instant kill chains: What does NZ’s future army look like?

New Zealand Herald November 08, 2026

NZ Army future fighting concept sets out AI, drones and autonomous warfare. Photo / Mike Scott

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

What does NZ’s army of the future look like?

A new report shows a potential combination of electronics and warfare in ways only dreamed about a decade ago.

The New Zealand Defence Force’s new 50-page Future Fighting Concept report – like its 2017 cousin called Future Land Operating Concept 2035 – dealt in the Army General Staff’s forecasts.

The former indulged in some pretty vague imaginings, while the latter deals with the emerging reality of weapons tech inflicting terrible damage in Ukraine and changing terribly fast in tests around the Pacific.

In 2017, the example on drones was how Russia put 13 fixed-wing drones and one type of quadcopter over Donbas, following its annexation of Crimea.

One drone linked to a rocket launcher “in particular ... could deliver fire-missions within 15 minutes of the drone identifying a target”.

Now, militaries have what the United States Pentagon calls the ‘kill chain’ down to seconds and the drones themselves can be the rockets, bearing down on Kyiv at up to 1000km/h.

The 2017 report mentioned drones a handful of times, although it foresaw that counter-drone systems would become vital.

Nine years ago, AI was not even a thing. In July 2026, artificial intelligence drove Human-Machine Integration as Australian and New Zealand troops tested ground drones in the Mojave Desert in the US.

This week, the US delivered more than a billion dollars’ worth of drones to its Central Command that covers the Middle East – 1300 kamikazes, more than 100 unmanned surface and underwater drones, and more than 24,000 counter-drones.

The speed of turning military dreams into reality is still hitting bureaucratic bottlenecks, think-tank studies overseas show.

However, it looks laser-fast compared with international efforts to rein in increasingly autonomous lethal weapons. A few weeks ago, for instance, 128 countries at the United Nations agreed on a text “defining” lethal autonomous weapon systems.

That is a record number – New Zealand was among them – but this was described as “a first step” towards talks on a possible international treaty to regulate them.

In 2017, the electronics to enable machines to talk to humans and each other, and across different militaries, and doing this by lasers between satellites, were the stuff of computer modelling.

Last month, they were tested in the toughest environment – the sea, where the physics of brine are difficult to surmount – in exercise Keen Sword.

It linked sensors to shooters – a Japanese underwater drone linked to an Australian ‘Rock Lobster’ surface drone, using US communications systems. New Zealand took part, a little, off the bench.

Keen Sword tapped into what a US commander called “a massive framework of integration on the US side that we have very rapidly rolled out to our partners during these recent exercises and persistently now”.

The NZDF is also part of a so-called Coalition Information Environment project, so militaries can see a battlefield the same way.

The Future Fighting Concept focuses on the Army, saying: “The NZ Army must prioritise investment in advanced capabilities that enhance agility, lethality, and responsiveness. Key focus areas include AI, Machine Teaming, Predictive Analysis, Distributed Decision-making, Network-Centric Warfare, Automation and Rapid Targeting, Cyber and Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations.”

Dominance in this last – electromagnetics – would be decisive, it said. However, NZDF has denied expanding into electromagnetic spectrum operations at a satellite-monitoring hub set up by the US in Auckland, although other US hubs are expanding this way.

Where do people fit in among all these capitalised electronics?

“One of the primary changes introduced by modern technologies is the increased speed of decision-making, lethality and precision in military operations,” the new report said.

“The concept of ‘human-in-the-loop’ systems, where operators retain ultimate control over critical decisions, is being complemented by increasingly autonomous systems capable of understanding complex operations independently.

“High automation will accelerate human-in-the-loop targeting through autonomous systems that identify, classify and engage threats.”

The future is about being more lethal and joining hands to do it.

“Our next-generation weapons systems will utilise NATO and ABCANZ partner forces systems.”

ABCANZ is a five-nation army interoperability agency of the US, United Kingdom, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand armies.

The report gets to ethics.

“Human-machine integration raises ethical concerns in warfare about accountability, and the moral implications of delegating life-or-death decisions to machines, marking a significant shift in the philosophical understanding of warfare.

“‘This also prompts a re-evaluation of international norms and regulatory frameworks governing warfare ... [and] the need for comprehensive dialogue among nations regarding the ethical and legal implications of deploying such technologies.”

The report also briefly mentions the politics of this.

“A future-focused NZ Army must train MDO [for multiple domains] and promote a change in policy to government for the rapid acquisition of new and rapidly evolving technology platforms.”

Rapid acquisition reflects the underlying theme of the need for speed.

There is also the need for money. On the election campaign trail, Labour raised the question of how New Zealand would pay to future-proof the military.

It said, if elected, it would take another look at that.

The path ahead is at least partially underwritten by a Pentagon budget line showing $60 million spent on its main project for integrating allies (called C5) in past years and another $110m for that out to 2031.

It is also underwritten politically by the White House, that says: “The United States will leverage S&T [science and tech] capabilities of international allies and partners as a force multiplier to advance national security objectives and outcompete adversaries. The Trump Administration is expanding co-operation in ... areas including AI, nuclear energy, quantum, advanced communications, PNT [positioning, navigation, timing], and space.”

The NZ Army’s future concept of weapons of war is not the only one. Armies around the world are thinking about this too.

The big difference between now and a decade ago is that AI is being prompted to think about this too.

- RNZ
