Election 2026: National’s Tom Rutherford elected as Mt Maunganui MP

New Zealand Herald November 08, 2026

Mt Maunganui MP Tom Rutherford and his wife, Hannah. Photo / Bijou Johnson

The contest of the 29-year-olds has come to a close with National’s Tom Rutherford claiming the Mt Maunganui seat.

Business as usual has already resumed, with Rutherford flying to Wellington today and “back to work”.

“It’s time to crack on with things.”

Twenty-nine-year-old Rutherford, who was Bay of Plenty MP for the last parliamentary term, won the new Mt Maunganui electorate over Labour candidate Rhieve Grey, also 29.

Rutherford received 21,579 votes compared with Grey’s 7520, giving him a 14,059 lead.

Party poll results, however, are deadlocked.

The Electoral Commission will announce the final count on November 27.

As it stands, National has received 29.2% of votes, which, alongside Act’s 10.9% and NZ First’s 9.8%, gives the centre-right coalition a National-led bloc of 67 seats compared with the Labour-led bloc of 57.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon has claimed “a pathway to forming the next Government”, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins told cheering Labour supporters on Saturday night “it may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve [New Zealand has] said”.

Rutherford said he felt “incredibly humbled” to be elected as the Mt Maunganui MP.

About 150 people gathered at Omanu Golf Club on Saturday night to celebrate the end of the campaign.

“My team and I have worked so incredibly hard this campaign, and I’m just so grateful for the really positive support we got from the community.”

He said he was “really grateful” to volunteers and “I just couldn’t have achieved this result without them”.

Rutherford said results showed there was “a mandate from the New Zealand public” for centre-right parties.

“We’ll obviously have to wait to see what happens with the official vote and the special votes that’ll come in the next few weeks. As we’ve always said, we wanted to complete the plan, stick with the plan, don’t leave it half done.”

Rutherford said he loved campaigning for his home.

A highlight from this campaign was knocking on Labour opponent Grey’s door.

“We weren’t campaigning against each other; we were campaigning alongside one another, and I just take my hat off to him for a really positive campaign.

“I’m not quite sure [if] I earned his vote or not, but I’ve got three years to try and win that from him.”

National faced several casualties on Saturday night, with deputy leader and Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee likely losing their jobs.

This was a result of National’s lower party vote compared with its high number of electorate seats, which led to an overhang possibly driven by vote-splitting strategies.

Rutherford said it was a “massive loss”, and he thanked the ministers for their service to the party and New Zealand.

His priorities for the first 100 days were to pass the council rates cap and extend paid parental leave.

Rutherford also said he wants to see “real progress” on Tauranga Hospital’s redevelopment and the continued delivery of Takitimu North Link and Tauriko West on State Highway 29.

“Expanding our access to quality, timely healthcare, but also the education infrastructure that our growing community needs, particularly in Pāpāmoa East. And so continuing to support that as the local MP.”

Rutherford also thanked his wife, Hannah, who he “couldn’t possibly do this job without”.

“I’m just so lucky to have her in my corner.”

Rutherford’s campaign manager and electorate chairman Mike Chapman said he “always knew Tom would do well”.

“We ran a really good campaign, and knocked on over 7000 doors.

“He’s done a really good job as Bay of Plenty MP, and because of that he’s got a fantastic profile.”

The MP’s father, Chris Rutherford, said he was “very delighted”, saying his son worked hard on his campaign.

“I am expecting my son to do what he has said he’ll do, which he did for the last three years, which is work hard for his electorate and represent everybody to the best of his ability.”

Rutherford’s mother, Sharon Nightingale, said there was “lots of positivity in the room” at Omanu Golf Club on Saturday night.

He was elected as Bay of Plenty MP in 2023, winning the seat with 23,303 votes over Labour candidate Pare Taikato’s 7898.

His main competition this year, Grey, told the Bay of Plenty Times on Saturday night he felt “really good” about his campaign.

Grey was joined by Labour list MP and Tauranga candidate Jan Tinetti at Tauranga Fish and Dive Club.

“We set out to run a strong, positive values-based campaign, and we’ve done that.”

This was Grey’s first political campaign. He came from a background in policy and foreign affairs and studied at the University of Oxford.

Other candidates were Pualele Westhead from the Greens, Act list MP Cameron Luxton, Tracey Coxhead from NZ First, Greer Young from NZ Loyal, and Caitlin Grattan from the Animal Justice Party.

National retained its Tauranga electorate seat with Sam Uffindell claiming victory. He received 19,117 votes over Tinetti’s 8843.

Act’s Luxton will also enter Parliament as a list MP.

What an uncertain election result means for households’ finances

New Zealand Herald November 08, 2026

Economists say many of the issues affecting household finances are out of the government's hands. Photo / RNZ

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

New Zealand’s election has delivered a less-than-decisive result, but what does it all mean for household finances?

With the election result still uncertain until the final count at the end of the month, economists say much depends on how those numbers fall and how coalition agreements are struck.

Massey University economist Matt Roskruge said, if National was able to form a coalition, as many pundits say it is likely to, it would probably mean more restrained government spending, particularly if Act was to take the finance portfolio.

“That could mean continued pressure on public sector jobs and services, particularly in Wellington, with knock-on effects for local businesses. It could also help contain inflation and interest rates, although that depends on the overall package, including any tax cuts.”

He said that if Labour had the numbers, there would be more support for public services and household incomes, which could help employment and those in urban areas.

“There could be trade-offs with inflation and interest rates, if it adds substantially to demand, but that isn’t automatic. It depends on how spending is funded and how much room the economy has to grow.”

He said global conditions would matter enormously, no matter who was in charge.

“Strong farm returns are helping support some regions, while many urban households are still facing a difficult job market. AI looks a lot like a bubble, and between political uncertainty and conflicts around the globe, there is only so much our government can do.

“Businesses might hold off on hiring or investment, until the policy direction becomes clearer. A narrow majority could make it harder to advance an agenda, although it doesn’t necessarily mean an unstable government.

“Longer term, I think the bigger differences for households will be access to healthcare, privatisation and how much they have to pay themselves, investment in infrastructure and whether we make meaningful progress on housing.”

University of Otago economist Murat Ungor agreed that some of the most important things to households were out of government control.

“I’d be cautious about expecting big near-term changes to household budgets either way. The things that matter most to most households right now, such as mortgage rates, rents, council rates, insurance and food prices, are driven largely by the Reserve Bank’s interest rate path, global conditions and the labour market.

“The real policy differences, such as Labour’s proposed capital gains tax and cost-of-living relief versus continuity under the current coalition, would take time to legislate and implement. Any multi-party arrangement tends to dilute headline promises, so I’d expect incremental change, rather than a sharp turn.

“In the coming weeks, I’d watch three things – the shape of the coalition or support agreement, any early signals on fiscal settings, and whether cost-of-living help is targeted at those who need it most or spread broadly. The first full Budget in May will be the real test of how far any promises survive.”

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said, based on the current numbers, major changes for households seemed unlikely.

“If you get a switch to Labour somehow and they manage to cobble things together, the policy direction starts to become a bit different. You have questions around what kind of additional tax may come in and then if there is any specific relief around the cost of living as well.

“It’s the sort of thing that’s not really going to start to have an impact until 12 months down the track.

“It’s been clear from both major parties’ points of view that they do recognise the tightness of the fiscal position that they’re working with. I don’t see government policy particularly adding to inflation depending on who gets in.”

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the result meant that whichever side was able to form a Government would not have a very strong mandate to make big changes.

He said a left-wing coalition could have had an impact on interest rates, if it changed the Reserve Bank mandate to require it to take employment into account in rate-setting decisions. Unemployment lifted in the most recent update, but business confidence was likely to be buoyed by a National-led coalition.

There could also be an impact simply because of the uncertainty of the result.

“Markets don’t like uncertainty, particularly in the foreign exchange market. Given the New Zealand dollar is already starting on the back foot, we went through the low point Friday night ... which is, aside from perhaps a couple of very short-lived episodes in the last 10-15 years, the lowest since the global financial crisis.

“We are in an environment here where you’ve already probably had a few factors leaning heavily against the New Zealand dollar and this uncertainty, I think, probably will add to those. That’s one of the things that makes it a bit tougher for the Reserve Bank, because you’ve got the potential of a bit more imported inflation filtering into the outlook, if you’re going to be building in a weaker exchange rate outlook.”

Auckland beach warnings after thunderstorms wash untreated wastewater into Waitematā Harbour

New Zealand Herald November 08, 2026

Mission Bay is among the beaches contaminated with untreated wastewater after weekend storms. Photo / File

About a dozen beaches on Auckland’s Waitematā Harbour have been left contaminated with untreated wastewater after weekend storms overflowed near popular bathing spots.

Eight inner-city bays have been deemed unfit to enter, while a further four on Auckland’s North Shore carry the same warning.

A handful of other beaches are also flagged as high risk, with modelling predicting unsuitable water quality for swimming.

A Watercare spokesperson said Saturday’s storm caused the poor water quality.

Severe thunderstorms rolled over the city for several hours on Saturday, bringing torrential downpours and flash flooding.

“It is international best practice to avoid swimming for 48 hours after heavy rain,” the Watercare spokesperson said.

Rain could send a “first flush” of dirty water through stormwater drains, onto beaches and into urban waterways.

Along for the ride could be animal faeces, oil, metals, rubber from tyres, microplastics and rubbish.

This morning, Safeswim deemed the beaches along Tāmaki Drive from Okahu Bay to St Heliers off-limits because of contaminated wastewater overflow. Orakei Basin and Te Tinana were also off-limits, as were Herne Bay and Home Bay, on the other side of the CBD.

Yesterday, the downtown Karanga Plaza Harbour Pool in the Viaduct Harbour was considered unsuitable for swimming but the alert had been lifted today.

A handful of beaches on Auckland’s North Shore including Narrow Neck, Milford and Castor Bay were also contaminated.

According to Safeswim, when a sensor detects an overflow on Auckland’s wastewater network a black pin automatically appears at the affected swimming spot for 48 hours.

The spokesperson said a red rating meant modelling indicated a high risk of getting sick from swimming.

Run-off after heavy rain was one factor that could make the water unsuitable.

A green rating indicated a low risk of illness.

Safeswim combined continuous monitoring of Auckland’s wastewater network with modelling to forecast water quality at individual swimming spots, said the spokesperson.

The service updated forecasts every 15 minutes.

Digital signs displayed the latest advice at beaches including Browns Bay, Takapuna, St Mary’s Bay and Herne Bay. Swimmers could also check their chosen beach’s water condition on the Safeswim website or app before heading out.

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Election 2026: National Party’s Todd McClay becomes Rotorua’s longest-serving MP after election win

New Zealand Herald November 08, 2026

The National Party’s Todd McClay may have become Rotorua’s longest-serving MP, but he says he’s as energetic as ever and is eyeing QE’s transformation on his to-do list for the first 100 days.

McClay took an early lead on Saturday night as results trickled in.

By the time the final votes were counted, he had a convincing winning margin of 5301 votes over Labour’s Fisher Wang. Special votes are yet to be counted but they won’t change the results.

While his winning margin so far is down from the 2023 election, when at the final count McClay was ahead of Labour’s Ben Sanford by 8923 votes, McClay said he had a clear mandate to continue as Rotorua’s MP.

Currently, the coalition parties – National, Act and NZ First - hold a slim majority in what is looking like a much larger Parliament, thanks to overhangs on both the left and the right.

About 399,365 special votes – those cast overseas or out of one’s electorate – are due to be counted as the Electoral Commission undergoes the official count, expected to conclude at the end of the month.

About 60 die-hard National supporters and volunteers celebrated McClay’s win on Saturday at Rotorua’s Pullman Hotel with McClay and his extended family, including mother Dawn, fiancee Anna Lillis and both of their children.

Saturday marked a year since the death of McClay’s father, Roger McClay, a politician and Children’s Commissioner, and McClay paid tribute to him and his mother during his victory speech.

McClay said on Saturday night that he had voted in Reporoa that day before going to a cemetery in the farming district south of Rotorua to visit his father’s grave with family.

Lillis said it had been a fantastic experience working alongside her fiance during this election. They had been together for about three years.

“He’s been very busy and energetic and is still loving it after 18 years.”

Yesterday afternoon, McClay was meeting with National’s leader, Christopher Luxon, and other senior MPs in Auckland to nut out what could happen with the Government in the coming weeks.

Before he left, he told the Rotorua Daily Post in an interview that one of his first jobs as a local MP would be to advance a plan to turn QE into a Rotorua health hub.

“We know our hospital needs up to four new elective surgery theatres. It is very hard to do it in the hospital, and it would be expensive and take a long time. We have a need for dialysis in Rotorua; we have people having to go elsewhere.

“If we can tick the box and get that going, then people get their operations sooner and those on dialysis will have a better quality of life.”

Jobs and opportunities for young people were also among the priorities, as well as reducing costs.

The way to do that was to grow the economy, create jobs and increase wages, he said.

“Over the last three years it has started to happen, but it’s way too soon for people to start feeling the positive effects of that.”

Having now won seven elections, McClay said he was now the longest-serving MP in the history of the Rotorua seat, surpassing fellow National MPs Paul Lapwood on 18 years and Paul East on 17 years and 10.5 months.

“That allows me to feel much greater responsibility and obligation to keep working hard and to repay the confidence that the people of this seat have shown me for now what will be 21 years [at the end of this term].”

He said it was pleasing that not just National voters had continued to consistently vote for him as the local MP. He vowed to “roll up his sleeves” and work for all local voters, irrespective of their party preferences.

He said Rotorua did well under National and National-led coalitions.

In the past 18 years, he said the city got funding for a new police station, new roading announced for all four entrances to the city, ultra-fast broadband in every house and a new courthouse.

The 58-year-old said he would treat his future in politics as he has done the past 18 years – by deciding a year out from the election if he would stand again.

“I say, ‘Do I enjoy the job? Have I got more to give? Am I doing a good job?’ If the answer is yes, then I continue.”

Wang said he was proud of his effort to close the margin and wished McClay all the best.

“They have a big job ahead, and he has my support as the successful candidate in this election.”

Wang said all candidates wanted to see Rotorua in a better place.

“It is now time to come together and back the winner.”

Wang said he appreciated it had been a “clean campaign” compared with the personal attacks seen in other electorates.

Despite the results showing from an early stage that he was trailing, Wang held an upbeat election party at Arikikapakapa Rotorua Golf Club with about 60 supporters.

The New Zealand First candidate for Rotorua, Billy Brown, who was watching the results from his home with his family, said he was rapt with the results.

While well out of the Rotorua MP race, he said it was always his goal to raise the NZ First party vote.

“I’ve told people you’ve got a great MP here [McClay] and to vote for him.”

The Opportunity Party’s Rotorua candidate, Finn Liley, said he was proud to help raise the party vote and described his party’s achievement of getting 6% party vote so far as “incredible”.

There are no traffic lights in my suburb, and the biggest motoring hazard is ducks crossing the road

Sydney Morning Herald November 09, 2026

As we drove towards the property, an enormous avocado tree sprawling across the front lawn came into view. That was all it took. “Sold!” I declared before even stepping inside.

My daughters thought I’d lost my mind. They may have had a point. Most people inspect the kitchen or check the plumbing, but I saw an ancient avocado tree and decided the rest was paperwork.

Having grown up in Brisbane, I thought I knew my own backyard. Yet, somehow, the islands just across Moreton Bay had remained a mystery to me.

While working in Italy, I began dreaming of a new chapter. One night, scrolling through the real estate sites, I spotted a property on Russell Island. Intrigued, I flew back to Australia, and arranged to meet the agent, who collected me from the ferry.

More than 20 years living in beautiful parts of the Gold and Sunshine coasts hadn’t prepared me for Russell Island. I hadn’t anticipated a place where I’d sleep better than anywhere else, become deeply involved in the community, and treat the mainland as somewhere I occasionally visit rather than somewhere I need to be.

Life here moves at a different pace. It’s like living in 1989, before everyone became permanently attached to screens and schedules. It takes just over 10 minutes to drive from one end of the island to the other, yet a quick errand can stretch into an hour after chatting with neighbours and collecting enough local gossip to fill a newspaper column.

There are no traffic lights, and the biggest road hazard is a family of ducks crossing as though they own the place. Curlews patrol the neighbourhood like disgruntled security guards, delivering their mournful night-time soundtrack. Strangely, I find their calls more calming than any sleeping app.

Cockatoos, kookaburras and plovers are also regular visitors. I’ve become a wildlife caterer, sharing my little patch of the world with feathered guests who seem to consider my property part of their real estate portfolio.

The houses are just as characterful: quirky cottages, colourful gardens and creative renovations accumulated over decades. I love that individuality, although identical new builds are beginning to appear.

At the Russell Island Bowls Club, two vodka sodas cost less than $15. You can sit outside, watch the afternoon unfold and enjoy a proper conversation without competing with televisions the size of garage doors.

And despite what some mainlanders might imagine, there’s always something happening. Markets, performances, creative gatherings and community events fill the calendar. Through my writing for The Friendly Bay Islander magazine and organising local events, I’ve become part of a community that continually surprises me.

Our greatest attraction isn’t a beach or a view; it’s the people. I’ve met an artist whose home is covered in artwork, a retired police officer who makes Native American-style flutes, and a 93-year-old woman who donated land to council for a public park.

There’s the couple who painted a massive tree blue in memory of their son, hoping to encourage conversations about suicide and asking others if they’re OK. Volunteers Robert and Shane, meanwhile, sit on the back of a ute at the IGA, helping elderly residents, caring for animals and children, and tackling mechanical problems. They’re reminders that some of the most valuable people in a community are simply those who turn up when someone needs a hand.

My most adventurous encounter involved a boat, a surfing dog and its owner. I wondered whether I’d accidentally sailed into a surreal pirate movie. You couldn’t make this stuff up.

I also started The Mooring, a Facebook media page, because online descriptions of Russell Island seemed so far removed from the place I was discovering. There was plenty about crime and undesirable characters, but little about the generosity, creativity and humour I experienced firsthand.

I’m not suggesting the islands are perfect. Ferry travel requires planning; infrastructure is under pressure; tradespeople can be difficult to pin down; and healthcare access is a genuine consideration.

I’ve also noticed an influx of new residents over the past year. Growth brings difficult conversations about development, parking and protecting the bushland that makes these islands so special. Loving a place also means caring about its future.

Still, the everyday pleasures keep winning me over. I can swim and picnic at Karragarra Beach, enjoy what I consider the best gelato at 8th Sense Kitchen on Macleay Island, and watch extraordinary sunsets from the Macleay Island Bowls Club. The passenger ferry between the islands is free, making it easy to explore our watery neighbourhood.

Contributor

My daughters thought I’d lost my mind buying a house on an island I’d never visited and where I knew nobody. Instead, I’ve found a community, work I love, stories to chase, and a front yard that doubles as a wildlife viewing platform.

Sometimes, overthinking stops us from finding the very things that make us happiest. There’s a lot to be said for trusting your instincts and seeing where they lead. In my case, it led to Russell Island, a community I adore, and a collection of stories I’m privileged to tell. Not a bad return on one impulsive decision.

And if the avocado harvest comes good, the investment might even pay dividends.

FA Cup roundup: Seventh-tier Wimborne shock Crawley to reach second round

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 20:15:53 GMT

Grimsby and Stockport survive scares but Wednesday out

Exeter upset League One leaders Huddersfield

Seventh-tier Wimborne heaped more misery on Crawley as the bottom side in the Football League lost 2-0 in the biggest upset of the FA Cup first round.

The Dorset part-timers took the lead after only nine minutes when the property surveyor Yang Seung-woo curled a superb strike from just inside the penalty area into the top corner.

Crawley came close to equalising when Kai Jennings flashed a low shot narrowly wide before Jonny Russell headed tamely into the arms of the home goalkeeper Cam Plain.

Crawley’s interim manager, Kevin Blackwell, made a triple change at half-time and Charlie Barker fired inches wide for the team 57 places above their hosts in the pyramid. The Southern Premier League South side got a huge slice of luck to seal victory 11 minutes from time. Jackson King’s shot hit Cameron Munn to send the ball squirming beyond the former Arsenal goalkeeper Vito Mannone.

Will Sutton scored a dramatic extra-time winner for Oldham as Dave Challinor’s first game in charge of Sheffield Wednesday ended in an upset. The homegrown central defender was up for a free-kick which the Owls failed to clear, with Sutton left completely free to nod home from six yards and secure a 2-1 win.

Calum Kavanagh put Oldham ahead in the 66th minute with a fierce drive after Mike Fondop headed on Noah Chilvers’ right-wing cross. Wednesday equalised 10 minutes later through the former Oldham forward Davis Keillor-Dunn.

The match ignited further in the 84th minute following a touchline fracas involving a large number of players. The Oldham manager, Micky Mellon, was sent off and Sheffield Wednesday’s Callum Slattery was booked. After Sutton’s winning goal, Oldham defended resolutely to close out the game.

Stafford Rangers were denied a historic win after losing 3-2 on penalties to Grimsby after they drew 3-3 after extra time. Two goals from firefighter Darrhyl Mason and one from the Aston Villa youth coach Jack Birch got the eighth-tier side – 89 places below League Two Grimsby – to a shootout.

Mason and Birch had put Rangers 2-0 ahead in front of a crowd of 3,130 at the Stan Robinson Stadium as they chased the second round for the first time since 2007. But set-piece headers inside three minutes from Harvey Rodgers and Maldini Kacurri sent the tie into extra time, where Mason and Géza Turi traded goals.

The home debutant Luca Navarro had to score to send the tie into sudden death but saw his spot-kick saved by Harvey Cartwright to end Rangers’ nine-match Cup marathon.

Lewis Fiorini’s extra-time penalty sent Stockport, who are second in League One, into the second round after they came from two goals down with 10 men to win 3-2 against Cray Wanderers.

Despite being 112 places below their opponents in the pyramid, it was the Isthmian Premier side Cray who took the lead after 21 minutes when Sammie MacLeod found the bottom corner.

Stockport were then reduced to 10 men in the 31st minute as goalkeeper Luca Ashby-Hammond was sent off for a dangerous challenge on John Ufuah. Alex Hernández bent a brilliant strike into the top corner from the resulting free-kick.

Depleted Stockport pulled one back in the 81st minute when Kyle Wootton tscored with a header. And the Hatters then sent the tie into extra time when Mikael Mandron was in the right place to nod home Jack Diamond’s cross. The decisive moment came in the 101st minute when Cray goalkeeper JJ Briggs clattered into Mandron to give away a penalty, which was dispatched by Fiorini.

Charlie Savage scored against his father’s team as Reading eased into the second round with a 5-0 rout of Peterborough at the Weston Homes Stadium on Saturday.

This all-League One tie turned out to be one of the most one-sided of the day, with the Peterborough manager, Robbie Savage, watching on in disbelief as his side were pulled apart.

Reading went ahead after 26 minutes as slick passing led to Andy Rinomhota playing in Daniel Kyerewaa, who found the bottom corner via a deflection. Reading doubled their lead in the 34th minute when a cross from Haydon Roberts was met by a diving header from top scorer Jack Marriott.

It was in effect game over in first-half stoppage time as Savage deepened his father’s misery when he took possession after the ball ran off Marriott, his deflected effort finding the top corner.

Jamie Reid added a fourth for the visitors in the 72nd minute when Paudie O’Connor nodded Savage’s free-kick into his path for him to lift over the Peterborough goalkeeper Alex Bass. Reading struck yet again four minutes later when Liam Fraser’s pass put Reid clean through to score his second.

Non-league Kidderminster breezed into the second round with a convincing 3-0 victory over League One Doncaster.

The National League club opened the scoring after 22 minutes when Maz Kouhyar pulled the ball back to Lewis Walker, and he fired home at the second attempt after his initial shot had hit the upright.

The Harriers striker continued to cause problems, putting an effort over the bar and another just wide, but in the 36th minute he turned provider, charging upfield before teeing up Kouhyar and the on-loan Notts County midfielder slotted home. Kouhyar was again involved in the third goal, having a shot that Josh Clarke could only parry and David Davis turned in the rebound.

The Kidderminster manager, Paul Wotton, said: “We started well, scored the goal and got the crowd up. It was just a really good day. They are a League One team at the end of the day, no matter what the scoreline suggests. They are two leagues higher than us, so they are going to have moments in the game, but we stood up to it.”

League Two Exeter pulled off an upset with a 2-1 win away to League One leaders Huddersfield. Exeter took the lead after 12 minutes, thanks to a perfectly delivered cross from the left from Luca Woodhouse, with centre-back Jack Taylor stealing in at the far post to finish it off.

Huddersfield looked a different team in the second half and found an equaliser within eight minutes of the restart as Ibane Bowat headed home Cameron Humphreys’ corner at the back post.

Charlie Cummins grabbed the winner nine minutes from time at the end of a well-worked move up the right, culminating in Reece Cole’s cutback and a good finish.

Altrincham were denied another famous FA Cup upset as they conceded an 84-minute equaliser against Notts County before bowing out in a penalty shootout.

County took the lead through Jacob Bedeau in the 28th minute but Altrincham responded well with Lucas Weaver grabbing an equaliser six minutes before half-time. Lewis Banks gave the hosts the lead just before the hour but Callum Roberts dashed Altrincham’s hopes of another cup scalp, having beaten 17 Football League sides in the competition, scoring with a first-time strike to force extra-time.

With neither side able to make a breakthrough in extra-time the game went to penalties and Aidan Barlow, Sam Taylor and Eddy Jones all missed from the spot for Altrincham as County triumphed 3-2.

Blackpool survived a scare at Hornchurch, needing to rely on a 118th-minute winner from Josh Bowler to secure a 2-1 comeback victory at the Hornchurch Stadium.

Fleetwood’s hopes of following up their memorable Carabao Cup upset against Premier League champions Arsenal with a long FA Cup run are over after a 2-1 home defeat by fellow League Two side Rochdale. Baba Adeeko’s goal in extra time at Highbury sent the visitors through.

Chesterfield withstood a second-half comeback from Yeovil Town to secure their place in the second round with a 4-3 victory. Yeovil recovered from 3-1 down to level at 3-3 before Joel Randall struck the winner for the Spireites a minute from time.

Late Mansfield goals from Rhys Oates and Jordan Bowery ended the plucky Cup resistance of National League North Macclesfield. Nathan Moriah-Welsh gave Mansfield a first-half lead but the Silkmen were still in the tie under Oates made it 2-0 in the 72nd minute. Bowery added a third three minutes into added time to wrap up victory for the Stags.

League One Plymouth eased through thanks to three goals in a late 11-minute spell in a 4-0 win against Southern League Premier Central battlers Alvechurch. Will Evans finally broke the deadlock after 50 minutes, winning the ball from Jessy Bavanganga before driving a low angled shot into the far corner. Further goals from Evans, Michael Baidoo and Ronan Curtis saw the Pilgrims through.

League One strugglers Barnsley booked their spot in the second round with a 7-2 win over Aldershot at Oakwell, with Cameron McGeehan grabbing a hat-trick.

Leyton Orient held off Harborough 5-1 to progress into the second round while League Two high-flyers Crewe beat Wimbledon 2-1.

Nick Powell and Adam Phillips scored twice as Bradford thrashed National League North side Marine 7-0, while a late goal from Joel Randall helped Cheltenham close out a dramatic 4-3 win over National League Yeovil.

Last season’s quarter-finalists Port Vale booked their place in the second round with a 4-2 victory over National League strugglers Scunthorpe United at Vale Park. MK Dons avoided an upset as they ground out a 2-1 win over League Two Swindon.

Southern League Premier Central team Worcester’s hopes of an upset were ended in a 1-0 defeat at League Two Colchester while Jack Bates scored twice in the first half as Dover progressed with a 2-0 win over Wealdstone.

Ollie Pearce scored after 10 seconds as York sealed a 4-0 win over Northampton. The City captain also bagged a second before Alex Hunt and Josh Stones completed the rout.

Jordan Thewlis’ stoppage-time penalty gave seventh-tier Guiseley a 1-0 win over Sutton at Nethermoor Park as Carlisle beat League Two leaders Salford 1-0. Ryan Graydon missed a penalty for the visitors before David Ajiboye’s goal just before the break proved enough to send the Cumbrians through.

Eighth-tier AFC Rushden + Diamonds slipped to a 4-0 defeat at Burton. Will Collar and Borges Rodrigues scored for the Brewers in the first half, with Charlie Webster and Zac Scutt adding two more late on.

Nathan Odokonyero scored twice as National League South Salisbury saw off seventh-tier Sholing 6-0 to take their place in round two for the first time since reforming in 2015.

Cruise ship pianist rescued after nine hours treading water miles from shore

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 20:13:09 GMT

Man taken to hospital after falling off Royal Caribbean ship in Pacific Ocean, with Coast Guard investigating incident

A pianist for a Royal Caribbean cruise ship is expected to survive after two Newport Beach, California, fishermen discovered him treading water in the Pacific Ocean nearly 20 miles (32km) offshore on Friday.

The unidentified man was taken to the hospital after the rescue, according to the US Coast Guard, which is now investigating how he went overboard from the cruise ship.

Authorities believe the man may have been in the ocean for approximately nine hours before he was spotted by Sean Norton and Grant Garrett, who were returning from a fishing trip near Catalina Island.

The two fishermen had spent the morning fishing for marlin when their trip took an unexpected turn. By noon, they had pulled the stranded man from the water.

“I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,” Garrett told CBS News, recalling the moment the boat’s captain first saw the man in the water.

The fishermen quickly worked together to bring the man onboard. Once the man regained his composure, Garrett said he identified himself as a pianist onboard Royal Caribbean’s 14-deck cruise ship, the “Ovation of the Seas.”

According to Norton, the rescued crew member had few words to describe what he had just experienced. “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,’” Norton said.

After the rescue, the fishing crew issued an emergency maritime call, prompting Newport Beach lifeguards to respond and provide assistance. Battalion chief Adam Yacenda said the man was found approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, according to CBS, or “pretty much in the middle of the ocean”.

Despite the extended time spent in the water, Norton believes unusually warm ocean temperatures may have played a significant role in the man’s survival.

“You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees,” Norton said. “A different year, no way he makes it.”

The circumstances surrounding the crew member’s fall from the cruise ship remain under investigation by the Coast Guard. Royal Caribbean Group acknowledged the incident and said it is assisting the employee following the ordeal.

In a statement to CBS, a company spokesperson said: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:54:56 GMT

Falkirk leapfrog their hosts with 5-2 rout at Tynecastle

Liam Scales gives Celtic 1-0 home win over Kilmarnock

Rampant Falkirk obliterated Hearts’ 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership with a stunning 5-2 win at Tynecastle on Sunday as they leapfrogged their hosts into third place.

Wouter Vrancken’s beleaguered side, missing 11 players through injury, were in disarray as swashbuckling Falkirk romped into a five-goal lead early in the second half through Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double. Hearts hit back through the substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Cláudio Braga penalty, but Falkirk were well worthy of making it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1995.

A stunned Vrancken said: “This is an embarrassment, the first half for sure. It’s crazy, crazy, and everybody – me, staff, players – have to take responsibility in those things. This is ridiculous.”

It was a first league defeat at Tynecastle for Hearts since April 2025 and they have won just two of their past 11 matches. Falkirk move into third, a point above Hearts, although they have played a game more.

Liam Scales provided a looping finish to earn Celtic a 1-0 home victory over Kilmarnock later on Sunday. The Irish defender hooked a Camilo Durán cross into the top corner in the 26th minute to restore Celtic’s four-point lead at the top of the table.

Celtic – and Kasper Høgh in particular – otherwise had a frustrating day in front of goal, with Benjamin Nygren missing a second-half penalty. Celtic manager Martin O’Neill said: “I thought Kasper was off the mark for about 35 seconds. I think he would maybe have scored the next chance if the first had counted, but he worked really hard for us.”

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win at St Mirren on Saturday.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two Scottish Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished their title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave Paisley without a mark on them.

The in-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before the returning skipper, Dan Neil, added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend Rangers’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

The Aberdeen manager, Stephen Robinson, insists he will face the challenge head on as his side go into the international break in real trouble at the wrong end of the table.

Hibernian started the evening three points behind Robinson’s side, but a dominant second-half performance in a 4-0 victory at Pittodrie allowed the Edinburgh club to overtake their hosts in 10th place on goal difference.

The hosts showed promise early in the game and the Hibs keeper Raphael Sallinger saved well from Jack Milne, who also hit the bar for Aberdeen before Jamie McGrath’s 25-yard strike found the target. Aberdeen went all-out in search of an equaliser, but quickly fell 2-0 behind to Callum Wright, sparking calls for Robinson’s head from the home support. Further strikes from Thibault Klidjé and Nicky Cadden completed the rout.

Robinson said: “It’s really, really disappointing, there’s no hiding away from it. It was an unacceptable performance and an unacceptable result. We haven’t taken our chances – Hibs had five or six chances and took four of them – [and] that’s always the difference in football. We got the result we deserved.

“It’s a difficult situation, difficult for myself, the players and the club. I will keep fighting until told otherwise. We have to be better than that, that’s not acceptable. We have to get players who want to fight and try to get us out of this situation.”

Jim Goodwin, the home manager, hit out at the decision to award the penalty that cost Dundee United dear in a 1-1 draw against Motherwell at Tannadice.

The referee, Ryan Lee, had initially given a free-kick for offside in the early stages of the game. However, he was then advised by the VAR, Andrew Dallas, to have another look at an incident where Tawanda Maswanhise had gone down in the United box under a challenge by the home skipper, Dylan Tait. After checking the pitchside monitor, the referee pointed to the spot with the Motherwell captain, Lukas Fadinger, tucking the penalty away.

The hosts ultimately salvaged a point thanks to Jesse Randall’s goal but Goodwin insisted his side should have had all three. “It’s a poor decision for me,” he said. “I know it’s going to be subjective and people will have their own opinions on it, but I don’t know what Dylan Tait is meant to do.” Unsurprisingly, the Motherwell manager, Alfred Johansson, disagreed with Goodwin’s assessment, saying: “He’s on the ball and gets down from a tackle, and it’s a penalty.”

Simo Valakari was thrilled to give St Johnstone supporters a 2-1 victory over Dundee to celebrate after recent Perth struggles against their Tayside rivals.

Josh Campbell headed the home side in front after five minutes. The substitute Joe Westley replied early in the second half after a mix-up between the keeper Ross Sinclair and Cheick Diabate. Kai Fotheringham, on his first Premiership start for St Johnstone, netted a deflected winner on 72 minutes.

Small plane crashes into pickup truck on busy Florida highway

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:29:05 GMT

No one was injured after emergency landing in Fort Myers 50 minutes after takeoff with two people onboard

A small plane crashed into the rear of a pickup truck as it made an emergency landing on a busy Florida highway on Saturday but miraculously no one was injured in the dramatic incident.

Video footage obtained from the sheriff’s office shows a Cessna 172 grazing over the truck as it approached the ground for a complete landing on a road in Fort Meyers at about 11.45am on Saturday.

The aircraft made an emergency landing after the pilot reported an engine issue, according to a Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) statement.

The plane took off from Sebring, Florida, around 11am on Saturday before it made the emergency landing about 50 minutes later, according to flight tracking data.

There were two people on board the aircraft and the pickup truck was traveling eastbound on Bayshore Road.

There were no reported injuries on the scene, according the Lee county sheriff’s office.

“Couldn’t have been a better outcome. Grateful doesn’t come close!” Carmine Marceno, Lee county’s sheriff, shared in a post to X.

LCSO Patrol & Florida’s department of transportation safely relocated the aircraft while the FAA is working to assume the investigation, Marceno added.

The FAA is the lead agency on the investigation into the incident.

The emergency landing comes one week after a business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a south Florida neighborhood and erupted into a giant fireball.

Dominant Lando Norris powers to victory in São Paulo F1 Grand Prix

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 19:12:32 GMT

Mercedes wrap up constructors’ championship

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen surges to second place

Lando Norris delivered a masterclass for victory at the São Paulo Grand Prix, taking the flag at a ­meeting marked by a series of ­striking comebacks.

Max ­Verstappen was once more outstanding at Interlagos by taking second from 21st on the grid and for McLaren it was a victory they have sought since mid-season. But of most import was confirmation of a definitive return from the wilderness for Mercedes as they claimed their ninth Formula One constructors’ world championship.

What it meant to Mercedes was clear, with as many of the team personnel as could be squeezed on to the podium in São Paulo celebrating the achievement. The drivers – the newly crowned world champion, Kimi Antonelli, and George ­Russell – and the team principal, Toto Wolff, ­sportingly allowed them their moment before joining them to share in the redemptive joy.

With it Mercedes have sealed their first drivers’ and ­constructors’ double since Lewis Hamilton last took the drivers’ title in 2020, and their first constructors’ championship at all since 2021. They needed to outscore second-placed Ferrari by three points in Brazil; Antonelli finishing fifth and Russell fourth proved more than enough.

The feat is even more impressive given how much Mercedes struggled under the last set of regulations. They endured four long years of battering away to little effect, a drought from which there was no guarantee they could return to winning ways.

The competitive edge might have been dulled, the operational execution in question, yet coming back at the first time of asking to close out with such control was a reminder of what a fearsome operation the Brackley-based squad remain and that they will finish the season as the early benchmark of this era in F1.

The achievement – tying them with Williams as the third most successful constructor in F1, behind only Ferrari and McLaren – is the culmination of a remarkable season for the team. The race at Interlagos was not their smoothest of the year – Antonelli had tyre temperature issues that cost him the lead and Russell spun on ­exiting the pit lane – but the hard work had long since been done.

Dominant for the opening half of the year, having developed both the best car and the best engine, they have taken 12 wins from 20 meetings. Indeed reliability has been their only real weakness, which was perhaps to be expected given the new regulations, and will be something the team can be expected to address going forward.

They rightly enjoyed the ­plaudits but Norris and Verstappen were also stars in an incident-packed race in Brazil, in difficult, mixed, wet and dry conditions.

Verstappen, after a grid penalty for taking a new engine, was hugely impressive and making it up to ­second ranks among his best comebacks on a track where he has already delivered some mighty performances, not least in winning from 17th on the grid in 2024.

This was a classic performance from the Dutchman, showing sharp decisiveness and touch to come through the field. Just taking ­podiums is not where he wants to be but the pace of the Red Bull indicated that the team, after starting the season well off the pace, are very much on course to be in the mix next season.

McLaren share that ambition, and they will be similarly buoyed by their showing. Antonelli had led for the opening phase of the race having beaten Norris off the line but had issues with his grip after his first pit stop, allowing Norris into the lead from where the British driver was all but untouchable.

The McLaren had immense pace even amid late tension when rain swept the track in the final 10 laps, causing a flurry of pit stops for wet rubber. Norris nonetheless had the conditions’ measure to the flag, where he ­finished with a 14-second lead.

The victory represents a real result for McLaren, as the final set of upgrades they brought to this round, notably the front wing, appear to have paid off. They have not won since Norris took the Dutch GP and were hoping these final developments to their car would prove they were going in the right direction for 2027. On this form they, too, have turned the corner, indicating that for all of Mercedes’s success they will surely have a fight on their hands when it comes to defending those well-earned titles next season.

Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar was in third. Hamilton, who marked his 400th grand prix by taking a grid ­penalty for an engine change, made it to ninth from 20th for Ferrari, with his teammate Charles Leclerc seventh.

Dorgu rescues point for Manchester United in eight-goal thriller against Aston Villa

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 18:54:23 GMT

Does this late, late comeback draw keep Michael Carrick in his job? He urged United to back up their breathless Roma comeback victory on Tuesday by building momentum and they did, kind of, by avoiding defeat.

Patrick Dorgu’s 96th-minute equaliser went off his head and in. Senne Lammens, up for the corner, knocked into his opposite number, Zion Suzuki, but no foul was given – to Unai Emery’s disquiet, Aston Villa’s manager pointing to this afterwards. This made it 4-4 to follow Joshua Zirkzee’s added-time finish as Villa were somehow pulled back by Carrick’s chaotic unit.

Chris Kavanagh soon blew for time but not before further bedlam as the referee sent off what appeared to be a member of Villa’s technical staff.

Before all of this Lammens (twice), Diogo Dalot and Leny Yoro were ­culpable for Villa’s goals. What can any manager do if a trio of players shoot the team in both feet with the schoolboy defending that allowed Alysson to score a barely credible 59 seconds in, and Nicolas Jackson to double the lead after four minutes?

Both these goals were ­Lammens’s fault. Then, after a rousing Roma‑esque first-half comeback to make it 2-2 via Bruno Fernandes and Youri ­Tielemans, Dalot’s chop on ­Alysson two minutes into the second period conceded the season’s clearest ­penalty, which John McGinn dispatched. Further farce followed via Yoro’s own what-are-you-doing moment: a ­flying header towards his own net that led to Leon Goretzka’s fourth goal for Emery’s team.

The bottom line is that United have still won three games all season, from 15, and only one of these in the league, on 30 August, when Ipswich were beaten 5-2.

Carrick may well cling on because Jason Wilcox has been reluctant to fire the head coach so far. Yet United enter the international break in a ­bewildering 18th place, so who knows? Carrick cuffed away a post‑match question that asked if he might walk away – for the good of the club. “I’m not,” was his curt reply.

For two minutes and 46 seconds his team were actually bottom of the table earlier in the day, when Sunderland went 1-0 up against Chelsea and before Liverpool took the lead at Crystal Palace.

The toxicity towards the United owners was summed up in the message, held up in letters and displayed in the Stretford End, to the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe: “Your funeral not ours, sell up”.

Villa’s lightning start was uber-professional from them and dismally amateurish from United: the ball arrived with Alysson and his shot went through Lammens’s legs.

United’s No 1 was in the dock again when Alysson’s effort went to ­the Belgian’s left and he pushed it out to Jackson, who smashed in for 2-0.

The joke beforehand was that even United could not lose by the 10‑goal margin needed to end the day in 20th place. The joke now was that United were in “hold my beer” territory.

Could they get a grip and retrieve a two-goal deficit, as they did ­versus Roma? Matheus Cunha, who scored twice against the Italian side, made a ­barnstorming charge into the right of Villa’s area that caused Boubacar Kamara to upend him. Kavanagh awarded the penalty and so ­Fernandes, as he did versus Roma, had the chance from the spot to pull a first goal back.

A hop-and-skip later it was game on again, Suzuki guessing the wrong way. This was 16 minutes in and the confusing rabble that is Carrick’s United took over as Villa were then pummelled until half-time.

United were all they had not been in the calamitous opening four ­minutes: slick, fast, and in charge in a 20-minute passage of pressure that was finally broken when Villa escaped their half, Pau Torres heading McGinn’s free-kick over.

United continued on. Their energy impressed and it said they still believed – in rescuing the match, and Carrick. Hard evidence arrived with Tielemans’s equaliser as Villa folded precisely as United had. Noussair Mazraoui’s cross came to the Belgian and he beat Suzuki. So, at the interval, the contest was all square after a breakneck opening half.

What might the second period ­conjure? The answer: Dalot’s ­feeble trip on Alysson, as Carrick was a ­picture of despair. McGinn converted, to Lammens’s right, and it was 3-2 to Villa.

They stretched their advantage further due to more ­slapstick play from United. McGinn floated in a free-kick from the right, Yoro’s header forced ­Lammens to tip the ball on to the frame of the goal, and it rebounded and ­Goretzka ­bundled in.

Carrick had not found a place for Shea Lacey despite his impact as a substitute against Roma but on 65 minutes the head coach did, the youngster joined by Dorgu and Mason Mount in a triple change.

Tielemans, Amad Diallo and Dalot came off and the Portuguese seemed to be jeered: if so a rare occurrence here for United to boo one of their own. Then came Zirkzee and Dorgu’s goals that grabbed a point for United.

“Sacked in the morning” had been the Villa support’s taunt of Carrick. We wait to see if this is prescient. It is a 50‑50 shot, maybe.

Riot breaks out at influencer boxing event attended by Tommy Robinson in Ireland

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 18:33:34 GMT

Two people arrested after Robinson’s presence inflames tensions in scenes witnessed by many on social media

Two people were arrested at an influencer boxing event that descended into a riot in Ireland after the presence of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson inflamed tensions in the crowd.

The riot took place at about midnight on Saturday at an event organised by the controversial internet personality HSTikkyTokky, whose real name is Harrison Sullivan, at the Hub events venue in Kilkenny.

Robinson, 43, is on bail after being found guilty in October of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence. He is due back in court on 16 December for a sentencing hearing, with a substantial custodial sentence possible.

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was a ringside guest and surrounded by a number of his supporters at the event, which was organised by Sullivan and fellow internet personality Ed Matthews under their Unhinged events company. Sullivan and Matthews earlier this year featured in a Netflix documentary about manosphere influencers. On Friday, Sullivan told the Guardian that Robinson would be attending the event.

A chaotic and violent press conference on Friday evening was a sign of the disorder to come, with competitors repeatedly attacking each other. They included streamers, fitness personalities, drill rappers, OnlyFans models, and Paul Flaherty, a convicted sex offender turned YouTuber.

The event, which was livestreamed on the Kick platform to about 1.8 million viewers, began without incident. The atmosphere grew tense when Sullivan and Matthews invited Robinson to the commentator’s desk before a fight by the Muslim social media personality Mo Deen, whose real name is Mohammad Kubba.

Robinson, who was holding a copy of his book The Grooming Gang Cover-Up, told Matthews that “Muslims have been raping our country for 100 years”, and cited false statistics about Muslim men and sexual offences. Many of the racially diverse people at the event took offence at Robinson’s comments.

After Kubba won his fight he climbed out of the ring and jumped on to Robinson, throwing punches. A scuffle was brought under control by security, with further competitive fights set to resume.

However, the event erupted into a riot after Sullivan demanded that Kubba, who had left the event, return to “face off” against Robinson in the ring. A reluctant Kubba was escorted back into the venue by the event’s security team. It appeared that Sullivan wished for the pair to have an unscheduled bareknuckle fight, with Sullivan repeatedly heard saying “let Tommy fight him”. Sullivan also allowed Robinson’s entourage, whom he referred to as “Tommy’s boys”, into the ring.

Upon Kubba’s arrival in the ring, which by now was filled with Robinson’s supporters, Robinson threw a copy of his book, which has Arabic-style lettering, at Kubba, and a fight broke out. The crowd erupted into violence, with chairs and barricades being thrown and attenders punching each other, as others screamed and ran for safety.

Interviewed by the Guardian after the riot, Kubba claimed he had been told to start a fight with Robinson, although he declined to say by whom. Before the fight began, Robinson had said he would be willing to “batter” Kubba if the Muslim personality started a fight with him, although he also said that he liked Kubba and bore no ill will towards him. There is no suggestion the riot was pre-planned.

Over the next 20 minutes violent scenes unfolded, as Sullivan pleaded unsuccessfully with the crowd to stay peaceful. The riot was eventually broken up by event and venue security and the gardaí, who had been called to the venue earlier in the night after disturbances.

A Garda Síochána spokesperson confirmed that a male in his 30s was assaulted and removed from the scene to St Luke’s hospital in Kilkenny, while another male in his 20s was arrested and detained at a police station. A teenage boy was also arrested and subsequently charged with violent disorder, and was due to appear in court on Sunday.

Footage of the riot spread on social media in real time. Before the live stream cut to black, some in the crowd could be heard chanting “Oh Tommy Robinson”. After police dispersed the crowds, Sullivan attempted to restart the fights for the live stream only, but was blocked from doing so by a visibly upset representative of the venue.

The Ministry of Justice and the Metropolitan police were unable to confirm whether Robinson’s bail terms prohibited international travel.

In comments uploaded to social media on Sunday, Sullivan acknowledged that he had erred by not hiring more event security. “Everyone makes mistakes when you are trying to grow something,” he said, before adding: “One thing I can say is it was a great night of entertainment and it’s gone super viral.” On its official Instagram account, @unhinged_promotions, footage of the riot was uploaded with the caption: “The Area started a RIOT.”

Outside the venue in the early hours of Sunday morning, the crowd, predominantly teenage boys and young men, filmed the aftermath on their phones. One attender told the Guardian that such things did not happen in Kilkenny city, which has a population of 27,000.

Lisa Nandy wary of ‘circular arguments’ about rejoining EU

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 18:20:06 GMT

Culture secretary pushes back against talk of revisiting Brexit but says closer ties would fulfil referendum promises

One of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said she wants to avoid “circular arguments” about whether the UK should rejoin the EU, underlining divisions at the top of government over revisiting Brexit.

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, appeared to suggest she was not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc, but she said the prime minister should still pursue closer ties to fulfil the promises made at the time of the referendum.

She is one of a handful of cabinet ministers who are concerned about Burnham’s plan for an “honest conversation” with the public about Brexit and who are privately warning it could reopen a row that would only benefit Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

“I do not believe that anybody wants to repeat circular arguments about in or out, leave or remain. I do think, though, that over the last decade we have let the British people down very badly,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

Nandy, whose Wigan seat voted overwhelmingly for leave in 2016, and who is one of the most cautious in the cabinet about reversing Brexit, was asked if she wanted to go back in. “I don’t know if that’s a choice we have,” she said.

However, she did concede that Burnham was trying to address the failings of the Brexit deal, telling Sky News it was important to “be honest” and highlight that “the deal that we got is not what we were promised”.

The culture secretary stressed there were “trade-offs and choices” to be made which involved a conversation with people across the country, indicating that Brexit would be a key theme of the next election campaign.

Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday. Downing Street sources said he would use it to get Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

In private, EU counterparts will be expecting Burnham to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to move beyond Labour’s “red lines” on the bloc after the next election.

Burnham said at the weekend there was more to come. “This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition,” he told the Sunday Mirror.

Officials will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) Safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and visas for touring artists.

Soon after the Brussels summit, Burnham is expected to give a speech setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU, arguing it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. No 10 sources said he wanted to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion.

Senior government figures say Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be solely confirmatory.

Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.

“We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court.

Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.”

He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister.

“My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said.

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.

During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.

Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.

Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.

He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.

If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday to settle a long-running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.

Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter, government sources say, helping British industry but setting up a potential fight with MPs and campaigners over the government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy.

The decision will be made just as Andy Burnham prepares to travel to his first Cop summit as prime minister, where he and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will champion electrification on a global scale.

With some MPs already upset by the decisions to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and to cut funding for green schemes to pay for higher defence spending, many see the upcoming decisions on the Rosebank oilfield and the EV mandate as critically important.

Lizzi Collinge, the Labour MP for Morecambe and Lunesdale, said: “The upcoming decision on the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate will have a huge climate impact, possibly the biggest one that’s on the PM’s desk.

“But it will also set the direction for tackling the cost of living and helping get our energy prices down over the coming decade.”

Catherine Fookes, the MP for Monmouthshire, said: “The government has some incredibly difficult decisions to make in the coming months and the prime minister will need to weigh up the consequences of each. We need the ZEV mandate to stay, and Rosebank to be rejected.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate and no decisions have been taken.

“We are committed to the phaseout of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this, and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

Under rules brought in by the last Conservative government, carmakers have to make sure they only sell EVs by 2035, gradually increasing the proportion over time to 80% by 2030.

The policy is expected to create greater emissions savings than any other, leading to nearly 14% of all the reductions to which the UK has pledged between 2028 and 2032.

Carmakers have warned for years, however, that the interim targets in particular are unattainable, arguing that higher inflation and a squeeze on living standards have pushed them out of reach.

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) says the industry will miss this year’s 33% target by a wide margin, with battery EVs accounting for 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year.

Those targets, however, do not take into account exemptions that allow carmakers to avoid fines even if they undershoot their targets, such as by selling more hybrid cars, or making up for lower sales of electric cars now by selling more in the future.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The gap between demand and mandated targets continues to widen.

“Meaningful change to the trajectory, alongside expanded flexibilities throughout the regulation, is essential to bridge that gap, safeguard jobs and investment while keeping the UK’s zero emission transition on track.”

With ministers already having diluted the targets on multiple occasions since the policy was first proposed, the government launched another review into the policy in August, proposing five main options.

That consultation kickstarted an internal battle in Whitehall. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has argued for the 2030 target to be reduced as far as possible, to 50%.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, is believed to want it to be approximately 60%, while Miatta Fahnbulleh and her predecessor as energy secretary, Ed Miliband, are understood to want it to remain at 80%.

“If the government does this, it must provide assurance that the mandate will not be weakened again in the coming years, the 2035 target for EVs remains in place, and it delivers a robust industrial strategy to build a strong EV manufacturing base in the UK that will protect jobs in the long term.”

The Guardian view on a tale of two activists: Joshua Wong and Au Kam San should not be behind bars

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 17:30:45 GMT

The latest vindictive prosecutions and harsh sentences in Hong Kong and Macau are further testimony to China’s ruthless suppression of dissent

One is internationally famous – he was once dubbed “the Face of Protest” by Time magazine – and the other is little known outside his home town. What Joshua Wong and Au Kam San share, beyond the harsh sentences they received last week, is that they represent the spirit of dissent that Beijing is determined to crush.

Mr Wong, who has been in prison for six years, should have walked free next January – not free to fight for Hong Kong’s rights, which China has suppressed so decisively, but at least to walk the streets of the city he loves. Instead, a court last Thursday sentenced the 30-year-old, an activist from the age of 14, to another 10 years. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the draconian national security law (NSL). The case’s timing means that he will remain behind bars until he is 40 because so little of his sentences overlap. It also came one day after the city’s annual summit for global financial leaders ended – avoiding awkward questions for companies such as Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, which long ago decided that it is business as usual, even as China turns the screw.

Mr Wong was sentenced after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” – the same charge used against the newspaper tycoon Jimmy Lai, a British citizen, who was jailed for 20 years this spring. Their crime was lobbying foreign governments to put pressure on China as they sought to safeguard Hong Kong’s way of life and high degree of autonomy – guaranteed for half a century in the international treaty that Beijing signed with London when Hong Kong was returned in 1997. Yet Mr Wong had mostly curtailed this activism before the NSL came into force. While high-profile targets have faced prolonged detention due to the stacking of charges, many more have been pursued by authorities. More than 300 people have been arrested for violating the NSL, a colonial-era “sedition” law and other legislation enacted two years ago.

One day after Mr Wong’s sentencing, a court in nearby Macau handed Mr Au a 12-and-a-half year prison sentence for subversion in the city’s first case under its national security law, which was held behind closed doors. Mr Au is a former primary school teacher and legislator who advocated for democracy and helped to organise annual vigils in Macau to commemorate those killed in the bloody crackdown on 1989’s Tiananmen Square protests. The extraordinary 2019 protest movement and unrest in Hong Kong never spread to Macau, but authorities still increased pressure on the casino hub and former Portuguese colony. Mr Au once spoke of “sowing seeds” in a bitter winter, in the hope they might one day sprout if the external environment changed. The intent of authorities is clear: to further chill any critics in Macau.

Leaders elsewhere must be clear in not only condemning the sentences handed to activists such as Mr Wong and Mr Au, but also calling for their release. The EU and Portugal condemned the sentencing of Mr Au, who also holds Portuguese citizenship, but did not call for him to be freed. Governments should consider imposing travel bans or asset freezes on officials involved in the crackdown. They must also do their utmost to protect activists who have fled Hong Kong and continue to press the cause of their home and their friends from exile, as they face increasing threats and pressure.

The Guardian view on Ordnance Survey maps: still a superior way to navigate the landscape

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 17:25:45 GMT

The 225th anniversary of the organisation’s first publication is an opportunity to celebrate its unique contribution to our sense of place

In his one-paragraph short story, On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication.

The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation, her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.

These days, the topographical legacy they left behind is updated through satellites, GPS and digital technologies. But just as significant has been the cultural impact of OS maps on the wider population, amid expanded access to leisure time. Science and art combined in the 20th century, as the commercial potential of small-scale productions for tourists and ramblers was recognised. Sales shot up as covers began to depict motorcars venturing down country lanes, pipe-smoking backpackers plotting a route through the Forest of Bowland, and couples wandering through the Chilterns.

One should not over-romanticise. There is a darker, controlling side to the history of maps, not least when it comes to who got to define borders and names. In his play Translations, the writer Brian Friel portrays the cultural impact of colonial power by following two British surveyors across Ireland, as they impose toponymic order on a recalcitrant Celtic landscape.

But viewed from the age of satnav instructions and Google Maps, there is a charm to cartography that the passive reception of a monotone order to “turn right after 50 metres” will never match. As well as being models of precision and order, the best maps are also a form of mysterious and evocative art, inviting us to proactively explore the world and firing up the imagination. Hewitt quotes from a 19th-century poem in which a woman yearning for her soldier husband “taught her finger” to “stray o’er the map”, tracing the represented distance between them. Countless map-readers have similarly immersed themselves in contour lines, symbols and coded colours, in order to visualise landscapes that they are about to encounter for the first time.

The rise of digital technologies means that the sight of a map poking out of a rucksack or spread awkwardly across the passenger seat of a car is less common than it used to be. But the tactile delights of vinyl records are being rediscovered and celebrated by younger consumers, amid a surge of nostalgia for the analogue age. Hopefully, the peculiar pleasures of attempting to tame an OS Landranger, as it flaps uncontrollably on a windy hillside, will also continue to be enjoyed by generations to come.

England had promised to do their talking on the field and so it came to pass. Maybe Borthwick should commission the Times to write his motivational pre-match speeches every week. On this evidence the ­Wallabies have some massive issues to address but, equally, England were com­fortably the better, more energetic side. Further improvement will still be demanded, of course, but this record number of points against ­Australia was easily their most satisfying all-round outing of the calendar year to date. Their three defining Ds – defence, discipline and desire – were conspicuous throughout and, at long last, they are starting to trust their exciting attacking talent out wide.

In the first half Manny ­Feyi‑­Waboso was a constant menace and when he failed to reappear for the second half England were able to whistle up the irrepressible Henry Pollock, who duly contributed two tries to ­justify his selection as a replacement winger.

There were also deserving ­first-half scores for the hard-working Jamie George, Ollie ­Chessum and Joe Heyes while Jack van Poortvliet also made it on to the scoresheet shortly after half-time to atone for the interception pass that presented the Wallabies with a ­relieving try just before the interval.

If England can maintain this sort of strike rate against Japan and ­New ­Zealand over the next two ­Saturdays they may yet have a chance of featuring in the Nations Champion­ship final on home turf at the end of the month.

At the very least this will give England the confidence boost they were seeking after the dismal Six Nations campaign that placed Borthwick’s regime under pressure.

The unselfish ability of Fin Smith and Henry Slade to put their teammates into space was also a big plus while Pollock is a player who just adores the big occasion. On the flip side the post-match sight of Feyi-Waboso in a medical boot was rather less encouraging.
