During such passages England look a more than decent team but ­consistency has too often eluded them this year. Much of that has been a consequence of the multiple cards they have been receiving; surprise, surprise they fare rather better when they keep 15 players on the field.

Australia were swiftly reminded of that same essential truth. At 19-3 down and reduced to 14 men it was hard to see the Wallabies finding a way back, hence England’s frustration when a telegraphed pass by Van Poortvliet was picked off by the lurking Max Jorgensen who sprinted half the length of the field to score. Ryan Lonergan’s conversion was the final act of a half in which the Wallabies had barely made it into the home 22.

Would the loss of Feyi-Waboso at half-time, though, be another blow to their momentum? No, was the answer as Pollock made decent yards with his first carry before England launched a searing attack on the opposite flank and Tommy Freeman threw a glorious long inside ball for Van Poortvliet to score.

At which point the 21-year-old ­Pollock decided it was time to start writing his own scripts. He was more than quick enough to beat the cover out wide for his first try after 54 ­minutes and within three ­minutes was again being mobbed by his ­teammates after a second electric burst to the line. It is unlikely to be the last time England fans see his now familiar “pulse check” celebration.

The Wallabies did at least leave with a couple of consolation scores for Filipo Daugunu and Jeremy Williams but the final word went to Ben Spencer, who snaffled an interception try of his own to complete the drubbing. One win does not completely change the world but it will make a huge difference to English self-belief.

Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:50:58 GMT

Bailiffs reportedly seized digital records before court case over alleged intellectual property breaches on Land Rover Defender

Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its “Defender clone” infringes intellectual property rights.

Bailiffs acting on behalf of JLR reportedly seized digital records from the offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp in August, according to the Sunday Times.

The raid took place before a court case in the The Hague this week which will decide whether the BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender.

Motoring experts have likened BYD’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year. The company is scheduled to launch the vehicle, which the BBC’s Top Gear magazine called the “Chinese Defender clone”, in the UK market in January at a price of £47,995, undercutting the Defender by more than £20,000.

BYD says on its website that “an unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look”.

The price of JLR’s seven-seat Defender 110 starts from £68,465and is one of the country’s bestselling cars. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, compared with 25,370a year earlier.

The raid in the Netherlands was carried out by court-ordered bailiffs, with JLR suspecting that BYD reverse-engineered some of the technology that could be used in the Ti7, the Times reported. JLR wanted to secure the digital records before they could be destroyed.

JLR and BYD declined to comment on the “ongoing legal proceedings”.

The dispute with BYD is not the first legal case JLR has pursed against a Chinese company over copycat allegations. It won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motor Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019 after a three-year court battle.

Met Office issues weather warning as UK conditions create ‘perfect recipe’ for fog

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:38:16 GMT

Travel may be disrupted until Monday morning in areas including most of southern England and across Midlands

The Met Office has said weather conditions in the UK are creating a “perfect recipe” for fog as it warned that travel may be disrupted.

A yellow weather warning lasting from 6pm on Sunday until 11am on Monday has been issued by the service, with the affected areas including most of southern England, excluding the south-west, and the entirety of the Midlands.

The warning also includes pockets of northern England and Wales, with fog expected in Liverpool, Sheffield, York, Cardiff and Wrexham.

Niamh Murray, a Met Office operational meteorologist, said: “There is still going to be patchy fog elsewhere, just not quite as dense or as impactful. Parts of the West Country could still see fog, Northern Ireland, really anywhere across much of the UK, even into the central belt of Scotland.

“With autumn and winter and getting fog during this time of year, we get much longer nights, and that allows temperatures to sort of fall away,” she told the Press Association. “We get a longer period of cooling and also the temperatures are much lower, so they’re much closer to the temperature that we need for the air to become saturated and therefore form fog.”

Murray believes recent weather conditions have created the “perfect recipe” for dense fog to roll across large areas of England and Wales.

“Another thing that we need to form fog is quite light winds, not absolutely no winds,” she said. “We just have the perfect recipe at the moment: light winds, clear skies, long nights, to allow that fog to develop. And particularly if we see the negative numbers, it can be quite stubborn to clear the next day.”

The Met Office said the fog may be densest overnight on Monday in rural areas such as parts of the Midlands, Wales and East Anglia, with air frost possible.

It also warned that delays to bus and train services could happen as visibility may reduce to as little as 50 metres or less in parts of the UK. Delays and cancellations for flights in and out of the country are also a possibility due to the heaviness of the fog.

Challenging the politics that brought Donald Trump to power

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:37:43 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial commenting on the Republicans’ rout in the US midterm elections

Your editorial on the US midterms (4 November) notes that culture war attacks, bigotry and smears failed this time. It is worth asking why they worked before. For a decade we have argued over whether Donald Trump’s support was about economics or culture. My research, combining a survey of 6,600 US residents with social mobility data, suggests the question was badly posed. Trump’s 2016 gains over Mitt Romney’s in 2012 were largest in counties where children born poor are least likely to rise, and people there describe success as luck and connections rather than effort.

The grievance was economic. The language it found was cultural. Factory jobs lost to China became Beijing; the end of the male family wage became feminism; the decline of coal towns became climate politics. Trump’s gift was to translate economic pain into identity, which is how his coalition absorbed tariffs, welfare cuts and tax cuts for the rich.

Last week the translation stopped working. Voters spoke plainly about grocery bills, petrol at $4.20 a gallon and electricity bills pushed up by datacentres. And an electorate supposedly gripped by a culture war sent the first out gay man and the first native American woman to the Senate, elected the first black and native American female governors in Georgia and New Mexico, and chose a black Republican as Florida’s first black governor. When the economy speaks for itself, identity stops doing the talking.

That is a warning too. You note that Democrats tied prices to corruption. That is the same story of a rigged game that carried Trump, and it punishes whoever is in charge. The only way out of this backlash is earned opportunity. No party has yet tried it. Dr Lorenz Meister Department of Social Policy and Intervention, University of Oxford Jonathan Freedland is right to warn that Trump’s electoral defeat does not mean the danger has disappeared (After the midterms, the global right is reeling. But the danger of Trumpism will never be gone, 6 November). But his argument that another Trump is possible because Trump happened once tells us less than it should about why he happened in the first place.

Ariana Baio’s report (Republicans hoping to succeed Trump in 2028 dissect midterm rout, 5 November) offers a revealing clue. JD Vance, Ted Cruz and Ron DeSantis are identifying the war, tariffs and the cost of living as reasons for defeat. They may represent different political futures, but their responses suggest adaptation rather than fundamental repudiation. The question is not simply who succeeds Trump, but whether the politics that made him possible are being challenged at all.

Trump’s defeat does not necessarily discredit the politics that brought him to power. His successors may learn from his mistakes, distance themselves from his excesses, and retain the grievances and discontent on which his movement has drawn.

Meanwhile, a Democratic victory, however emphatic, is not itself evidence that those underlying conditions have been overcome. Rejecting Trump is not necessarily embracing an alternative. Freedland warns another Trump is possible. The more uncomfortable question is whether US politics has produced the forces capable of making another Trump unnecessary. David Eaton Sunderland

President Trump’s policy of bringing about regime change by bombing Iran has proved to be successful. The only problem for him is that the regime he changed was his own. Phil Bramall West Bridgford, Nottingham

Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:31:13 GMT

Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole

I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing (‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief, 2 November). Here is a woman who doesn’t feel obliged to turn ageing into another self-improvement project. She can be angry, grumpy, less adventurous than she once was, and still enjoy her life.

We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job we are expected to perform.

As a 69-year-old psychologist who researches and writes about later life, I question this narrative. Of course, looking after our health matters. But ageing isn’t a competition, and we shouldn’t have to demonstrate that we’re making the most of every remaining year.

I was particularly struck by Brand’s comments about older women being treated as though they are all alike. We are as varied, contradictory and individual as we have ever been. Some of us want adventure; others want a quieter life. Some are still working, others are delighted to have left employment behind. And our feelings about ageing can change from one day to the next.

Perhaps what makes Brand’s interview so appealing is that she doesn’t offer us a formula for growing older. She simply describes her experience, with humour, honesty and a willingness to acknowledge what is difficult.

We need more of that. Less instruction on how to age successfully, and more freedom to grow older in our own way. Dr Denise Taylor Chartered psychologist and author of ThriveSpan

I would like to reassure Jo Brand that approaching 70 is certainly not too old to get fitter and healthier. My partner (aged 73) and I (64) were dedicated couch potatoes. Our evenings were spent with wine, cheese and chocolate. Neither of us had ever done any sport or fitness activity until April of this year when we began the Couch to 5K challenge.

We now run 5km three times a week, every week. We’re not quick (40 minutes) but we do it and feel so much better for it – so virtuous that my halo lights our evening runs. Louise Mothersole Bournemouth, Dorset

Wirtz provides quality as Liverpool leave Crystal Palace propping up table

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:16:18 GMT

It was the moment when ­Liverpool knew they would win here in south London and so move on from the ­Premier League defeat against ­Arsenal at Anfield last Sunday and the one in midweek at Fenerbahce in the Champions League.

Florian Wirtz had timed his run as Liverpool broke up the right and Bradley Barcola’s low pull back was made to measure. Wirtz had to take on the shot first time and it was a test of his technique under pressure. He never looked like failing it, not least because smoothness in this area is his calling card. Liverpool were 2-0 up, Alexis Mac Allister having headed them in front towards the end of the first half from a Dominik Szoboszlai free-kick, and all you could hear was the eruption of delight in the away supporters’ enclosure.

In the Crystal Palace seats there was silence and it seemed to go on for an age. The atmosphere inside this stadium has been diminished since the Holmesdale Fanatics stopped their activities during matches in protest over the general treatment of fans by the club. There was no rallying cry from the stands. Only resignation. Acceptance. There were 54 minutes on the clock but they knew as well as everybody that this was done.

Palace were good in the first half, Yéremy Pino their stand-out ­performer. What a lovely player he is to watch. Pino rattled the crossbar and there were other moments when his team threatened. After the Wirtz goal, there was next to nothing from them, only a Pino effort after a quick break that Alisson blocked.

Liverpool eased home and it was no surprise when Alexander Isak glossed the scoreline towards the end. When he lashed a shot past Dean Henderson from Wirtz’s touch, it was the prompt for thousands of Palace supporters to make for the exits. Their club are in a parlous position as they look up at everyone else from the bottom. It was a fourth league defeat on the spin and the late penalty from Eddie ­Nketiah, on as a substitute, barely seemed to register. It was Palace’s first goal ­during that run of losses.

There was no anger, no boos for the players at full time. And there does not appear to be any appetite from the crowd for the manager, Pierre Sage, to be dismissed even if that is surely looking like his destiny. The problems are not all of his making; the recruitment was simply not good enough in the summer. It was certainly telling that he mentioned afterwards how he wanted to “adjust a few things in the winter transfer window.”

Sage spoke well, insisting he was confident he would remain in charge for Palace’s matches after the ­international break – Coventry (away), Hull (home). “I have not gone from the dream to the nightmare,” he said. “I know we have to push more things, especially in our level of ­playing. We have a lack of efficiency.”

Palace were reasonably secure when they defended in a low block. The problems came after they conceded the opening goal with yet more lax marking on a set piece. ­Thereafter, Liverpool had the spaces they craved in the transitions. Even at 0-0, the visitors looked more ­dangerous in open play on the counter. When they broke with numbers in the 26th minute, Palace were indebted to Adam Wharton for a ­saving challenge on Isak after Wirtz had pulled back from the right.

Liverpool began with a flurry. They took shots from distance. Barcola wanted a penalty following a nudge in his back from Óscar Mingueza; there was not enough in it. In a sign of things to come, Mac Allister darted for the near post onto a Szoboszlai free-kick and flashed a header wide. There was the moment when Cody Gakpo volleyed across the face of goal only there was nobody there.

Palace almost took the lead in the 18th minute with their first forward thrust. Tyrick Mitchell played the final pass, clubbed in low from the left and Pino did well to bring it under his spell. His shot flew over Alisson and crashed against the crossbar.

Palace did not deserve to trail at the interval. They threatened up the left through Mitchell and Pino. ­Jørgen Strand Larsen had a goal ruled out for offside while Daichi Kamada was denied by Alisson after ­catching a volley sweetly. After the Mac Allister goal, Wharton had Alisson scrambling to touch behind after he stretched to reach a Pino ball in. Following a few recent wobbles, ­Alisson’s performance was a major plus for Liverpool.

Barcola had blazed a volley high when well-placed from a deep ­Szoboszlai cross just before the Mac Allister goal and it did not feel as though the breakthrough was coming for Liverpool. There was fury among the Palace support because they did not think the referee, Tony Harrington, ought to have penalised Jefferson Lerma for a foul on Gakpo.

It was a soft award but the decision was right. It did not excuse Palace’s inability to defend the Szoboszlai set piece. It was just too easy for Mac Allister to direct the free header. Liverpool might have scored from yet another Szoboszlai free-kick in first-half stoppage time only Ronald Araújo could not properly reach a Jérémy Jacquet flick.

Palace felt the belief crumble after the Wirtz goal and it became a gentle slide towards the inevitable. Isak was denied one-on-one by Henderson but not when opportunity knocked for him again shortly afterwards. “We needed this win, definitely,” said a relieved Andoni Iraola. “It was important to score first and we controlled the second half.”

Is this the most rubbish Christmas present ever?

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:00:44 GMT

I thought I knew all about disappointment, having received one of the very worst presents as a child. Then I heard about ‘data gifting’

One Christmas when I was a child, my parents wrapped the presents in shiny paper. Unlike the matt kind I was used to, with this stuff you could slowly peel off the sticky tape without ripping the paper or leaving any trace, unfold the end of the package, peek inside, and reseal it – so that’s what I did, to all of mine, as soon as they appeared under the tree. Don’t worry, my comeuppance is coming right up.

The jubilation I felt at pulling off such a stealth move – being basically a master criminal in the manner of those movie jewel thieves who dodge laser tripwires – was almost immediately negated by the sinking realisation I’d ruined my own Christmas. I’d been too impatient to bear the wait, but now, with weeks still to go, all anticipation and excitement had been extinguished. Not least because my main present was – how to put this delicately? – crap.

I always struggled to get up for school, so Santa had stitched me up with an alarm clock. A fun, razzy alarm clock, but an alarm clock all the same. To clarify: no kid wants an alarm clock. It was the very definition of bleak times.

Until this week, I believed this was the most depressing Christmas present in the history of the nativity. But then I heard an advert for a mobile phone provider, which offered the suggestion of “data gifting”. This is where, brimming with festive spirit, you transfer your unused or spare data to somebody else’s device or plan, ho ho ho. A virtual, imaginary present so entirely practical the recipient probably won’t even realise when they use it.

As tangible items increasingly cease to exist in the world, perhaps this is where we’re heading, and it’s too late to turn back. So in future, Christmas will be less about the three wise men, and more the 300 wise MB. Even an alarm clock is preferable to that.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

What are you yearning for? We took to the streets to find out

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 16:00:44 GMT

Longing for someone – or something – can be even more thrilling than getting what you want. That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for? We asked the question in Glasgow

In a world of instant gratification, is it any surprise that many of us have fallen back in love with the idea of “yearning”? Running counter to much of today’s on-demand culture, yearning melds desire and distance, nostalgia and uncertainty; longing for something, or someone, can sometimes appeal in a way that getting exactly what you want cannot.

The resurgence of yearning – especially in the romantic sense – has been one of the biggest entertainment themes of the last couple of years: from The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heated Rivalry to the latest big-screen adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, the allure of unmet desire and slow-burn love has topped hasty happy-ever-afters. TikTok remains awash with recommendations for those who want to #feeltheyearn.

But yearning encompasses more than just romantic infatuation. You might be pining for a particular place or longing for a different time in life. With this in mind, we took to the streets to ask: what are you yearning for right now?

I’m from the north-east of England, so I yearn for a place beside the sea. I yearn for somewhere that I lived before that is probably no longer there anyway – it’s more the idea of it: something I had that wouldn’t necessarily be there if I went back. I think yearning can be seen as a weakness, so if people are pining more than they used to, they may not want to share it. Elizabeth Kennedy, 63, retired

I feel as if I pine for things I have a lot – I place so much value on my friendships and my relationships, and I yearn for them in the quiet moments, even though I have them. I think people have always yearned – Virginia Woolf was pining for things, for example – but I feel like people are pining more openly these days, especially on social media. Adam Hamill, 24, student

I would say I yearn for things, yeah. I’m a mixed martial artist and I’ve not been able to go to my gym in a while, so I’m yearning to go right now. It’s natural to yearn for something – you learn to enjoy the process. If I haven’t been to the gym for a week, it can feel more worthwhile when I finally do go than if I had been every day. Erys, 26, student

Recently, I’ve been yearning for home, back in Oman. Hopefully I will get to go for Christmas or the holidays. I feel like, lately, people have been romanticising yearning a lot – it may have been present before, but now people are labelling the feeling and emphasising how much they enjoy the act of yearning. Manar, 21, student

I’ve been working quite a lot, so I’m yearning for a day off! I think people are yearning for human connection a lot more definitely because everything is online these days – shopping, dating, whatever. I think the human touch is missing for a lot of people – a bit of loneliness maybe. People are longing for something a bit deeper. Declan, 30, actor/salesman

I don’t yearn; I know a lot of people who do, but that’s not me. I just take each day as it comes and I believe that what is for you will not go by you. It’s a mindset: if I can’t afford something – a bigger house, for example – I don’t get it. I’m quite happy with what I’ve got. A lot of the things I think people yearn for are materialistic, but I keep my things for years and years, rather than following the fashions. Ann Walker, 67, retired

Whether I have a small goal or a big dream, I would plan step by step to reach the thing I am yearning for. For example, I’m a K-pop fan and there are some idols that I really like – especially Anton from Riize; he is very handsome. I yearn to work with these idols, and currently I am studying contemporary art theory. I think yearning can be enjoyable, as long as you are not too anxious about it; you just have to wait. Yuntan, 22, student

I just yearn for our family get-togethers – I miss all that. I’ve just been organising a get-together next year, because you’ve got to book these things in advance. But I don’t think I’m longing for anything any more than usual. I’m quite happy – I’ve got my health, I can get out and about, and that’s the main thing. Elizabeth Harvey, 72, retired nurse

I see a lot of people yearning for a mythical UK that they think existed about 50 years ago, although it never really did. It’s like a really low-grade nostalgia. On a personal level, I don’t really yearn – I’m extremely content. That may be because I don’t have a television. I do go online, but I believe life’s too short to spend it staring at a gogglebox. Steve, 63, self-employed stage manager

I yearn for my best friend – even though she is here! I want her under my skin. I sometimes yearn to go to places, but with a specific somebody, a special somebody – I yearn more for people than things. Everyone is different – and not everyone enjoys the experience of longing, but it can be fun. Delchie, 19

I think people maybe yearn for other people, but not so much for “things” because everything is so accessible now. People don’t like to wait for anything; they’re not really patient any more. I like the idea of yearning, that it can take time to appreciate an experience. I’m on holiday with my friend just now – celebrating 10 years of our friendship – and we have been yearning for this trip! Madeline, 24, student

I’m not yearning for anything specific right now. I think the idea of yearning has become overused – people will be single for, say, four months and they’ll say they’re “yearning” to be in a relationship again. But you can tell when someone is really yearning for something, and when it’s just a buzzword. Reece Ruddick, 18, student

‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 15:37:54 GMT

Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling

The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.

The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.

They are part of an initiative that aims to sow confidence and resilience by teaching them to wrestle and to create stage personae – personae whose feats in the ring, it turns out, inspire them in real life.

“I’ve been slagged and made fun of because I was overweight and went to a special school but I’ve proved that I’m somebody,” said Keelan O’Hagan, 24, who has an alter ego called Kellio, before the show.

“He doesn’t step away from any challenge, he always accepts the mission. No matter what, he doesn’t quit,” said O’Hagan, who transformed his diet and fitness to play Kellio. “To anybody who has tried to bring me down, I’ve been able to get back on my feet and come back stronger.”

Brian Walsh, 44, who is blind, plays a character called Brian Brogue who vanquishes opponents with wrist locks and head locks and by pinning them to the floor. “Before, I wouldn’t have had the strength,” he said. “The training was scary at the start, then I got the hang of it. To be a blind person who does wrestling is the best thing ever.”

The Foyle Rumble is a joint initiative of the Tuned In Project, a Derry-based NGO that creates opportunities for disabled adults, and Complete Anarchy Wrestling (CAW), an event promoter based across the border in County Donegal.

The goal is to give disabled people more independence and agency, said Phil Conn, the Tuned In Project’s programme manager. “We challenge them to be the best they can be. It gives them purpose and a support community. It’s a reason to get out of bed in the morning.”

Participants train for months and know there is an element of real risk and danger, said Conn. “It’s a choreographed performance – if this was an actual fight, we couldn’t do it – but we’ve had students bruised and battered. The throws and hits have an impact.”

The inaugural rumble was in 2024, and Saturday was the third and most ambitious show, with hundreds of spectators and dozens of performers, including some without disabilities. There were smoke machines, dramatic entrances, elaborate stunts and a storyline that pitted the heroic characters against a black-clad entity called The Fault.

“It’s mad how far it has come,” said Sean Curran, of the Tuned In Project. “Wrestling is great. It’s basically your personality pushed up to 11. We’ve seen them grow in confidence and sort of become the characters.”

after newsletter promotion

The idea originated when Curran, as best man at a friend’s wedding, hired Stephen Campbell, a gymnastics teacher and wrestling coach with CAW, to choreograph a stunt at the reception.

Campbell started to coach the Tuned In Project students, instructing them in moves, and discovered they had the ability and desire to create characters and to perform. “They got more talented and one thing led to another,” he said.

On Saturday, Campbell fired up the performers with a rousing speech before they entered the hall. “Tonight is your night,” he told them. “Fuck WrestleMania. They never had a blind wrestler.”

Kiernan McLaughlin, 27, who played a benign monarch known as King Kiernan, gave a shy smile. “I’m spearing somebody tonight,” he said.

SJ Murray, 25, who has a learning disability, admitted to nerves. “I’m petrified,” she said. However, her character, Siren, is fearless. “She’s a badass that is brave and protects the one that she loves.”

Murray has learned combat moves and studied wrestling theory and strategy. “You need stamina and to know what you’re doing,” she said. “My family think I’m mad but support me no matter what.”

On stage, Siren grappled foes who eventually fled the ring, only for their nemesis to fly over the ropes and topple them to the ground.

Abdul El-Sayed’s Oxford years: PhD, political influences and sporting distinction

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 15:26:04 GMT

Michigan senator-elect’s former peers recall his time at university in Britain – and his love of coronation chicken sandwiches

In the cold, twilight days of 2008, inside the University of Michigan’s fortress-like Fleming administration building, one student was given a particularly adulatory sendoff.

Mary Sue Coleman, president of the university at the time, convened a ceremony for the latest Rhodes scholar heading to the University of Oxford: Abdul El-Sayed. “There is no doubt among anyone who crosses his path that he will achieve all he sets out to accomplish and more,” she declared to a room full of the university’s leaders, calling the medical PhD student the “epitome of the engaged intellect”.

She even recalled Bill Clinton’s response to a speech made by El-Sayed in 2007, with the former US president remarking: “I wish every person in the world could have heard you speak today.”

For those who ran into El-Sayed months later in autumn 2009 when he finally crossed the pond, these words of praise rang true. “He always seemed very driven,” says Elias Rothblatt, who played lacrosse alongside Michigan’s senator-elect more than 15 years ago. El-Sayed was captain of Oxford’s lacrosse team and student journalists at the time described him as a “defensive master” in the sport.

Rothblatt, 36, who works in fintech, says El-Sayed was a “very fierce competitor” on the field and a “wonderful” captain. “He had a great sense of humour. He struck a really good mix of being friends with other people on the team but also setting the tone and helping lead the team and keep things, keeping serious.”

Off the field, Rothblatt says, El-Sayed was equally “fun and friendly”. He says: “It was always a pleasure to run into him. He was with his wife sometimes and she was wonderful too.” El-Sayed also had a fixation on a resolutely British sandwich: coronation chicken. Speaking to the Times, Ricardo Chasebi, owner of a now-closed cafe in Oxford’s covered market, recalled El-Sayed’s order as a grilled ciabatta filled with coronation chicken, cheddar, peppers and red onion that was topped with lettuce and tomato.

He eventually placed El-Sayed’s version on the menu, naming it “the Abdul”. The senator-to-be was so keen on Chasebi’s sandwiches that he would call ahead from the airport and say: “I’ll be in Oxford in two hours, don’t shut until I get there.” El-Sayed even handed Chasebi a copy of his doctoral thesis, where he thanked the cafe owner in the acknowledgments for “nourishing my stomach and my soul”.

Rothblatt has tried the Abdul sandwich. “It’s good,” he says. El-Sayed also had a penchant for Nando’s, organising meetings there with his fellow Rhodes scholar cohort.

While he eventually settled into Oxford life, things didn’t start smoothly for El-Sayed. He did not enjoy his course at first and flew back to Michigan two weeks before his first term ended. And based on a recent outburst, where he told a Sky News reporter: “You know how many votes I want to get in the UK? Zero,” you might assume he was, at best, apathetic about his time in Britain. But that is not the case. In his memoir, Healing Politics: A Doctor’s Journey into the Heart of Our Political Epidemic, El-Sayed wrote: “My classmates in Oxford taught me more than I could learn in any classroom.” And in several articles El-Sayed wrote for the Guardian, he expressed an appreciation for Britain and, in particular, its political system.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

In one piece, where he declared that UK democracy had the “upper hand” on the US, El-Sayed expressed his awe at a parliamentary hustings in Tower Hamlets, east London before the 2010 general election where all of the candidates were of Bengali heritage, reflecting the demographics of the local area. He opined: “As an Arab-American, the likelihood of ever having the opportunity to vote for an Arab-American candidate for national office during my lifetime is minimal.”

But this week, he did have the opportunity to do so, being able to cast the ballot for himself. He was joined by more than 2.5 million others who followed suit and elected El-Sayed as the country’s first Muslim senator.

Rothblatt is “very excited” to see what El-Sayed will do in the Senate. “I think he’s going to do a fantastic job. Back then, he was a talented, ambitious person who had some really good ideas about what he wanted to do in the world. Now he’s continuing to bring those to life,” he says.

‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how Ted Scheinman finally broke through his depression

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

Troubled from the age of three, by 35 the American journalist viewed himself as ‘the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth’ – and neither therapy nor drugs seemed to help. But there was one thing he hadn’t tried …

Ted Scheinman can date the origin of his depression with laser accuracy. It was the day he went to the fair, aged three, and returned to his home in upstate New York clutching a Batman toy that he’d won. In the bathroom, he swooped his new doll over the sink. Scheinman had a vivid imagination; in a few years, he would want to become a playwright. To add sound effects and drama, he turned on the tap. There was a whoosh – and the unthinkable happened. Water landed on Batman’s pristine boot in a darkening, enlarging spot that for young Scheinman triggered several rapid thoughts, the last of them being: “I am going to die.”

Now 41, Scheinman, a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine, has written a memoir of his “life as a depressive”. Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness charts his path from toddlerhood to the point in 2020, at the age of 35, when he referred himself for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). By then, he was in “a much darker place” than he had ever been – and regarded himself as “the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth”. The treatment was “not so much a last resort … as my only hope”, he says.

Jolt is really “a view from the other side of the tunnel”; a travelogue – which somehow manages to be amusing – of the journey towards an experience that for many remains taboo. During ECT, an electric current passes through the brain, triggering a brief seizure. In those seconds, affected neurons fire simultaneously and repeatedly, triggering the release of neurohormones and neurotransmitters (such as dopamine). Despite the treatment being steeped in horror – as in artistic depictions such as One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and The Bell Jar – Scheinman’s main worry was that “it wouldn’t do shit for me”.

Literary references are never far from view in Jolt – or in Scheinman’s life, for that matter. They were there in utero: his mother assumed he’d be a girl and planned to name him Jane, after the novelist Austen. (His younger sister acquired the name a few years later.) Bookishness pervades Jolt and, fittingly, on our video call, Scheinman sits before a row of bookcases.

“Write this down!” his mother kept saying before he was admitted to the psychiatric ward of Sibley memorial hospital in Washington DC in 2021. “This is great material.” They’re perhaps not the words many mothers would offer a child about to embark on ECT. “It might sound sort of clinical or heartless,” Scheinman says, “but it was the opposite.”

His mother, who died last year, was a professor of English at Colgate university in New York, specialising in 18th-century English literature. (His father was a doctor and medical researcher.) What does Scheinman think she was trying to tell him? “If you could make meaning out of this … you would have power over it. Or at least, a sense of agency within the illness. She knew who I was,” he says.

From Jolt’s title on, of course, the reader knows where this memoir is leading – and maybe, somewhere in his head, that’s how Scheinman felt, too.

“Sympathetic portraits of people with mental afflictions were very common in our household,” he says. “I think I heard about ECT very, very young.” Some of his mother’s friends had benefited from the treatment. And she held a correspondence with Alan Bennett who, in 2006’s Untold Stories, describes the effects of ECT on his own mother as “a miracle”.

At dawn on 12 May 2021, Scheinman was taken for his first treatment. Having the electrodes attached to his temple was scary, he says, “but the fear almost felt distant because I was pathetically hopeful”. Actually, more than hopeful: “I felt this intense sense of need.” Because if it didn’t work, what then?

“It’s such a dramatic thing, right? You go on this table, you picture yourself convulsing more than you will. And if you’re lucky, you get up after however many treatments and walk out a changed or restored person … I was attracted to the sheer apparent extremeness of this treatment.”

Perhaps the extremity implied an ending that, in turn, implied a solution. In any case, Scheinman can recall lying on the hospital bed, the squeeze as the blood-pressure cuff tightened around his left ankle, the prick of the needle administering general anaesthetic, and the pervading sense of relaxation bordering on euphoria as he tried to count down from 100 in line with the anaesthetist’s instructions. He remembers exclaiming “Oh boy!” and waking with a headache. But what happened between those moments, the “jolt” – nothing like the arching back of cinematic portrayals, a mere twitch of his left big toe – remains “a black box”.

What he does know is that at some point over the five months of mostly outpatient treatments – 11 unilateral, 14 bilateral (meaning that electrodes were applied to both temples) – his illness began to improve. His friends, driving him to and from the appointments, noticed before he did. For about 18 months after the ECT ended, he felt “much better than I realised I could” – and the next year, better still. Now, five years on, “I feel more myself than I have felt in years. Most of my days pass without depression.”

Scheinman qualifies this: “I mean, I do still consider myself a depressive.” His fondness for verbal precision makes him prone to self-correction. “According to my history, by the diagnostic and statistical manual, I am a major depressive.” Prior to the ECT, he was diagnosed with agitated depression with bipolar characteristics. “But the further and further I get from the worst of 2020 and 2021, the happier I get, the more settled.” In May, he got married (to Tara Ganapathy, an attorney specialising in congressional investigations).

In a funny way, Jolt reads like a coming-of-age story with a zany timeline. Scheinman was such a precocious intellect that he seems to reach graduate-level discourse by age six, then spends years waiting for his body, wardrobe and emotions to catch up. “I felt marooned between being a tiny adult gentleman and the big feelings of a child,” he says. The book is full of descriptions of young Scheinman dressed in his grandfather’s hand-me-downs, old before his time. Today, although he’s wearing a Patagonia fleece, his assertion that he has gone “full hippy” itself sounds a bit tweedy.

Some of Jolt’s most comedic – and disturbing – moments come from the dissonance between his biological age and his mother’s parenting of him. When, for instance, Scheinman enters a germophobe phase at elementary school, she warns him: “You’ll have a very disappointing sex life if you go on like this.” Another time, she soothes his tears with the words: “A lot of sensitive and creative people have a period of depression.” To which six-year-old Scheinman protests in anguish: “But that’s such a cliche!” He was thinking of consumptive Romantic poets, he says, which surely alienates him from many first-graders. Does he feel any regret at not having been a more childlike child?

“I think that would have been really nice. I probably would have had a little bit of a smoother go of it,” he says. “If and when I raise a child of my own, I’m really going to try to give them a properly delineated childhood. I’m going to be very careful about not even hinting that there’s an expectation or possibility of being too precocious.”

“Delineated” is a telling choice of adjective given how the boundaries between Scheinman and his mother vanish as the memoir goes on and his parents’ marriage declines. They separated while Scheinman was at college, at which point his mother’s phone calls intensified. “Often, it seemed she didn’t wish to listen so much as talk and be confirmed in her martyrdom. So I confirmed it,” Scheinman writes.

His father is the book’s more classic villain: he had an affair, but beyond that, his blithe optimism appears to grate on mother and son. Scheinman professes much less tolerance of his father’s shortcomings than his mother’s overcomings, and in Jolt’s most moving scene, he shares a heartfelt, peacemaking boat ride with his father. He gets “goosebumps” just talking about it.

“I kept doing gradations of forgiveness and acceptance with my father,” he says. “We were never estranged. But that’s very different from having a true, frank, uncluttered relationship.” His father has read Jolt four times and is, says Scheinman, “a big fan”.

Alongside his depression, the book shows Scheinman to be not only functional, but successful. He gets his growth spurt, excels academically, wins parts in plays, has friends, girlfriends, a place at Yale (to study English and classics), does a PhD and becomes an academic before pivoting to journalism. He wrote his first book, Camp Austen: My Life as an Accidental Jane Austen Superfan, in his early 30s (his mum called it “a Mom-oir”).

“I think that overachieving is probably bound up with my particular flavour, or flavours, of mental disorder, which is trying desperately to do all the right things or just anything that could get you internal forgiveness or internal peace. Or to get some laurels and be like: ‘Well, now I can rest on these,’” he says. The book shifts between these drivers with a perennially unquieted self-questioning that feels both exhaustingly dramatic and quotidian.

Scheinman tried many treatments before arriving at ECT. He had his first talking therapy at the age of eight – his father’s suggestion – and further courses followed over the decades. There were drugs too, recreational and prescription. He self-administered alcohol, ran cross-country. And although ECT was “a last resort”, he now wonders if it’s necessary “to wait quite as long for people who are really in straits”.

No one knows exactly how the treatment works – whether the shock or its aftermath causes the “reset” effect. In 2023, the Royal College of Psychiatrists reported that of 1,835 patients to have received ECT in the preceding 12 months, 68% were found to be “much improved” or “very much improved”. According to the American Psychiatric Association, 70-80% of patients experience substantial improvement after ECT.

However, the treatment can cause memory loss. Scheinman struggles to access stretches of memories during the ECT course, “as well as significant stretches of the six months leading up to those treatments” – gaps that must present a challenge to a person’s sense of continuous selfhood. So does he feel his treatment restored or changed him?

“I think restored is probably closer to the mark,” he says. Later, he emails to say that his reply may have been “overly glib”, and that the process of writing the book, which entailed many hours of interviews with friends and relatives, as well as scouring medical records and diaries dating back to when he was five, “ended up helping profoundly”.

“I’m still myself!” he writes. “I just feel less trapped by myself.”

About a year ago, he unpacked his hospital “go-bag”. “I stand ready to go back under the electrodes if I have to, and I’ll do it quicker this time,” he says. “Without engaging in any horrible recovery cliches” – I can’t help thinking of his harrowed six-year-old self, when he says cliche – “I’m keenly aware, especially because I now have a wife whose life I don’t want to make difficult or unhappy, that I might need ECT again. I don’t try to evangelise for it in any way, but one of the things that surprise people is that I wish I’d gotten it sooner. I really think I would have lost fewer memories.”

He has informally coached a few people who are considering ECT, and is in the process of volunteering through the National Alliance on Mental Illness “as a person who can be contacted”. In the meantime, he has belatedly begun meditation. He stays active with what he calls “a reasonably strict regimen of exertion and movement” and plays music “as though it is a prescription”.

“I try to live very, very fully,” he says. “I feel like my sense of adventure is back.”

Jolt: Depression, Memory and My Electric Journey Out of Darkness by Ted Scheinman is published by Wildfire (£16.99). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Monica Dolan looks back: ‘I was repulsed by Rose West, yet I had to work out what made her tick’

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

The Bafta-winning actor on her toughest roles, teenage crushes, and the joy of finding her people at drama school

Born in Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire, in 1969, Monica Dolan is a TV, film and stage actor. She trained at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama and won a Bafta for her portrayal of Rosemary West in ITV’s Appropriate Adult in 2011. She won the Laurence Olivier award for best supporting actress for her role in the West End production of All About Eve in 2019. Her other television credits include Mr Bates vs the Post Office, W1A, Sherwood, Alan Partridge: Alpha Papa, and Smoggie Queens. She stars in Onwards and Sideways, in UK cinemas from 6 November, ahead of its release on BBC iPlayer later this year.

That’s me staging a puppet show with a Waldorf Muppet, my head poking through the very 1970s-looking hatch in our house in Woking, Surrey. There’s a somewhat neglected Sindy on the side. I think she was an ice-skating one – I wasn’t massively keen on dolls, but I liked that you could move her legs around quite acrobatically, and if you bent her knee too far the plastic would snap and a wire would poke through.

I was teased for having chubby cheeks a lot at this age, and it was right before the dentist sent me to get the gap in my teeth closed in hospital. I could have been Madonna if I’d kept it. Or maybe I’d have never got a job as an actor.

I wasn’t one of those extrovert performer types as a child, but I remember recognising how useful having a sense of humour was in terms of connecting to my family, especially as I was the youngest of four. Once, after my dad had sent me to my room for being naughty, I decided I would come downstairs in my red dressing gown. As I strode through the door I did a few karate chops and delivered some lines from Hong Kong Phooey, the cartoon I liked to watch after school. The whole family laughed. Dad might have even laughed a little bit, too. It certainly made it harder for him to carry on being mean.

My teen years were complicated. People at school were forming groups, and I was never that sort of person – I was more of a satellite when it came to friendship circles. I wasn’t into boys in the way that the other girls were. I’d get massive crushes on some poor person but always from afar. But I was quite a joker as well – someone who was outspoken in class. It didn’t always go down well, and I am sensitive, so it wasn’t easy being told to stop talking.

My parents met at University College Dublin while studying sciences. There was a certain expectation that I might follow in their footsteps, because science was so important to them – basically, Mum thought if you didn’t study science you weren’t very bright. When I was choosing O-levels, they had filled in a form and underlined my options for me: physics, chemistry and biology. When I saw it, I absolutely blew my top. They came to my room to talk to me and genuinely couldn’t see why they’d done anything wrong. I said to Dad, “This is a life decision. It is like getting married. It should be mine to choose.” Eventually he said he’d Tipp-Ex it out. I did end up doing those subjects, but I wanted it to be my choice, not theirs.

In contrast to my school days, university was a place I flourished. I had finally found my people. I was in my final year when I met an agent. I asked her, “What should I do if I get a job before I leave drama school?” She said, “Well, that’s not going to happen to you.” Anyway, it did. I’d met the head of Northcott theatre, in Exeter, who offered me a season there. We did a variety of plays, everything from Outside Edge to To Kill a Mockingbird and The Merchant of Venice. My parents came to see me in all of them; they were so supportive. Even Mum, who found a lot of cultural things a real chore.

After that I had quite a long period of unemployment. I sat around and got impatient. Then I went back to Guildhall to be part of someone’s final‑year production. My agent wasn’t very pleased – he thought it was a bad look for a new actor to go back to university to work free of charge. I said, “Well, you’ve not got me anything. And I want to do something.” I was right because, to return the favour, the Guildhall told me about a director who was looking for people for their production of Jane Eyre. They said they’d make sure I got an audition. I got the part. That was the start of everything.

When I worked with Mike Leigh on Topsy-Turvy, he would get cross if you referred to your character as “I”. “Always call the character she or he,” he’d say. “They’re not you!” It was releasing, because acting can become very involved. But it wasn’t until I played Rose West that I understood how much that distance matters. I was repulsed by her, yet I had to work out what made her tick and what her priorities were. So I got the transcript of the case from her solicitor and treated it like a play, focusing on the technicalities. That let me stay objective and at a distance.

after newsletter promotion

Even so, after that performance I was a bit of a husk. A bit rubbed out as a person. When that happens it’s important to remember basic things that you like, to keep you connected to who you truly are. For me that was getting a dog. Having a dog is earthing, as they live in the moment and you have to go out for a walk every day, to spend time with this being who isn’t bothered about what’s going to happen next. As I’ve got older I’ve realised you shouldn’t work all the time, either. Dad helped me with that. I told him I was unemployed and he said, very firmly, “No, you’re resting.”

I’ve played a lot of characters who are real people. It is probably awful to admit, but I’ve never thought in terms of disappointing them. But I can’t pretend that I don’t get very nervous, particularly when I played Jo Hamilton [the subpostmaster in Mr Bates vs the Post Office]. When we did the first screening, the subpostmasters were there, people who felt so broken by what they’d been through. I thought, “What if they just think, that’s not me; that’s not my story at all?” There were real‑life consequences, and I felt a lot of pressure.

The stakes are lower with comedy but it is still demanding. There’s nowhere to hide if the timing’s not right, and it can be humiliating. One day shooting W1A, I was on take 11 of a scene and [writer and director] John Morton was clearly thinking, “This still isn’t right” while I kept thinking, “What am I doing wrong?” I got there in the end.

One thing that’s remained a constant is how much I care. The girl in the photo wanted to have an effect on people, to make people laugh. If you look closely at her, there’s a little bit of hope – something eager to be liked. I still feel that now. A need to entertain. To be seen. That seven-year-old is trying to make a difference and so am I.

My ideal man? I’ll take a carer over an adventurer, any day

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

Is it ever OK to leave your family – including small children – to live in the wilderness or walk around the world?

The latest season of Alone – the US TV competition in which cocky survivalists are dropped into a remote, inhospitable wilderness only to be rapidly humbled by squirrels and their own colons – has just ended. I love Alone. The landscapes are spectacular and their implacable hostility to humans obscurely cheering; plus, I get real atavistic satisfaction from watching my favourite contestants make shelters or manage to trap rabbits (grim, but at least every scrap of every creature is usually used – someone even ate a hare’s partially digested stomach contents once). I’m also gripped by what it says about being a man.

Obviously, the contestants aren’t all men, and anyone who goes on a survival show confident they can outlast 11 others living off shrews and moss is a particular personality type. But they are mostly men and it’s striking how many seem better equipped to tackle starvation and grizzly bears than “experiencing emotions” or “being a father and partner”. Contestants are always suddenly remembering, filthy and shivering, that they have families and agonising over what to do about it. On day three this time (spoilers ahead), David, a man with a baby back home, tapped out – Alonespeak for admitting defeat – declaring: “I know the kind of father I’m committed to being; a good father doesn’t take days off from that.”

He got there fast: it usually takes chaps weeks of self-inflicted suffering and near-fatal constipation to reach this revelation; some stick it out whatever the physical, mental or relational cost. Towards the bitter end this time, another contestant talked about missing his son, and fatherhood. “I think about my relationship with my dad growing up and I get this sense of just … absence,” he mused. “If I want to be a better dad, how about just spending more time with your son?”

Then he stayed, because Alone was “an amazing opportunity to be able to have a body of work he’ll always be able to look back and see”. (Has anyone on a reality show who says they’re doing it so their kids will be proud actually met a child? They’re not proud: they’re pissed off you can’t take them to netball.)

A third miserable, cold, hungry man talked about wishing he could talk to his estranged wife and how they were trying to work things out, concluding: “We have to suffer.” Do we, though?

It’s unfair to extrapolate this from a handful of hardcore survivalists, and of course the massive potential paycheck ($500,000) skews their thinking. But that adventurer ideal of manhood – the notion that there’s admirable, selfless nobility to being away from home, facing physical challenges – serves no one well. There’s an obvious parallel with Karl Bushby, whose recent return to Britain after walking round the world for 28 years garnered only a partial hero’s welcome. Many expressed discomfort at lionising a man who abandoned his family for decades. I’m always baffled by mountaineers with families taking on deadly peaks; the same self-destructive impulse has inspired a meme about cave divers with loving wives and three children choosing to squeeze into high-fatality-rate crevices.

This isn’t most men. Fathers do more childcare than ever before; they’re present and involved and regularly express a desire for more family time. But it’s an ideal of manhood that won’t quite die: in March, research from King’s College London found 21% of gen Z and 19% of millennial men thought men engaged in caregiving were “less masculine”. Anecdotally, I often hear about men taking on extreme physical challenges with pregnant partners or new babies at home. Guys, just wait till you try the punishing physical and mental challenge that is amusing a toddler and comforting a colicky newborn on 13 minutes’ sleep!

Partnering and parenting are about presence, time, attention. “Talk to anybody on their deathbed and … all they want is time,” David mused, abandoning the wilderness. It seems a lot more admirable to me to stay home and put in those boring, precious hours. My stepfather did – he looked after my sister as a baby, nappy pins jangling from his belt loops, and he’s been quietly there for both of us over decades. I reckon that makes him a better male role model than any Alone warrior.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

‘I just got AI emails rejecting my application – or no reply at all’: this is the soul-crushing reality of being a Neet

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 13:27:33 GMT

Alan Milburn describes them as a ‘lost generation’. Those I spoke to just want to know what they have to do to finally get a job – and a chance in life

Callum Atkinson is 23 years old, and lives in the Greater Manchester town of Rochdale. Until very recently, he was one of hundreds of thousands of young people in the UK reckoned not to be in education, employment or training: what officialspeak rather coldly terms a Neet, and therefore part of a huge national problem being investigated by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn, whose final report on young people and work is due any day now, and will be a big, hyped-up political event.

Milburn – quite rightly – thinks the UK’s estimated 981,000 Neets represent the profound risk of “a lost generation” and a “moral crisis” that is already upon us. If you are interested in matters of finance as well as ethics, you may also be aware that the annual cost of maintaining such young people was recently put at £125bn, which is more than the British state spends on either education or defence.

Until a month or so ago, Callum told me last week, he was one tiny element of those statistics. He has three A-levels graded at A, B and C, respectively in maths, further maths and computer science: although educational failure is a major factor in the current crisis, 21% of Neets have at least one A-level or its equivalent, and 15% have graduated from university. What his life so far does point up, however, is the labyrinthine lunacy and callousness of the modern labour market, and how its serial failures are often only finally mended by small, ground-level organisations.

Six months ago, his last spurt of employment – working in finance, “organising invoices, making sure suppliers got paid on time, doing Excel reports” – lasted three months, before he collided with problems in his personal life and fell into a spell of depression. When he was let go by his last employer, he was put on universal credit. Most days, Callum told me, he sat in bed applying for jobs using his phone. “Maybe 600 or 700 at least. And the most I usually got back was an AI email saying, ‘I’m sorry, we’ve decided not to go through with your application, please try again next time.’ Or there was no reply at all.”

And so to some good news. Not long ago, Callum was pointed in the direction of a new Manchester-based charity called Breakout. The people there arranged mentoring sessions and work experience placements. He is now an undergraduate at the University of Salford, studying computer science and artificial intelligence – but what his life experience so far seems to have left him with is only the vaguest sense of his own future. When I asked him for his thoughts on the subject, there was an uneasy silence. “My plan is just to get through university,” he eventually said.

Breakout was founded by Roman Dibden, a spirited 30-year-old who himself has experience of being a Neet. When we spoke last week about the Milburn review, he said he had one big concern: that the kind of outsourcing corporates who tend to land government contracts would be the main beneficiaries of its recommendations. The fact that Milburn wants local authorities to deliver his recommendations, Dibden said, may well force such companies into a cosmetic reinvention: “My fear is that will see the same big providers putting on a grassroots badge and carrying on like before,” he said. “But these are real human lives we’re talking about. We need people who actually get it.”

Humanity, however, is a waning factor in the UK’s increasingly bamboozling jobs machine. Dibden told me he was getting an increasing sense of recruitment systems in which applications written using AI are then robotically read by machines that respond with automated knock-backs, a process that renders trying to get a job about as meaningful as buying a scratchcard or lottery ticket. “People can give the jobcentre evidence of so many hours of job search because they’ve scattergunned it out,” he said. “But it leaves young people completely at their wits’ end.”

The day after that conversation, I spoke to another 23-year-old on Breakout’s books: Raihan Ali, who last did any paid work at Christmas in 2025, when he temped at a discount store for 16 hours a week. Like Callum, he is no academic slouch: though the pandemic meant he didn’t sit any formal GCSE exams, he got the second-to-top grade – an eight – in maths and combined science, and a B and two Cs at A-level in maths, physics and chemistry. Once he had decided to take a vocational rather than academic post-school route, it took him nearly a year to get an apprenticeship, doing admin for a chemical company. He was paid £12,000 a year: soon enough, he realised that he wanted to get into accountancy, but an apprenticeship in that line of work lasted only a matter of months.

“It was kind of the dream job for me,” he told me. “But it was fast-paced; very demanding. And going in with basically little-to-no experience, I just couldn’t keep up. Six months later, I’m sat down with a senior manager and HR and they tell me, ‘We can’t keep you.’”

That rupture happened in early 2024. In Hyde, on the eastern edge of Greater Manchester, Raihan lives with his mother – who, like him, currently depends on universal credit – and two siblings, who are still in education. He has long felt a deep responsibility to provide for all four of his family. “I just thought, ‘Oh my God, what am I going to do now?’ I had money coming in, and suddenly there was nothing.” He then began a purgatorial two years of constant job applications, broken only by his brief spell of part-time retail work.

“I’ve just ended up thinking that the good things that have happened to me have been sheer luck,” he said. “And all the bad things have been more like, ‘Well, yeah, no one wants me. I’m not good enough for that.’” On countless occasions, he has been told that he was effectively the runner-up. “And that’s just a terrible feeling, because what can I do to make someone believe that I’m actually the one that they want, rather than always being behind someone else?”

I had two last questions. The first was about his Bangladeshi heritage, and a grim fact cited in the interim report Milburn published in May last year, which pointed out that although Neet rates for young people from Pakistani and Bangladeshi backgrounds run at just below the national average, total adult unemployment among those in the same category currently runs at three times the rate of those classified as white British. “I’ve worried about things like that,” Raihan said. “When they see the name ‘Raihan Ali’ on my CV, do they not actually want me from that alone? I try not to think about them, ’cos it’s out of my control.” He paused. “But yeah. Yeah.”

We were talking via Zoom, and I noticed another of my open tabs, a report about the Milburn review, which bluntly pointed out that our cash-strapped prime minister will “need to find billions of pounds more to fund employment schemes if he wants to get young people back to work”. On an invest-to-save basis, Burnham agreed with that suggestion last week; by Saturday, there were news stories about an extra £6bn.

After 45 minutes spent talking about a country that seemingly cannot offer a future to even some of its comparative achievers, Raihan hinted that from his perspective, one other thing was needed: deep change to some of the most basic ways in which our economy works. Did he, I asked him, have any faith that things might get better? “I think the solutions will just need to be, like, big enough to actually make a difference,” he said. “You can’t take small steps here and there, can you? There’s going to have to be a gigantic amount of change for anything to actually work.”

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

1-0 to humankind? US midterms vote puts AI, datacentres and the broligarchy back in their box

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 12:05:58 GMT

Election results appear to have turbo-charged an already growing social, political and financial market rethink about AI

‘AI clog’: UK battles onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints

Editorial: the AI backlash – Silicon Valley’s political power is cracking

Last week’s midterms may not have cowed Donald Trump, but they should be a wake-up call for the grinning tech broligarchs who lined up at his inauguration two chaotic years ago.

Clearly, the cost of living squeeze unleashed by Trump’s war in Iran was a big driver of the Democrat wave. But AI was also on the ballot – in many places, literally.

Dozens of measures calling for limits on datacentre expansion were passed. And elsewhere, reining in the unchecked expansion of the power-hungry mega-sheds was a rallying cry.

At a campaign event, the Texas senator-elect James Talarico recalled meeting a mother who told him the lights from the neighbouring datacentre were so bright, her son thought it was daytime in the middle of the night.

Whether the tech sell-off resumes this week remains to be seen; but the anti-AI sentiment evident in last week’s results appears to have punctured at least one narrative that was sustaining the market boom.

Every bubble needs a story, and for AI, one chapter involves carpeting the US in debt-funded datacentres, which will become necessary – and viable – as demand for the technology increases.

That looks a lot less feasible after last week. It turns out, chucking up hundreds of these humming warehouses, while simultaneously warning workers they may be superseded by an army of superhuman bots, is not great PR.

The public were meant to set aside their qualms, for the greater good that AI would bring the economy. But the positive benefits many people may derive from interacting with chatbots – the shopfront of AI for most of us – coexist with very obvious downsides.

Just to name a few: the sea of online slop; those pervert glasses; and tech firms’ insistence on shoehorning the technology unbidden into every app, platform and device – the latest example of what tech writer Cory Doctorow calls “enshittification”.

At the same time, voters have watched the leaders of the big tech firms become obscenely rich, while average consumers continue to be hammered by inflation. So perhaps it should not be surprising that the US electorate seems to have decided: enough.

Ultimately, all businesses in a democracy – even those embraced by the US president – have to operate within the bounds set by society. And the tech bros have done a terrible job of winning over the public.

Elon Musk’s approach in Texas, where he poured billions of dollars into trying to buy the electorate, just became a selling point for the Democrats.

It remains to be seen whether objections to datacentres are the start of a more radical shift in opinion that will eventually tame the tech companies, redolent of when Teddy Roosevelt swept into the White House at the turn of the 20th century to set about breaking up the oil and railway monopolies.

However, at the very least, the opposition seems likely to put the brakes on the hectic pace of investment in building out AI’s physical infrastructure.

And this shift seems to have accelerated a market rethink that was already under way. As Joe Maher of Capital Economics put it last week: “Sentiment towards the AI trade was already looking fragile and the US equity market was showing many late-cycle signs. As such, this [the midterms] could plausibly become the catalyst that leads to a more long-lasting unwind of the AI equity boom.”

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Two things can both be true: AI is a transformative technology that will bring welcome productivity benefits; but they won’t be big enough to justify current market valuations.

As the economist Dario Perkins, of TS Lombard, put it in a brilliant recent note, written in the past tense as if in the aftermath of a future AI crash: “What people who worked in tech and finance didn’t realise was that people outside the ecosystem – you know, regular people – just weren’t that interested in AI.

“Yes, it made web search easier (sort of); but contrary to the assumption in Silicon Valley, regular people were never going to use AI to organise their lives or ‘run workflow’. Tech insiders were living in a bubble – in at least two senses of that phrase.”

Perkins described the industry in late 2026 as essentially “$200bn in current revenues supporting more than $1tn in future commitments from just two companies [Anthropic and Open AI]”.

A reckoning was already in the offing, even without the intervention of US voters. The tech-heavy Nasdaq peaked a month ago; and a growing number of voices were sounding the alarm.

As just one example, the International Monetary Fund pointed last month to“growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and that “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.

The IMF highlighted the growing capabilities of lower-cost Chinese models and pointed to the circular financing that has become rife within the AI sector.

More recent reports have also highlighted a string of corporate AI users either slapping limits on staff use of costly products such as Anthropic’s Claude, or turning to much cheaper models, hosted on their own servers.

The datacentre backlash appears to have brought new focus to some of these pre-existing concerns. Whether the stock sell-off persists or not, opposition has thrown down the gauntlet for the AI lobby to prove what the tech can do for societies – including those well beyond the US – which are reluctant to accept the very obvious costs.

Zohran Mamdani has a mustache now. We cannot take this lightly

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 12:00:40 GMT

The once-bearded New York mayor has downsized his facial hair. Does it work?

I’ve battled with facial hair almost my entire adult life.

I started growing it early, turning me into a pubescent villain from a spaghetti western. I was told by my parents not to shave it off, lest it grow back more furious than before. I just had to walk around high school looking like a hungover bond trader, which did nothing for my popularity.

Once I hit proper adulthood, I grew a real beard, one that could effectively hide my chubby infant face. Now, I shave regularly, so that passersby don’t get a gander at my prodigious gray hair. Yes, my temples are whiter than the Lakers’ starting lineup, but a full-on Santa beard just exacerbates the problem. I am old, and getting older.

I could follow the lead of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and grow a mustache instead. Mamdani rose to political prominence with a thick, black beard. The mustache is like Teddy Roosevelt shaving his own mustache off and settling for a soul patch.

The beard made Mamdani’s already sunny face even more “cool dad” adjacent. It made him look both more rugged and somehow more approachable, like the most affable econ professor the East Village had ever known. But that nice guy beard is gone, replaced with a 70s-style mustache. I’ll be monitoring the situation for increased thickness, volume, and contour variation.

Whenever a public figure changes their look, it’s a shock. A famous actor goes blonde and it’s headline news for the gossip industrial complex. A new piercing or a bit of plastic surgery can launch a thousand memes. But a mustache is another thing entirely. A mustache evokes a very particular reaction, considering its association with retired baseball players, sleazy used car dealers, and 20th-century union-busting oil barons. On a politician, it’s a bit undignified.

Look, I’m no class traitor. I’m not fully anti-mustache. I believe in the working person’s right to a Tom Selleck special on their upper lip.

My father, an air force master sergeant, had a mustache for most of the 1990s. When he left home to go fight in the Gulf war, he had the ‘stache. He came back with it, plus a Tabasco bottle filled with Kuwaiti sand. Mustaches are in my blood. They’re my birthright, but I can’t even begin to dream about a world where I have one.

It runs counter to everything I believe myself to be – a man who can’t even figure out how to properly put air in my tires. I’ve tried to use a hammer on the wrong end more than once. I haven’t cleaned a single gutter in my entire life. For me, a mustache would be the lowest form of stolen valor. The only way I could be more disingenuous would be if I started dressing like Bruce Springsteen on the Born to Run cover.

I grant Zohran his mustache, even if I see him on MS Now and think for a second that it’s Bob Hoskins in a toupee. Zohran’s mustache isn’t even the facial hair of the year – that title goes to Oliver Reed in the recently re-released 1971 film The Devils. But it has grown on me (pun intended), and I accept his decision to alter his personal brand ever so slightly.

With that said, we must be steadfast in who we, as a culture, allow to wear a mustache.

John Waters is grandfathered in, as the filth-monger director without his wispy facial hair would be as sacreligious as all of his movies. Timothée Chalamet grew a mustache for Marty Supreme, but if he wore that thing permanently, I’d have to send him a strongly worded letter. Barack Obama with a mustache would conjure images of the bartender from The Love Boat. We must hold the line.

The mustache will always have blue-collar connotations. There are always outliers, but the vibe is the vibe. The mustache is powerful, it’s direct, and it is unequivocal.

As a tool of personal identity, it might be unmatched. If you have one, you are guaranteed to be “the mustache guy” in your circle of friends. Some people might even keep your number in their phone as “Mr Mustache”.

So, unless you can confidently go on Morning Joe and be called “Magnum PI”, then don’t do it. Don’t let GQ or some other style magazine pressure you into following the inevitable Mamdani-led trend. You are not him. You are not Jacob Elordi. Don’t make the decision lightly. Study, ponder, consult. Sure, you can shave off a mustache in a few minutes, but you can’t undo the damage to your social life if your facial hair flops.

You must accept this. You have to embrace it, otherwise the mustache will consume you. This is why I will never wear one. Mustaches wear you.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist
