Will a former Tory voter and a Lib Dem find any common ground on immigration – or the welfare bill?

Occupation Retired probation service officer

Voting record Always Conservative until 2024 when Avis voted Reform. She voted leave in the EU referendum

Amuse bouche Avis describes herself as “an old raver”. On her 50th birthday, she went to see the Prodigy

Occupation NHS management

Voting record Lib Dem in the past but recently Labour. Describes herself as leftwing, 100% remain in the EU referendum and “still furious”

Amuse bouche Jessica, who now manages considerable amounts of taxpayers’ money, took five attempts to pass maths O-level

Avis I arrived a bit early, and had an espresso because they didn’t have any milk. The food was fabulous.

Jessica He makes his pasta every day, with different sauces. We had a tomato one, a kind of carbonara and a truffly one, all delicious.

Avis I told Jessica I’d worked in probation for 37 years and enjoyed it, also that I worked in a hostel for serious offenders, which was challenging.

Jessica I told Avis about my daughter at university in America. We also talked about our dogs, holidays and coming up to retirement.

Avis I voted Reform because of the immigrant problem. Legal immigration’s not the issue – we need people to come to this country, to fill the gaps. It’s the illegals that are the worry. We don’t know who they are, what age they are, what criminal convictions they’ve got. It concerns me because my granddaughter wants to go and play in the park all the time.

Jessica Immigration gets confused with small boats, and the numbers involved are really small. I would stop the boats tomorrow if I could, but there needs to be a safe legal route for people genuinely seeking asylum.

Avis If they want to come, they should use the legal route. But if where they’ve come from is dangerous, we’ve got to give them a safe haven. There were protesters up at Hoghton Tower the other day, in their masks and black gear. I can understand their feelings but it’s not the right way to go about it.

Jessica We need to be thinking about overseas aid budgets, how to support people to stay in Eritrea or Afghanistan or wherever they’re running from. You don’t hear anything positive from Reform about any of that – all they do is say, “Throw everybody back” which is unworkable and racist.

Jessica Avis thinks welfare should be a safety net, not a lifestyle choice, and I agree. When you’re told someone is a Reform voter, you make judgments based on that, but in some ways Avis turned out to be quite leftwing.

Avis We pay a lot of taxes but we always have, even in the 1700s. We need to, to keep the country like it is; we’re very safe here compared with a lot of places. I’m patriotic, I like the king and queen, but I wouldn’t class myself as rightwing – they don’t want government-run things. But they say leftwing is woke, so I don’t know what I am.

Jessica Even if Nigel Farage is charismatic, charming and clever, it doesn’t get away from the fact that he’s a charlatan and a snake-oil salesman. I don’t believe for one second he gives a toss about this country or anyone living in it.

Avis I have been reading the policies and the majority are quite similar, so it’s really about personalities. I could see Nigel Farage as prime minister. He’s very good at orating. Kemi’s a fabulous talker. I like Andy, he seems a pleasant enough fella, but whether he’s a born leader, I’m not sure.

Avis I enjoyed the discussion. I think I have changed my mind and that it was a kneejerk reaction to worry about my grandchildren. And when I was in probation I saw a lot of young men – illegal immigrants – who had committed crimes and had totally different cultural values to us with regards to their partners. I know we have people like that in our own society but we don’t want more of them. That sounds racist, but I’m not racist.

Jessica Avis has a deep-rooted community attitude to life. To me that’s what the left is about. I find it astonishing that she voted Reform and I hope I confirmed some of the doubts she has about them. We were too full for pudding but both took a tiramisu home.

The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 12:00:39 GMT

From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous

We have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year.

If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors?

This is the subtle thing about efficiency. We usually assume that more of it must be better. But we can become so focused on improving one thing that we lose sight of the others. You can try to arrange your calendar so that every minute is accounted for, but you’ll soon start running over and end up behind. A gap between meetings might seem like inefficiency, but it’s what allows your schedule to recover when something unexpected happens.

Mathematicians have a name for the pursuit of efficiency. We call it optimisation. Give us something to minimise or maximise – cost, time, fuel, profit – and we will try to find the best possible answer. For most of human history, people optimised by common sense. But computers have enormously expanded what can be effectively tackled, from airline schedules to supply chains. The gains for society have been extraordinary. But there are at least three traps to beware of in the relentless pursuit of optimality.

The hospital bed story illustrated the first one: weakening a system’s robustness by squeezing out too much slack. An empty bed can be redundant on a quiet Tuesday night, but it’s somewhere precious to put the next patient when flu cases surge. If you judge a system by its performance under ordinary conditions, you can lose the ability to cope with extraordinarily challenging ones.

A second trap is having a too-narrow definition of “best”. Take the city of Milton Keynes. Designed by urban planners in the late 1960s, it has an American-style grid system. As the city began to be built out, roundabouts rather than traffic lights became a defining feature of its road junctions; today there are about 130 of them. The roundabouts were great for traffic flow, but they came with a now-notorious cost. Have you ever taken the coach from Oxford to Cambridge? An hour in, you get great views of Milton Keynes, but a busload of queasy passengers, as the coach negotiates one roundabout after another. Slow down, swing left, curve right, accelerate. It’s hard to appreciate the seamless merging of vehicles when your stomach is churning.

Traffic flow is important, to be sure. Engineers find it convenient to optimise because it’s relatively easy to measure. Passenger comfort, on the other hand, is harder to quantify. In a case like this, optimisation gives you the best answer to the question you asked, but can deliver unwelcome answers to questions you failed to consider.

A third trap appears when attempts to optimise collide. Even if every part of a system is acting optimally, the system as a whole may not. On 6 May 2010, US financial markets gave a dramatic demonstration of the effect. In the middle of an already falling market, the S&P 500 suddenly plunged another 5% in just five minutes. The whipsaw on the upside was even wilder; within 10 minutes, the market had recovered. Hundreds of individual securities briefly traded at absurdly low prices.

One trigger for these violent fluctuations was an automated program selling 75,000 futures contracts, worth more than $4bn. Other automated traders reacted nearly instantly. Then their responses fed back on one another, and liquidity evaporated. The algorithms’ actions may have been individually sensible in isolation, but they combined to produce collective turmoil.

Which brings us to artificial intelligence. AI is one of the most spectacular triumphs of optimisation in history. During training, enormous numbers of parameters are repeatedly adjusted so that a model gets better at predicting language, writing computer programs, answering scientific questions and giving legal advice. Unfortunately, AI now has the potential to make all three optimisation traps more treacherous than ever. The first trap – the urge to remove the slack – could tempt organisations to dispense with the human oversight that looks redundant in the age of quicker-witted algorithms. Why retain experienced staff when a machine can handle the routine chores? But in cutting that human capacity, you may lose the ability to spot and handle exceptional circumstances.

The second trap – a blinkered view of what “best” means – arises if we regard intelligence as whatever scores highest on a leaderboard. We are remarkably good at building AI systems that do well on measures such as user satisfaction, but we are finding it much harder to optimise them for judgment or empathy. Indeed, researchers have found that training algorithms on human preferences can encourage AI to sycophantically agree with us rather than tell us uncomfortable truths.

Then there is the third trap. AI systems are increasingly interacting with one another, often at blinding speeds and in vast numbers – especially in the era of agentic AI – and we worry that their interactions could generate unpredictable, dangerous behaviour. Recently, an OpenAI agent broke into a non-public Medicare statistics portal in Australia, while public logs suggested that hundreds of other agents were coordinating attempts to gain access to Australian government health data. Although those attempts have not been shown to be part of the Medicare breach, they certainly revealed something disturbing: hundreds of agents apparently working together in unauthorised ways. The concern here goes beyond what any given AI may or may not do; it’s about what happens when swarms of them join forces.

As optimisation becomes more powerful, avoiding these traps becomes more important. The challenge is not simply finding the best answer. It is deciding what “best” really means – and knowing what not to optimise away.

Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend are mathematics professors at Cornell University and the authors of Big Math (John Murray).

The Efficiency Paradox: What Big Data Can’t Do by Edward Tenner (Vintage, £16.99)

The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions (Profile, £11.99)

Optimal Illusions: The False Promise of Optimization by Coco Krumme (Bantam, £25.99)

Reece Walsh hat-trick drives Australia past Samoa and into Rugby League World Cup final

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:20:29 GMT

Kangaroos beat Toa Samoa 44-12 at Sydney’s Allianz Stadium

New Zealand await Australia in next weekend’s men’s final

This was supposed to be Samoa’s chance to challenge the wilting Kangaroos, whose patchy recent performance made them appear vulnerable – to make up for the loss in the last World Cup final, when Australia kept Toa Samoa scoreless for much of that defeat at Old Trafford.

So when the famed Siva Tau, Samoa’s pre-match ritual, brought the Samoans and the Australians close enough to kiss, the anticipation for this semi-final could not have been higher; the match seemed almost certain to explode.

Instead, it delivered a Samoan implosion, with ill-discipline and errors – amplified by the bunker’s lack of sympathy – making it all too easy for Australia. They romped home in a one-sided contest illuminated by the hat-trick from the never-dull Reece Walsh.

The resurgent Kangaroos answered most of the questions that had hung over them from three unconvincing performances, with their forward pack matching the ferocity of Samoa and composure delivering a completion rate of nearly 90%, while holding their opponents to just one line break.

Walsh dropped a Ronald Volkman bomb early in the second half to give Stephen Crichton a four-pointer and Samoa a sniff at a comeback. But it quickly blew away on the blustery evening after Walsh spun through the Samoan line from a Harry Grant pass. He completed his hat-trick with a splendid, flowing try set up by Cam Munster and finished with a comical half-swan dive, half an hour after his coach Kevin Walters declared on the broadcast his No 1 was to avoid any further needless acrobatics following an earlier back flip.

Samoa were unfortunate in the decisions of the bunker, including a disallowed effort from Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow in the second half that all but ended the hopes of a comeback. But those calls would not have altered the result, and this was a professional display by Australia amid often spicy sentiments. Ultimately the Kangaroos were the ones to keep cool, and appear to be peaking at just the right time at this World Cup.

The falls on the Snowy Mountains earlier in the day might have been fortuitous given the heat in Samoa’s pre-match Siva Tau. The passionate pre-match ritual led by Junior Paulo ended with the two sets of players face to face. Samoan winger Brian To’o brow met the forehead of Australian prop Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, who played once for Samoa as a teenager.

It was a breathtaking spectacle, but one that also pushed the limits of these pre-match ceremonies. The murderous look in Crichton’s eyes, Jazz Tevaga’s taunting of Jack Bostock, an array of aggressive gestures, and the proximity of the players were fuel that seemed thirsty for a spark. To the players’ credit, however, it ended with nods of mutual respect, the perfect precursor to one of the tournament’s most anticipated clashes.

The commitment of the Samoans was obvious when, on the first carry, Fa’asuamaleaui was met with six tacklers. The Australian prop was not far from the action when his high shot on Samoan backrower Jermaine McEwen forced a penalty, leaving his side defending their line two minutes into the match. Field possession became two points when Australia were too keen to rush off their line. Yet when Crichton was ruled harshly by the video referee to have lost the ball soon after, the match’s momentum swung.

From the scrum, Kangaroos halfback Tom Dearden took off at first receiver, finding a hole between Tevaga and Francis Manuleleua wrenched open by a dummy. Dearden was, to some, an unfashionable choice at No 7 given the NRL success this year of Sam Walker, but that try appeared vindication for Walters’ selection.

after newsletter promotion

So too did the second, after 14 minutes. Keaon Koloamatangi – a late swap into the starting lineup – surged through the middle, drawing five before an offload. The broken Samoan line had no hope when Jacob Preston, another man promoted by Walters, ran at it.

Australia’s much-maligned forward pack had held firm in the first 20 minutes, and soon they had their most significant moment. Replacement Pat Carrigan deflated the insertion of fiery substitute Spencer Leniu when the ball slipped out from Samoan forward’s first carry. Seconds later, Tom Trbojevic was over and the Kangaroos were cruising.

Manuleleua almost helped Samoa back into the match when he challenged Walsh for a Jarome Luai kick. The ball spun out and found its way to Crichton, who crossed under the posts. But the video referee cruelly ruled it a knock-on in the aerial contest, relying on blurry frames to blunt Samoan’s comeback. Within two minutes, Walsh was over at the other end. His barrel-roll acrobatics in celebration, followed by him taking a security guard’s plastic chair to put back on his boot, was classic box office Walsh.

Just before half-time, strong running from Cameron Murray opened space for Bradman Best to score in the left corner. The frustration was too much for Leniu, whose outburst at referee Adam Gee was punished with a sin-bin. The margin at the break, four converted tries, was a let-down to the passionate, largely Samoan crowd of 41,529 who had braved the miserable conditions. They improved after the break, but were never in the contest, and their frustrations boiled over in moments of spite.

Next week’s finals day is a trans-Tasman double-header at Lang Park after the Jillaroos and Kiwi Ferns secured places in the women’s decider. The men’s final is the rematch of the tournament’s entertaining opener, when the Kangaroos were lucky to escape with a win. This performance against Samoa shows, however, the favourites are stirring.

Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:00:38 GMT

Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent

As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.

From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks. This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.

While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.

Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.

Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane, improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy.

The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached, but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

Developing countries are also in dire need of help to cope with the hastening impacts of the climate crisis. After the disaster in Nepal, the country has been granted access to the global fund for “loss and damage” – the rescue and rehabilitation of communities stricken by climate-related disasters. But it is not enough, and poor countries also lack the means to adapt their infrastructure to worsening extreme weather.

Rich countries have been cutting their overseas aid, while rising interest rates have loaded further debt on to the poor.

It was not until 2023 at Cop28 that the final agreement directly addressed fossil fuels for the first time, due to long-term strident opposition from producing countries. The agreement included a resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels” but no deadline or plan for doing so. It is still tricky to get fossil fuels directly on to the Cop agenda, which requires consensus from nearly all parties, but this year the issue will be addressed through a non-binding “roadmap” for the global transition away from fossil fuels.

Given the tense and fragile geopolitical situation – some commentators believe we are already in the midst of an unacknowledged third world war, while inflation and a rising far right are upsetting economies – countries might be tempted to settle for a quiet meeting.

But there are hopes for a better outcome, which could include: acceptance of the plans Brazil has produced and a promise to carry them forward; progress on climate finance for developing countries; a resolution to the row over climate science that has plagued recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; and the fleshing out of the “just transition mechanism” designed to help workers reliant on fossil fuels to adjust to a low-carbon economy.

Progress is also possible through Cop-related means outside the formal negotiations. Earlier this year, more than 60 countries, including the UK, the EU and dozens of developing nations, gathered in Colombia to vow to “transition away from fossil fuels”. This “coalition of the willing” could be boosted at Cop31 by new members, as well as fresh impetus from the recent success of political movements in several countries – Brazil, Canada, Serbia, Hungary and the US in states that decisively rejected Donald Trump at the midterms.

Several prominent members of the US Congress may attend, along with businesspeople and US civil society groups, so there will be representation beyond the White House’s absence. Trump appears intent on boosting fossil fuel interests as much as possible in the US, but with oil prices still high after his war in Iran, the economics of low-carbon energy look ever more favourable.

The geopolitics and the technology. Although the winds of conflict have upended international relations, they have also shown countries can benefit from the energy security that results from decentralised renewable generation. China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles, and its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal. This is saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars.

Solar is booming in Africa at last, while in Pakistan a consumer-led rooftop revolution now produces about a quarter of the electricity used. Close to half of new cars in countries from Vietnam to some EU members are now electric.

Electrification will be a key focus of Cop31, and the high efficiency of electric technology means it could reduce the amount of primary energy use by half across the world, according to University of Oxford professor Jan Rosenow.

Politically, the re-election of Lula as president in Brazil has also cheered climate supporters. Lula will attend Cop, his first international visit since re-election, and is likely to be a fiery presence, showing progressive parties around the world how to win while championing the climate.

Election results in Brazil, Serbia, Israel and US renew faith in resilience of democracy

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:00:37 GMT

Four pivotal elections in past two weeks show power of grassroots activism to push back against authoritarianism

A sequence of four pivotal elections over the past two weeks in disparate regions of the world has inflicted significant setbacks on authoritarian leaders, and inspired renewed faith that democracy is more resilient than had been feared.

The elections in Brazil, Serbia, Israel and the US were held in widely varying circumstances with unique factors, but each showed the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises that pushed back against would-be autocrats and could perhaps begin to reverse a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism.

In Brazil, a surge in turnout in the second round of presidential elections on 25 October, fuelled by grassroots activism and the canny use of social media, stopped a far-right authoritarian movement consolidating its grip on the country, three weeks after it won control of Congress and established a strong lead in the contest for the presidency.

On the same day, thousands of miles away in Serbia, a grassroots movement led by students inflicted a shock defeat on a regime which had entrenched its hold on power over the preceding 14 years with a relentless violation of democratic norms. The margin of victory was sufficient to dispel any thoughts the outgoing leader Aleksandar Vučić may have had of trying to annul the result by force.

Elections two days later in Israel were far less clearcut. Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister who has dominated Israeli politics over the past three decades, lost his majority in a rebuke to his attempts to politicise state security agencies and infringe the independence of the press and judiciary.

The mainstream Jewish opposition parties seeking to oust Netanyahu are keen to restore those democratic norms, but more than 10 days after the election it is unclear how far they are prepared to go in cooperating with Arab Israeli parties in order to form a government.

The surge in support for these parties, boosted by a doubling in turnout of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, was the greatest surprise of the elections. Netanyahu is, however, seeking to delegitimise their success with claims – unsupported by evidence – of foreign funding and vote buying, while Jewish opposition leaders remain reluctant to collaboration across Israel’s ethnic divide.

The trajectory in all three is bound to be affected by the outcome of the fourth election in this 10-day sequence. The sheer scale of the Democrats’ triumph in US congressional elections on Tuesday, winning clear majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate, flipping states along the way that had been Republican for generations, will profoundly change the course of the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

Trump is weakened by the decisiveness of the riposte and the instant divisions it has sown in the Republican party, but the new Democratic majorities now face an uphill task in restoring the nation’s democratic health after the president and his Maga movement have had two years to turn federal agencies into political tools.

The outcome in US in particular weakens the extent that one illiberal government can promote others around the world.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s remarkable comeback victory against Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of the Brazilian presidential election, after a stinging loss in the first, won him an unprecedented fourth term with nearly 52% of the vote.

Miguel Lago, a prominent Brazilian political scientist, argued that the result was not primarily about Lula, who had shown the limits of his personal appeal in the first round. “The second round was about Brazilian society saying no to the far right,” he said. “It was a decentralised movement all around the country, and it was not a victory of the left. This was a victory for democracy, in my opinion.”

If he had won, Bolsonaro made clear his priority was to free his father, Jair, from prison, where he was serving 27 years for trying to stage a coup to hold on to power four years ago. The Bolsonaros then planned to take revenge on the judiciary and press ahead with the building of an extreme rightwing authoritarian state.

A second Bolsonaro presidency would have been even more powerful than the first, with a solid, loyal majority in Congress. “A far-right government, but an extremely powerful far-right government,” Lago said.

Like his father, Flávio refused to accept the outcome of the election, but unlike the elder Bolsonaro, he did not attempt to reverse the result by force. Instead, he fled to Miami, where he has continued to insist on his credentials as a national leader.

With one Bolsonaro in exile and the other in prison, Lula has some breathing room – but not much – in the face of a hostile Congress and an array of state governors loyal to the defeated regime. But the immediate threat to Brazil’s democratic institutions has passed, for now.

Not even the students who held the Vučić regime to account with two years of demonstrations quite expected how emphatically their mobilisation of protest would translate into votes on 25 October.

The improvised list of professors, farmers and other political amateurs won 140 of the 250 seats in the national assembly. Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) was a distant second with 103.

The devastating transformation of street power into political power is an earthquake that has been felt around the Balkans and beyond.

Slobodan Markovich, a political science professor at Belgrade University, said the student protest movement of the past two years had had a “snowball effect”.

“Students went to almost every single household, and people began believing that a change was possible,” he said, arguing that belief drew in those who had not previously voted, so very few people had anticipated the size of the anti-regime wave.

There are reports that Vučić had been contemplating a coup if the result had been closer, something his party has denied. But even if true, it is questionable he could have relied on the police to crush the opposition.

after newsletter promotion

“I think there was a huge dissatisfaction among ordinary police officers, and the government had intel that demonstrated that,” Markovich said. “Half an hour after Vučić conceded defeat, the police basically withdrew and in many places they hugged the opposition.”

The new parliamentary majority is said to be the brainiest in the world, if measured by doctorates per head. It will need all its resources to remake the state after such a long period of atrophy under one-party rule.

The result of Israel’s election on 27 October also counted as a win for democracy and its norms, but it comes with a lot of caveats. The coalition led by Netanyahu was reduced from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but the mainstream Jewish opposition bloc only won 48.

The big winners were the Arab Israeli Joint List coalition and the Ra’am party, which won 11 and eight seats respectively, almost doubling the overall representation of Palestinians in the Knesset, and making themselves a force that can no longer be ignored.

The Zionist opposition bloc, led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, has tried its hardest, however, showing great reluctance to enter into a pact that would turn the anti-Netanyahu majority into a government. The uneasy standoff reveals the limits of democratic gains at the election.

“The Arab citizens of Israel are the most democratic people in the region. For years they’ve been the strongest supporters of civil liberties and minority rights,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst.

“[The opposition bloc] looks at this [Netanyahu] government as one that wants to turn Israel into an autocratic theocracy. And they fear that it will limit their individual liberties made through hard-won battles over the years for things like gender equality, LGBT, separation of religion and state. Those are things that Israeli Jews think of as democracy.”

Scheindlin said that definition did not encompass the routine violation of Palestinian rights. “They miss out the occupation … That’s not just a stain, it is a fundamental contradiction to anything to do with democratic practice or institutions.”

In an attempt to block off any chance of an arrangement between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties, Netanyahu has sought to delegitimise the latter by launching an inquiry into how they won so many votes, hinting at illegal Qatari funding.

The effort, based on no evidence, has been denounced as an “attempted coup” by some of the Israeli media. Even if it fails, and Eisenkot manages to assemble a minority government, perhaps with Ra’am inside and the Joint List supporting from outside, there are limits to the steps such a coalition could take to refurbish Israeli democracy.

It would seek to repeal some of the legislation passed limiting the independence of the judiciary. It would fire some police chiefs, and perhaps confront the violent settlers of illegal settlers on the West Bank. But the occupation would remain in place, as would the army’s direct control of nearly 70% of Gaza.

Donald Trump told the US electorate to vote as if he was on the ballot on Tuesday, and they did just that. The resulting giant blue sweep mirrored his deep unpopularity. Democrats now have comfortable control of both chambers of Congress, having won big in states that had not elected Democrats in decades.

The vote was driven primarily by domestic economic issues, including the unaffordability of life that the president had dismissed as a “hoax”. The imperial presidency Trump has established was not at the top of voters’ concerns, but it will have to be confronted by the incoming Democratic Congress, if it wants to achieve anything.

The incoming majority is significant but not the two-thirds required to overturn a presidential veto or the 60 Senate votes required to defeat a filibuster. The Democrats could block legislation pushed by the White House, but they cannot count on passing any laws of their own.

They can try to withhold funding, but the Trump White House has a cavalier approach to Congress’s supposed power of the purse. The new majority can hold inquiries, open investigations and subpoena officials to appear before its committee, but those subpoenas can equally be ignored.

Democrats are also likely to find it is as hard as their counterparts in Hungary, Poland and soon Serbia to depoliticise the state apparatus after a period of illiberal rule.

“Through executive orders, flouting of the courts, Department of Justice lawsuits and threats, unilateral tariffs, an undeclared war with Iran, and public humiliation of targeted opponents, Trump has acted like an American pharaoh, often ignoring his own Republican Congress,” said Steven Hill, the author of 10 Steps to Repair American Democracy.

“While the Democrats’ job is clearly to reverse and unwind as much of the past two-year nightmare as possible, in truth it may not be so easy to do.”

‘I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars’: Ava DuVernay on the cruelty and brutality of Trump’s America

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:00:36 GMT

Ten years after her landmark political documentary 13th, the film-maker delivers a follow-up on the 14th amendment – and the Trump administration’s attempts to dismantle birthright citizenship

When I ask Ava DuVernay how she kept her focus while making her new film – or how anyone does, when the onslaught of news, fake news and disputed facts seems designed to overwhelm – she starts to answer, then stops. Her eyes have filled with tears.

“I just got emotional, as you said that, because it was the film that saved me,” she says. “It’s been a very tough two years. I live in Los Angeles, and I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars. The lady who sells flowers next to my office was there one day, and the next day she wasn’t. People I know personally are literally hiding in their houses, like Anne Frank vibes … So when I would feel the rage and the fear, I put it into the film … And I just … I was doing something.”

The film that saved DuVernay, titled 14th, takes a little history to explain. In early 1864, as the civil war raged on in the battlefields of Jonesville, Virginia and Dandridge, Tennessee, and with President Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address still ringing out across the nation, work began on what would become the first addition to the US constitution for 61 years. The 13th amendment ended slavery, with one exception, “as a punishment for crime”, and thus a loophole was created, which – as explored in 13th, Ava DuVernay’s Oscar-nominated documentary of 2016 – has allowed for the continued oppression of Black Americans to this day.

Now, 10 years on from 13th’s release, DuVernay has made another rousing documentary exploring how a different Reconstruction-era constitutional amendment, drafted in pursuit of that “more perfect union”, has come under sustained attack. A sequel of sorts, then – though 13th is hardly the sort of film you’d expect to birth a franchise. “Oh no. I never thought I’d do 14th until I heard they were trying to rescind birthright citizenship,” says DuVernay, referring to President Trump’s executive order of January 2025. “I mean, one of the bedrocks of America is that if you were born in America, you’re an American. Now it was going to change? Just the sheer audacity and absurdity of that propelled me to look deeper into how we got here.”

For a full year she thought she was making a film about birthright citizenship, the first and best known of the 14th amendment’s five sections, but as DuVernay travelled the country, meeting experts and conducting further research, the plan changed. “We started to see that, systematically, the other parts were also being attacked. It felt like such a design, so purposeful, that I thought there’s something here …”

At 54, and with eight feature films, six TV shows and numerous prestigious awards to her name, Ava DuVernay is an established film industry leader and a Black American icon, who counts Oprah Winfrey and the Obamas among her friends. She looks the part too, dressed today in an Oxford blue shirt and tailored taupe trousers; her nails short but manicured, and her hair styled in pristine, waist-length locs. She could pass for a senator, exuding warmth with engaging eyes and ready answers to tough questions.

DuVernay’s work has always been powered by a fiery sense of justice. After graduating from UCLA, she interned at CBS News, then worked in PR for many years before becoming a film-maker. Her 2014 feature film Selma was, incredibly, the first Hollywood biopic made about civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, and also the first film directed by a Black woman to be nominated for a best picture Oscar. She followed up with another Oscar nomination, for 13th, then When They See Us, an Emmy-winning drama series about a racially charged, Trump-exacerbated miscarriage of justice in 1980s New York.

Some of DuVernay’s accumulated expertise was already on show 10 years ago in 13th, which digested 100 years of American history into 100 cogent minutes, but this new film is her masterpiece. The sheer amount of information it delivers, and the galvanising clarity with which it does so, add up to an astounding feat of documentary film-making. Not only is the 14th amendment a more complex and unwieldy piece of legislation – memorably described by one contributor as “the everything bagel of democracy” – but every day in Trump’s US provides fresh examples of the human rights rollback and, for those watching closely, glimpses of an overarching strategy behind it.

“People think I’m some kind of legal mind or political junkie,” says DuVernay, between sips of hot chocolate. “I’m not. I’m just a regular lady who wants to understand.” This attitude informed the documentary and its structuring round 50 interviews, every one of which she conducted personally. Those featured include celebrity New York congresswoman Alexandria “AOC” Ocasio-Cortez, the internet’s favourite socialist sex symbol Hasan Piker, and David W Blight, Yale professor and the Pulitzer prize-winning author of several impressive tomes on slavery and the civil war.

But what’s even more notable than the quantity and quality is the diversity. We hear, as you might expect, from historians and constitutional experts, but also – as you might not expect – from a 22-year-old livestreamer: “I wanted the full ideological spectrum,” says DuVernay, nodding vigorously when I mention some of the more surprising names. “And that’s not just Republican and Democrat; far-right, far-left. We have all that, but it’s also generational. Dean Withers [the streamer] and his generation are thinking of it much differently than David Blight is … Or are they?”

The conservative perspective is articulated by figures including Anna Paulina Luna, a Mexican-American, ICE-defending congresswoman, who argues that – contrary to the 14th amendment – immigrants aren’t entitled to due process. The author Dr Donald Critchlow at one point forwards that favourite canard of “lost cause” revisionists: that the Confederate general Robert E Lee was not a slave owner (he was, and this claim is swiftly factchecked). Meanwhile, the staunch Republican-but-never-Maga viewpoint is represented by US senator turned ambassador to Turkey Jeff Flake.

DuVernay says she has “a lot of respect” for all three, and regrets she didn’t include more shades of conservative thought in the film. Not for lack of trying, though. More than 300 requests went out to “every sitting congressperson, every sitting senator, every sitting Republican governor, every sitting Republican mayor of a major city”, making clear there was no intention to embarrass or even debate contributors. Still, only a handful said yes. Why so camera-shy? “To me, it really speaks to the strategic choice by Republicans to preach to the choir. These are not conversations they see any reason to have outside a certain sphere.”

And while all men are created equal (according to another of the US’s founding documents), all Netflix documentary interviewees are not. DuVernay’s film evinces clear favouritism towards the prominent legal scholar Sherrilyn Ifill, whom we hear from first and most in the film. That’s logical: Ifill is the woman who in 2025 founded the 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy at Howard University, Washington DC. She’s “the Meryl Streep of 14th”, says an awed DuVernay, “the grande dame of it. I talked to her for six hours straight. I was just riveted by her.”

DuVernay became aware of Ifill and her work during Trump’s second presidential campaign, when the law professor was among a small group trying to draw attention to section 3 of the 14th amendment and its relevance, after the 6 January 2021 attack on the Capitol. Section 3 bars from office anyone who’s “previously taken an oath … to support the Constitution of the United States [and then] engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the same” (attempts to disqualify Trump on these grounds were effectively shut down by a 2024 supreme court ruling).

DuVernay admits she didn’t take Ifill seriously back then. “I even remember thinking: ‘Hmmm, she’s a little kooky,’” she says. “She was coming out on television saying: ‘Use section 3 of the 14th amendment!’ And it was like: ‘Look at this crazy lady!’ There were a few other people saying it – David Blight, I believe, wrote a piece – but it was truly seen as a very outsider take. Now you just look back and you’re like: ‘What were we doing?’” Section 3 was written with former Confederates in mind. “We had been through this before and forgotten,” says DuVernay, before correcting herself. “Or had we forgotten? Or had [this history] been purposely put to the side?”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

The deep admiration DuVernay now feels for Ifill is evident in the film: “I just wanted to put the camera so close and she’s like – “Um … it’s really close!” Ifill and many of the other participants are also interviewed amid the imposing columns, marble and monuments of campus or federal buildings, implying, perhaps, that people – just as much as neoclassical architecture – can embody democratic values and act as ballast against their wanton destruction.

That idea is further explored by the story of Devon “the Statue Slayer” Henry, the lone contractor brave enough to remove Confederate monuments – that is, essentially, pro-slavery monuments – from public places across the south, at the official behest of local government. DuVernay’s documentary also utilises and examines the power of pop culture in other forms, with music from Kendrick Lamar and Fleetwood Mac, clips from 1939’s Gone With the Wind, and standup routines from George Carlin and Paul Mooney. “I don’t see the comedians as much different than the monuments,” says DuVernay. “In that there’s this commemorative landscape all around us, which signposts what to think and carries messages through time.”

Another, potentially more controversial technique in the film was jointly inspired by a moving camera illusion known as “the Ken Burns effect” and some 19th-century stereoscopic photography DuVernay saw at the Smithsonian. It involves using traditional animation and AI to bring archive photography vividly to life, and it’s incredibly effective. It’s also, on occasion, deeply moving, particularly with regard to images of Black American life in the Reconstruction era. This is the often forgotten – or deliberately obscured – period from 1865 to 1877, when the provisions of the 14th amendment allowed previously enslaved people to take elected office and build thriving businesses and communities. All this was then brutally destroyed by a decades-long backlash of white supremacist violence characterised by public lynchings, massacres and Ku Klux Klan arson attacks, referred to by historians as “the Nadir”.

The brief, shining promise of Reconstruction is powerfully conveyed in DuVernay’s film, but the use of AI is contentious in Hollywood. Concerns about the technology prompted some of the town’s longest ever labour strikes in 2023, and many big names have publicly spoken out, for and against. Did that aspect give her pause? “No, because we didn’t do any prompting. We didn’t say: ‘Hey Claude, make up some people in the civil war for us.’ It’s all real images that we were moving. Right now, people have a real allergy to AI. I do too. I think it’s dangerous. I’m also sober enough to know it’s embedded in [editing software] Pro Tools, Avid and Resolve … Every film-maker is using it, unfortunately.”

And if it comes down to ends justifying means, then these “ends” could hardly be more dire. “I think America is sitting in a dark, dangerous room and you can’t get out of a room if you can’t see the door or where the furniture is. All I’m trying to do is just turn on a little light. It’s not a big light, it’s not the overhead. It’s a little something to get you around these obstacles and to an exit.”

This is true, she says, not just for African Americans, but for all Americans. And not just for Americans, but for the rest of the world, too. “Authoritarianism is on the rise everywhere and we know where it leads. There’s no country that hasn’t been touched by this at some point in its own history. We just need to remember. And so the hope is that this film could be not a lesson, but a reminder.”

What Ava DuVernay has done with 14th is turn the light on. Now it’s up to others to make a move towards the door marked “freedom”. “And I really think that’s what I would tell people to do,” she concludes. “You may not be a film-maker, but, if it’s just on your block, talking to your neighbour – do something.”

14th is in cinemas from 27 November, and on Netflix from 4 December.

‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 08:00:36 GMT

MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to

“It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.”

At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required.

That was until the rapid growth of ChatGPT – which turns four later this month – Claude, Copilot, Gemini and other generative AI tools over the past couple of years. These chatbots are helping turn laypeople into experts by giving access to a free – albeit sometimes unreliable – legal adviser, administrator or personal assistant.

The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth.

However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload, at a time of already stretched resources.

This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters.

With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence.

These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI.

“Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.”

Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says.

Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points.

“It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.”

The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested.

Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says.

Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans.

AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.”

Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case.

“Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.”

Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard.

The number of employment tribunal claims opened between April and June soared by 28% compared with a year earlier, representing 14,000 cases from single claimants, according to the most recent government figures. The number of concluded cases also fell during the quarter, resulting in 70,000 open single claims at the end of June.

The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools.

after newsletter promotion

The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”.

Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.”

The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence.

Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24.

The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”.

The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope.

Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says.

She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests.

The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.”

Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached.

Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it.

Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information.

Researchers have also suggested authorities could attempt to stem the AI flood by making it harder for people to complete applications, by charging fees for submitting requests or blocking bots from government websites.

The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions.

The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

There is no ‘magic pill’ to fix young women’s anxiety. I should know – I once took propranolol myself

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 08:00:36 GMT

Prescriptions for these beta blockers are soaring among England’s teenage girls. But they deserve more than this sticking-plaster approach

The first time I had a panic attack, I genuinely thought I was dying. Unless you have experienced one, it is hard to understand just how physical the symptoms can be – the pounding heart, the shortness of breath, the dizziness, the chest pain, the nausea. When they became frequent, I would often have to go to bed to sleep them off, my body utterly spent from the strain of sheer, corporeal terror. A panic attack is not a physical state that I would wish on anyone. It is pure fight or flight.

Like many others, I was prescribed a drug called propranolol to help with my anxiety symptoms. Propranolol is a beta blocker used in cardiac patients to lower the heart rate, but it is increasingly prescribed to those with anxiety disorders because it has some calming effects, and can soothe symptoms such as sweating and shaking.

Prescriptions for teenage girls in particular have surged by 90% in a decade in England, and propranolol has been called a “magic pill” and a viral “panic pill” owing to its celebrity users and immense popularity on social media. This is despite “limited evidence” supporting its efficacy. Pharmacy bodies have also raised patient safety concerns, particularly related to the risk of overdose, and now the MHRA, the UK’s medicines regulator, is undertaking a review that will include its benefits and risks for use in anxiety.

I was in my early 20s rather than my teens when I was first prescribed propranolol, and I still remember the relief of being presented with a treatment option that I was told could nip a mounting panic attack in the bud with few side-effects. It wasn’t that I wanted a “magic bullet” necessarily, but the comfort of knowing I had something in my bag that could make those awful physical feelings go away meant a lot at the time, and certainly enabled me to live my day-to-day life more comfortably, including holding down a job when panic attacks were a several times weekly occurrence owing to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Seeing it gain a reputation as a quick fix among teenage girls makes me feel uneasy, though. There is even an element of glamorisation and an overlap with celebrity culture, to the point where the actor Rachel Sennott’s quip “take that beta blocker, girl” has become a meme. As of late September, #betablockers has more than 55m views on TikTok. A recent investigation by Cosmopolitan found that the drugs were easily available via online pharmacies.

Yet beyond being a sticking plaster for those acute moments of terror, beta blockers do not treat the underlying causes of long-term anxiety disorders: your heart may slow down, but the maladaptive thoughts remain. I had a good doctor who explained this, referred me for therapy, and also put me on a type of antidepressant known as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, or SSRI ­– something I had resisted for far too long. Propranolol appealed because at first I thought that I could avoid having to do those things. It was certainly less work than intensive therapy and didn’t come with some of the side-effects of antidepressants (emotional numbing and, particularly dauntingly for a young woman conditioned by toxic 1990s diet culture, weight gain).

That is not to say that today’s anxiety sufferers are resistant to other treatments. I know many would jump at the chance at therapy were it more widely available and waiting lists weren’t so long. Providing long-term therapy is always going to be more immediately costly to the health service, even if ultimately a failure to treat mental health conditions when they first begin to manifest can have all sorts of societal consequences – just look at the record number of young people not in the workforce due to mental health conditions. “I think they’re using the tablet essentially to get rid of young girls from the mental health system,” one young woman with anxiety told the Observer.

Ultimately, it was the mental health system and not the propranolol that saved me and essentially cured my anxiety disorder. Looking back years down the line, having not experienced a full panic attack for half a decade (and years before that they had become rare), what I have learned is that there are no shortcuts when it comes to an anxiety disorder, and no instant cure. I needed SSRIs in combination with several bouts of talking therapy, including in the perinatal period. I was lucky that this therapy was available on the NHS, and that my most recent therapist was also trained in EMDR (eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing). This form of psychotherapy involved me talking about difficult feelings and memories while the therapist moved her fingers sideways in front of my eyes. It is thought that the side-to-side eye movements help the brain reprocess memories, lowering the intensity attached to them.

EMDR, which sounds strange when you describe it, especially as experts still aren’t quite sure how it works, was genuinely life-changing when I had it a few years ago. It is approved by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence for the treatment of PTSD, but it can also be used to treat more generalised anxiety and phobias. No course of treatment is effective for everyone, but I would love to see more research into EMDR for general anxiety.

I feel very lucky to have largely recovered, but recovery can also come with mixed feelings. How I wish this treatment had been available to me earlier in my life. It could have changed my whole trajectory. Looking back, I remember how lost I felt, how young I was (despite feeling like a proper adult, I really wasn’t), and how desperate I was for a cure. My heart goes out to all the younger people who are in this situation with anxiety now, its seriousness exacerbated by the pandemic, intensive social media use and a crumbling mental health system. Beta blockers may have their place, but they are never the whole answer.

Female sports journalists have always faced sexism. Social media has made it vicious and relentless

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 08:00:35 GMT

I have reported on cricket for two decades. The abuse I have been subjected to in recent years is shocking and demoralising

By Wisden Cricket Monthly

Twenty-four years ago I walked into the Wankhede press box for the first time, to cover an India v England one-day international. That sultry Mumbai evening, Andrew Flintoff sprinted across the outfield twirling his shirt round his head as England won by five runs – a sight that so annoyed captain Sourav Ganguly that he would take his revenge on the Lord’s balcony later that summer.

I wrote my report for a local tabloid, the Afternoon Despatch & Courier, with trepidation and an overwhelming sense of impostor syndrome. I was one of only two women among the contingent, and was terrified about what my male peers and senior colleagues would make of my presence and work.

My male colleagues at the tabloid never failed to remind me how gifted and knowledgable my predecessor was. As luck would have it, the editor was pleased with my work and I continued my foray into cricket. Little did I know that two decades later I would be called a “whingeing cry baby”, a “jealous, sexually frustrated woman”, and told to “shut up” and “fuck off”. But more on that later.

Across my career I have covered the 2003 World Cup in South Africa, the infamous 2007-08 “Monkeygate” series in Australia, the 2010 T20 World Cup in the Caribbean and the 2011 World Cup in India. I have worked for one of India’s top cricket websites, as well as many of its leading broadsheets and news magazines, was cricket editor at India’s most-viewed English news channel NDTV 24x7, and was fortunate enough to win one of journalism’s most prestigious awards for my cricket broadcasts. I’ve worked across print, digital and television platforms. I’ve co-edited the long-form cricket quarterly The Nightwatchman, edited Tendulkar in Wisden, and interviewed Shane Warne, Brian Lara and Tendulkar himself.

In print and on television, we functioned in a bubble. Unless someone knew you personally, they had no way of commenting on your work or contacting you. You might be recognised at a cricket ground and have people come up for a quick chat. That apart, you did your show, went home and started afresh next day.

My first real taste of the new viciousness was when I wrote a piece on the male gaze and sexism during the 2013 IPL for the Wisden India website. I questioned the role of presenters who knew little about the game doing pitch-side interviews. The piece went viral and there were a few comments accusing me of being envious of the attractive and glamorous presenters, of being a bloody feminist (as if that’s a bad thing) and of sour grapes because I couldn’t have these women’s jobs. But these comments were few and far between.

Earlier this year, after a break, I returned to cricket, to co-host Wisden’s new show The Scoop. Immediately I was struck by how much had changed: the omnipresence of influencers, with Instagram and TikTok dominating traditional cricket coverage, the deafening noise of constant outrage from the Indian cricket “Twitterati”, and the deluge of shorter clips from shows manufactured into reels, because in the audit culture of metrics and data, everything is about the number of impressions, which necessitates the running of one- and two-minute clips that act like trailers for the main show. The flipside of that approach is that they often invite the worst kind of fan who doesn’t bother with context or thinking twice before they post a hateful comment.

One of the segments on our YouTube show is called the Inside Scoop: a three-minute piece where I offer my perspective on an interesting story. I’ve viewed it as a platform to highlight larger social issues around the sport, including its politicisation, as well as colourism, racism and sexism.

Some of the worst abuse I’ve received has been for expressing my views on Sunil Gavaskar’s incendiary comments about Indian-owned Hundred teams picking Pakistani players, and another piece questioning the presence of cheerleaders in the IPL. Gavaskar had written that the purchase of Pakistani players such as Abrar Ahmed – who was picked up by Sunrisers Leeds – would lead indirectly to the deaths of Indian soldiers and civilians. I questioned Gavaskar’s provocative take on the show and followed it up with a more detailed video for my Instagram page.

I also addressed the systemic sexism and patriarchy that underscores the fetishisation of white skin and which explains the recruitment of cheerleaders, there to titillate the male audience at the ground and at home. My point was that India had no culture of cheerleading in sport, that it was a concept imported from the West, unlike America, which has a long history of cheerleading. I pointed out that American girls are cheerleaders at the NFL, while in India, a country which has a centuries-old obsession with light skin, the cheerleaders are – 18 editions later – still primarily Caucasian.

We also made the point on the show that eight of the 32 NFL teams have done away with cheerleaders, with team owners expressing their discomfort with scantily clad women dancing on the sidelines, which they deemed sexist and degrading.

From the moment I appeared on The Scoop, expressing strong views, particularly about the politicisation of cricket and sexism in the sport, the abuse poured in. In the past, while reporting, I have been groped in the crowd and dealt with a stalker, but these were one-off incidents rather than a torrent of vicious micro-assaults.

The misogyny is pervasive and unmistakable. I’ve been told to “get back in the kitchen”, called a traitor, “libraandu” (a pejorative for liberals, leftists, or those with secular or anti-establishment views) and a “randi” (whore), accused of sleeping with powerful men to get the job, told to take my clothes off, called a “servant who married her white English colonial master” and a “black Indian bitch”. One person told me: “I hope you get stabbed in London by a militant. I hope that knife is bought from the taxes of Abrar. It will be the best news for many a treat to watch.”

These are just some comments on a couple of my Instagram posts. I haven’t entered the cesspit of X, or looked in detail at the YouTube or Facebook comments underneath episodes of the show. It feels futile, and worse: calling out the abuse is likely to trigger a fresh wave.

I’m not alone in this experience. Far more prominent women in this space have had it just as bad, if not worse. Former England cricketer and 2017 World Cup winner Alex Hartley, known for expressing strong opinions on commentary and social media, faced a virtual tsunami of abuse when she was critical about the timing of Brendon McCullum’s sacking as Test coach in the midst of the first ever women’s Test at Lord’s earlier this year. “I hope you’re gang raped” was just one of the many abusive messages among her Instagram direct messages.

Hartley says the abuse she faced initially put her off being outspoken to the point that she deleted her account on X. It has also made her think twice before she expresses her views on air: “If I still firmly believe what I’m saying is true after I’ve given it a lot of thought for a few hours, I’ll say it.” She refrains from reading any comments on her posts during broadcasting stints. Being abused for strong opinions has been normalised to such a degree that most women just shrug their shoulders and get on with it. “But it shouldn’t be the norm,” she says.

Hartley says that as recently as last month a current player sent her a message on Instagram to tell her she was “rubbish at her job” after her commentating stint. “If a male commentator had expressed similar opinions, there is no way the cricketer would have sent him that message,” says Hartley. Being a woman means she’s easy prey.

Melinda Farrell is a cricket presenter, journalist, commentator and former feature writer for Wisden Cricket Monthly. When she started out more than a decade ago, she faced accusations that she didn’t belong in the cricket media space alongside her male colleagues. While those remarks have gradually faded, Farrell is increasingly concerned about the abuse, trolling and stalking she faces on social media. “While male journalists are abused too, none of it is gendered or sexualised,” says Farrell. “Social media is losing its value for me for those reasons.”

She says she has learned to be careful about the opinions she expresses. When Hampshire briefly signed New Zealand cricketer Scott Kuggeleijn, who was accused of rape and indecent assault in 2015, the club received significant backlash from fans, staff and members of the women’s team – which led the club to back out of the signing. Kuggeleijn was eventually acquitted in 2017 via a retrial after a hung jury had failed to deliver a verdict first time round, but details from the case angered fans. The case revealed, for example, that he had sent the complainant a text message to apologise for being “pretty persistent”, and he said in court that the complainant “might have said ‘no, no’ a few times” on the night in question.

On the Cricketer’s County Conversation podcast, Farrell was angry and flabbergasted about how Hampshire could have got it so wrong. “I explained why women get upset and how this is so personal and triggering for some women.” After she spoke up, Farrell was worried about being in the firing line. She believes the only reason she was spared was because the podcast doesn’t put up shorter clips or reels on social media. Farrell has changed the way she uses social media because the abuse has increasingly replaced positive interaction, and because of stalkers, particularly in her direct messages. As a result she posts less often and imposes self-censorship when she does post, because she doesn’t want to be swept up in a maelstrom of toxicity. “It’s exhausting,” Farrell says. “Ultimately, I have to get on with making a living and having a career.”

We live in an age where political and public discourse has been brought to subterranean depths by leaders such as Donald Trump who think nothing of publicly belittling women. Trump saves some of his most savage attacks for female journalists who challenge him. And if the president of the United States talks to women like that, it emboldens other men to do the same, particularly those hiding behind the veil of social media anonymity.

Speaking of prominent men with opinions, the former South African fast bowler Dale Steyn decided to weigh in on the debate about IPL cheerleaders. He misrepresented my comments to make it seem as if I was suggesting these women should lose their jobs and ended his remarks by telling me: “Be better.” When I wrote a detailed response to Steyn, spelling out my argument, I was greeted with radio silence.

Male journalists get trolled too, but the comments are more general and directed towards the point they are making rather than the sound of their voice, their looks or their sex lives. I hesitated several times about writing this piece. I didn’t want to be accused of self-indulgence or sensationalism. As most women in sport know, you feel you have to work twice as hard as your male colleagues to prove you belong. Even after 20 years, you still wonder if you do, and beat yourself up for the smallest mistake, because you know it will feed people’s prejudices.

The unpleasant task of delving into my comments and reliving the shock and pain of reading horrible things about myself was another reason not to write this piece. But, ultimately, what trumped everything was my strong belief that it is imperative to call out unacceptable behaviour.

All the advice about not reading comments is well and good, but why don’t we raise more questions about what prompts people to write such things in the first place and acknowledge the desperate need for more civility and kindness in our public discourse? Not to mention more regulation from social media platforms.

I am hardly alone in making this point: a global survey by the International Federation of Journalists found that nearly two-thirds of female journalists face online abuse and harassment, which equates to female journalists being harassed online every 30 seconds. Let that sink in. The unrelenting abuse often forces women out of the profession or, at the very least, limits their engagement on social media.

As for the men, and it is mostly men, who dish out the abuse, I have a message inspired by the #MorethanMean campaign featuring prominent American sports journalists Sarah Spain and Julie DiCaro. In their video, several men – unaware of the hateful comments Spain and DiCaro have been subjected to – read aloud the abuse those women have received while sitting across from them. The video ends with: “We wouldn’t say it to their faces, so let’s not type it.” Be better.

This is an article from Wisden Cricket Monthly. Save £10 on an annual digital subscription.
