Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:00:33 GMT

As AI exposes flaws in IT systems and geopolitics plays out on the cyber frontline, some experts say the events of recent weeks could soon be a common occurrence

Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd.

The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same.

As he approached his biggest unit, its defrost light also blinked on.

It was at this point that Pearce thought: is this a cyber-attack? He walked over to the box connecting the units to the internet and yanked out the cable.

He was right.

On the same day, retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported similar problems, with refrigerators and freezers in some shops soaring to as high as 50C (122F).

“If it had happened on a Saturday morning, when I don’t tend to be here, it could ultimately have led to a fire,” Pearce said.

But it is not just Pearce and a disparate group of retailers, as well as French blood banks, that have been suffering.

The hacking attack was one of three over a number of days. On 30 October, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, was robbed of $6.3bn (£4.7bn) in a record heist and on 1 November hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app, sending people in Kyiv a fake nuclear strike alert.

The official message after the fridge attacks is: expect more disruption. We are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said this week.

Referring to flaws in IT systems that are being exposed by AI technology, the NCSC boss, Richard Horne, said: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.”

He added: “The most serious risk we face in the short term is just a huge rise in the volume of incidents … and I think you could probably point to the last few months and say we’ve started to see that.”

Websites around the world were temporarily taken out of service as a precaution last month when AI technology from the ChatGPT developer OpenAI helped discover a flaw in PHP, a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. French supermarket fridges were also attacked last month in what could have been a trial run for the more expansive foray this week.

To Azeem Azhar, a tech entrepreneur and commentator, the way AI models were discovering flaws that assailants could harness recalled China’s Covid ground zero. This was, he said, a “Wuhan moment”.

Azar’s assertion headlined a Substack post that also quoted the cybersecurity executive Matthew Prince, who said last month: “We’re going to have a couple of years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

Not long afterwards, Pearce’s defrost lights went on.

There are two factors underpinning the NCSC warnings: geopolitics and AI. At least one expert has said the fridge attacks bear Russian hallmarks, while the Binance hack has been attributed to the North Korean state, and Russia is naturally a suspect in the Ukraine incident.

The NCSC said last week that AI-powered malicious software was “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028. AI would help attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, the organisation said.

But there are caveats. The NCSC’s director of operations, Paul Chichester, said the cold storage hackers “really didn’t need” to use AI to discover the fridge flaws because they were already out there, including default access passwords that were published in one fridge operating company’s manuals.

Sophos, a leading cybersecurity firm, said it had not seen any major incidents among its clients related to the PHP glitch, although – like others in the industry – it had seen a significant number of attempts to take advantage of the vulnerability.

And one expert said we had been here before. Ciaran Martin, the founding chief executive of NCSC, played down the “Wuhan moment” comparison. This was not the first time the world had faced a concerted threat, he said, pointing to the NotPetya and WannaCry cyber-attacks in 2017, which have been blamed on Russia and North Korea respectively, and a surge in ransomware attacks in 2021. North Korea, hobbled by sanctions and starved of cash, has a well-established reputation as a crypto hacker.

“It’s a bad run, but it’s not unprecedented,” Martin said. “The idea that we are having a Wuhan moment is not true. We are having one of those waves of incidents that happen every few years.”

Nonetheless, AI is exposing vulnerabilities. This is the term for a flaw in an IT system that a hacker can exploit, a door that is ajar and unnoticed or ignored by its owner. Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which has a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eight-fold.

Attacks have not increased by the same volume, however. The cybersecurity expert Tal Be’ery has speculated that criminal hackers are struggling to make money from these flaws, as shown by a recent decline in revenues from ransomware attacks.

“It seems that currently the surge in vulns [vulnerabilities] does not translate to a surge in breaches,” Be’ery wrote last month.

The fridge targeting is carried out by attacking the companies that provide operating systems for commercial refrigeration units. These systems are connected to the internet, giving the hackers a remote access route to the ultimate victims. The Danish firm Danfoss, one of the affected system providers, said most of the affected equipment was old and no longer received security updates. It said it had “long recommended” customers install updates or replace obsolete software.

The NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, said the hacks were a reminder of the vulnerability of everyday objects with internet access, from smart speakers to broadband routers. Ollie Whitehouse, NCSC’s chief technology officer, said this week it was “quite clear” that such devices could be “susceptible” to hackers. Manufacturers need to invest more in making their products secure and consumers need to be willing to pay more for the most robust products – and to keep updating them.

A key flaw targeted by hackers, including in the fridge attacks, is “end of life” versions of products that are no longer being produced by companies or receiving glitch-eradicating software updates.

Referring to the prospect of more attacks on internet-connected domestic devices, Whitehouse said: “To be worried, I think, is [too] strong. But we need to be more mindful, definitely.”

Pearce said he now realised his fridge monitoring system, by the US firm Copeland, which was installed in 2018, would need updating.

“Have we learned a lesson? Yes,” he said. “There is a vulnerability we probably should have been aware of, but luckily the ramifications for us were not severe.”

The need for mindfulness is heightened by the nation state threat. Criminal gangs carry out ransomware attacks, where a victim’s computer files are encrypted and assailants demand a cryptocurrency “ransom” to unlock them. But there is a cyber frontline where nation states operate too. Geopolitics, exemplified by Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against Europe, have made this conflict grey zone a particular source of concern.

Last month, the UK government launched the Be Ready campaign, urging people to stock up on three days’ worth of food and up to nine litres of bottled water in case of a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the country needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” targeting everyday infrastructure.

One expert said he believed the fridge attacks, for all the simplicity of the weaknesses they exploited, showed Russian traits. Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said his startup set up “honeypot” traps involving the same fridge controllers targeted by the Europe attackers. The techniques used by the lured hackers included using internet service providers that were particularly tolerant of malicious activity – a tactic linked with previous malicious activity carried out by Russians.

“Are we certain they are Russian groups? We are not. But elements of this point in that direction,” he said.

On the frontline of the grey war, there is no shock at recent events. Experts and officials in Finland said the fridge attacks were not a surprise, but part of a pattern they had seen growing for years.

Finland shares a 1,340km (832 mile) border with Russia. Since the 2022 Ukraine invasion, cyber-attacks of all kinds have escalated. Last year, the country’s national cybersecurity centre recorded nearly 21,000 incidents – targeting a population of fewer than 6 million people. In 2022 it was about 13,000 incidents.

This year, hackers managed to compromise up to 50,000 Finnish government mobile phones; last year, they took down the website of the country’s ministry of defence.

It is a trend across Europe and Nato countries but is especially pronounced in nations that border Russia.

However, Russia was not the only reason cyber threats were increasing, said Samuli Bergström, the vice-president of WithSecure, a Helsinki-based cybersecurity company. AI was boosting attacks as well and he echoed the warnings about internet-connected appliances.

“These attackers are mostly opportunistic,” Bergström explained. “When they see something that is facing the internet, they will probably attack it. [If you have a device] connected to the internet, you have to assume that it will be attacked, sooner or later.”

Bergström and others also emphasised that Russian state actors were not the only culprits – or even, necessarily, the most sophisticated ones.

There is a vast, unseen economy of hackers in the world. Some are activists. Some are mercenaries, in it for money. A good number of them have links to states, such as Russia and Iran. But this affiliation could be loose, which makes it difficult for officials to concretely attribute a motive to a given attack.

What does this mean for Europe? The world’s cyberthreat actors are growing more sophisticated and more resourced – better able to spot vulnerabilities, more capable of exploiting them. These advances invite doomsday speculation: could an entire nation’s power grid flicker out in -mid-winter, or could commerce grind to a halt?

Finland – and most European nations – have plans in place for disrupted payment systems, or an attack on the grid. But cyberthreats are not the same as kinetic war.

Bombing a power station could take out an electricity grid for months, or even longer, given the years-long wait to buy transformers. Cyber-attacks won’t necessarily have the same effect. Software is more quickly patched; it is usually possible to disconnect a device from the internet.

The goal – at least for state actors – in mounting these cyber-attacks could be more psychological than anything, some officials said. Turning fridges into ovens, or compromising a blood bank, is dramatic; it sears itself into the memory. But those vulnerabilities are likely to now be patched. There is no guarantee that a criminal group might be able to mount that exact attack again.

Still, there are many vulnerabilities, and legacy systems, left for malevolent actors to exploit. These attacks “are more frequent, and they continue to happen”, said Bergström.

Pearce has not reattached the internet cable but said his Langridge Organic business was otherwise unaffected. He said even after the French fridge attacks last month, he did not expect his company to be next.

“Hacking for the sake of being disruptive is a strange concept to most people.”

Donald Trump’s power is on the wane. What next for Russia, Israel – and the rest of us?

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:00:32 GMT

With the global tide turning against him, the US president’s lame duck status could still aggravate old tensions and spark new explosions

It was a victory for the world, too. People in the many countries that suffered pain, loss and cruel indignities at the hands of Donald Trump over the past two chaotic, fearful years celebrated a moment of glorious, shared redemption. The monster, like others of his kind, still lurks in his gilded White House lair; far-right authoritarianism still casts a dark shadow over many nations. But the power of this most destructive of presidents is shattered, his malignant spell broken. The triumphant roar of US midterm voters was a rallying cry of democratic defiance that, echoing the American revolution of 250 years ago, reverberated around the globe.

For Iranians, Trump’s electoral humiliation raised hopes, perhaps misplaced, that his murderous war of choice against Tehran’s oppressive regime may soon cease. In Israel, many among the majority who voted for change last week will welcome the humbling of the foremost supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu’s as-yet-unvanquished extremist coalition. Ukrainians voiced optimism that a Democratic-controlled Congress will curb the sickening appeasement of Vladimir Putin’s Russia. In Europe, the beginning of the end of the Trump era brought a sense of relief – and hope that toxic transatlantic relations can be drained of Maga poison.

It’s clear Trump is now weaker internationally as well as domestically. Despite his fanciful denials and contemptible attempts to shift blame, the sweeping Democratic successes represented an unmistakably personal repudiation. For foreign friends and allies, as for many Americans, the miasma of menace, the aura of invincibility surrounding Trump since 2024, has been blown away at last. In a self-flagellating act of egotism that ignored his rock-bottom approval ratings, he asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They obliged in huge numbers – and, acting as proxies for democrats the world over, offered him a tumescent middle finger.

Trump’s diminished lame duck status, and frustration that he is no longer the centre of attention, could aggravate old tensions and spark new explosions. For all his talk of deal-making, he rarely compromises. If thwarted, he gets angry, doubles down, lashes out. That’s why Iranian celebrations may prove premature. Egged on by Netanyahu (as long as he’s in power), commander-in-chief Trump could yet defy chastened Republicans such as the vice-president, JD Vance, and resume and expand the war – not least to avenge the Tehran-engineered Middle East oil shock that so alienated voters.

Settling the decades-long Iran nuclear standoff is a key legacy issue for Trump, increasingly obsessed with his place in history. Another legacy issue is Russia. He has gone to embarrassing lengths to reward war criminal Putin and punish Ukraine for being invaded. Trump regards the conflict as an obstacle to normalised ties with Moscow and lucrative bilateral energy, investment and trade deals. He clings to a vague idea of performing a “reverse Nixon” – befriending Russia to strategically disadvantage China. He’d like a Nobel peace prize, too. But ending the war for the sake of Ukraine’s besieged people is not Trump’s motivation. He cares little for the thousands of civilians killed, maimed or traumatised by Russian bombs.

Paradoxically, Trump’s weakness could hasten a ceasefire. Putin, beset by battlefield failures and deepening economic problems, knows his best chance of a face-saving outcome is to cut a deal while Trump remains in office. Herein lies grave danger for Ukraine and its allies. Trump’s amateurish negotiators may redouble their push for territorial and other concessions from Kyiv, disregarding its sovereign rights and Europe’s wider security. To force Kyiv’s capitulation on his terms, Trump may double down on his withholding of weapons and intelligence support and refusal to offer credible security guarantees - and to hell with the consequences and the precedent.

Trump retains huge latitude in directing US defence and foreign policy independently of Congress. But after Democrats take charge of both chambers in January, he and senior officials are certain to face intense scrutiny over executive actions, budgets, and alleged corruption and abuses of power. One early political casualty could be his pet weasel, the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth (although he’ll probably escape public execution). If Trump is impeached again, as some Democrats demand, he will have less time to worry about his international legacy.

Most US policies will not shift significantly between now and 2028. Any new Israeli government is likely to continue to deny basic Palestinian rights in Gaza and the West Bank, more or less supported by Washington. Trump could make nice with Europe and Canada by de-escalating tariff wars. Or he could enact previous threats to abandon Nato and the common defence of Europe – for him, another twisted “legacy” issue. There’s a risk he could foist Venezuela-style regime change on Cuba. Meanwhile, an altogether smarter autocrat, China’s Xi Jinping, will continue to run rings around him. Urgently needed agreements to halt nuclear weapons proliferation are nowhere in sight; nor is an end to White House climate emergency denial. On the other hand, the Democrats, once they hold the purse strings, could and should move swiftly to fully restore the overseas aid budget.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

At this tantalisingly uncertain moment of global redemption, can Trump redeem himself? It would be nice to think that, stung by an unambiguous national vote of no confidence and a powerful popular reassertion of American democracy, he will atone for his sins. It’s not so hard, Donald. Take the advice of the rapper Ice T, who said: “Redemption just means you just make a change in your life and you try to do right, versus what you were doing, which was wrong”. Yet such late-stage metamorphosis is improbable. Aged 80, stuck in his ways, learning nothing, never listening, slipping into senility, profane, vulgar and hugging outdated prejudices like a comfort blanket, Trump, “the angry duck”, is too far gone to change.

In prospect are two more years of presidential overreach, interference in other countries’ affairs, egotistical foreign policy posturing, damaging economic rows and overseas military adventurism. Yet the tide is turning against him. Progressive election victories in Hungary, Serbia, Brazil and now the US have reinvigorated and refreshed global democracy. Next up, Spain, then France in 2027. More historic defeats for the far-right, ultra-nationalist populists who believed Trump and Maga were invincible are now a glorious possibility. It’s all about trumping Trump.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

From Wild Horse Nine to Kings of Leon: your complete entertainment guide for the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:04 GMT

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell team up in a typically offbeat Martin McDonagh comedy, and the Followill brothers reach album No 10 in rustic mode

Wild Horse Nine Out now John Malkovich looks set to be nominated for an Oscar for his portrayal of an ageing CIA agent with terminal cancer who is sent to Easter Island with his younger colleague (Sam Rockwell) in this dark comedy drama from Martin McDonagh (The Banshees of Inisherin).

La Bola Negra Out now Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi were inspired by Lorca’s unfinished four-page fragment of the same name to create this epic Spanish queer drama spanning three timelines, with an international cast including singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close.

I Play Rocky Out now Back in 1975, a struggling actor by the name of Sylvester Stallone wasn’t getting the parts he wanted – so he gave himself three days to write a juicy role. The result was Rocky and the character was so good he had to fight to play it. Anthony Ippolito stars as Stallone in this feelgood dramatisation of the story behind one of cinema’s most famous roles.

One in a Million Out now Winner of the audience award at the Sundance film festival, this documentary follows a girl across an extraordinary decade in her life: from her childhood in Syria to adult life in Germany. Directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes. Catherine Bray

Simple Things festival Various venues, Bristol, 7 November For the first time in its 12-year history, Bristol’s festival celebrating boundary-pushing music has employed guest curators in the shape of Squid, Shabaka, Jeremy Deller and Cobrah. Alongside their picks are the likes of Hannah Diamond, My New Band Believe and the Avalanches. Michael Cragg

London jazz festival Various venues, 13 to 22 November This ever imaginative 10-day festival’s opening night includes spectaculars such as the star-packed John Coltrane centenary celebration (Barbican Hall) and vocal showcase Jazz Voice (Royal Festival Hall), while small-band gems such as saxophonist Jean Toussaint’s JT5 (also Friday, World Heart Beat Embassy Gardens) will be happening all over town. John Fordham

SBTV20 The O2, London, Wednesday The great and the good of the UK grime scene will appear at this 20th-anniversary celebration of the pioneering music platform SBTV. The event, which features Chip, Ms Banks and Tinie Tempah, will also honour the legacy of SBTV’s founder, Jamal Edwards MBE, who died in 2022. MC

Elgar’s Dream of Gerontius The Glasshouse, Gateshead, 8 November The epic oratorio at the heart of the 2025 film The Choral is a blockbuster even without Ralph Fiennes and co. The Royal Northern Sinfonia, local amateurs and a vast choir perform this choral favourite with top-flight soloists Sarah Connolly, Benjamin Hulett and Roderick Williams. Dinis Sousa conducts. Flora Willson

Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires V&A, London, 7 November to 9 May This big, ambitious exhibition looks at 1,600 years of art, design, antiquities and rarities such as the 11th-century Enkolpion of Constantinos, from a city that acts as a cultural bridge between Europe and Asia, east and west, and Islam and Christianity.

Georg Wilson Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, 8 November to 18 April Young painter Georg Wilson takes an ecological, folkloric, atmospheric approach to landscape painting, which means she should fit in perfectly in the historic surrounds of Thomas Gainsborough’s old gaff.

Ade Adesina City Art Centre, Edinburgh, 7 November to 11 April Aberdeen-based printmaker Ade Adesina uses woodcuts, etchings, linocuts and screenprints to tackle big themes of colonial history and the climate crisis, all with dramatic starkness and intense detail.

Katie Shannon Goldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 13 December The latest artist to take over GCCA’s experimental Episodes series, where they give a platform to young creatives, is Katie Shannon, with a new body of work looking at lost musical histories and “feminist rereadings of time and space”. Eddy Frankel

The Adam and Joe Show Royal Albert Hall, London, 11 November; Beacon Hall, Bristol, 5 December It has been 30 years since Buxton and Cornish’s cult comedy series was first broadcast. To celebrate, the duo revisit its highlights – toy movies; BaaadDad et al. Rachel Aroesti

Cloud 9 National Theatre: Lyttelton, London, to 13 January Dominic Cooke revives Caryl Churchill’s typically inventive, time-bending, mind-boggling play. It begins in Victorian colonial Africa then jumps to 70s London, with the cast performing theatrical gymnastics along the way. Miriam Gillinson

Owain & Henry Wales Millennium Centre: Donald Gordon theatre, Cardiff, to 28 November Michael Sheen stars as Owain Glyndŵr, a Welsh lord who rebelled against Henry IV after being declared an outlaw. Written by Olivier winner Gary Owen with a cast including Sophie Melville, Linus Roache and Rakie Ayola. MG

Humanhood: Vortex Sadler’s Wells East, London, 10 to 14 November Hypnotic movement from the Birmingham-Barcelona-based duo Humanhood and their company. Artistic directors Julia Robert and Rudi Cole have developed a method that’s somewhere between dance and a spiritual practice. Lyndsey Winship

12 12 12 Apple TV, 13 November A heist: 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute and 12 days to see whether you’ve got away with it. That’s according to this neat, numbersy cat-and-mouse thriller starring Jamie Dornan as the criminal mastermind behind a Zurich bank vault robbery and Anthony Mackie as the FBI agent on his tail.

Hunting Alice Bell Channel 4, 11 November, 9pm The Guardian’s film critic Peter Bradshaw and his schoolmate David Baddiel once co-starred in a sitcom; now they’ve reunited to create this internet vigilante thriller about a group of women who are all rumoured to be the accomplice of an infamous serial killer (Simon Pegg) living under a new identity.

The Good Daughter Sky Atlantic & Now, 12 November, 9pm Rose Byrne lends her exceptional acting chops to Karin Slaughter’s own adaptation of her characteristically disturbing 2017 novel about the secret truths behind a horrific attack that continues to haunt two sisters. Cunk on Cinema BBC Two & iPlayer, 12 November, 10pm It has been 13 years since “computer typist” Philomena Cunk first appeared as a talking head on Charlie Brooker’s Weekly Wipe; since then Diane Morgan’s alter ego has found fame as a very confused documentarian. Her latest series sees her grill doyens of the film industry in bewildering style. RA

The Devil’s Due PC; out 10 November It’s a classic story: you’ve lost a card game with the devil, and now you must make your way out of hell by defeating all of his minions at poker. Inventive cheating and a characterful collage-esque look make this a trip to hell worth considering.

Shrek 2: Remastered All platforms; out 10 November I’m not sure anyone expected this rerelease of the 2004 movie tie-in, which was surprise-announced just a few weeks ago, but it’s here to capitalise on the run of Shrek nostalgia that has already resulted in an immersive experience, a musical and several Shrek-themed raves. Keza MacDonald

Kings of Leon – O My Beloved Out now On their 10th album, the Followills get reflective. Self-produced, rustic and rooted in nostalgia, O My Beloved looks back at their career, their family life and the moments that shaped them, with the sweet, country-tinged My Whole World a painting of domestic bliss.

Shygirl – Swallow! Out now The artist born Blane Muise channels the likes of the Prodigy, William Orbit-era Madonna and the more interesting aspects of indie on this second album. Songs such as lead single Alyse also bolt on plush string arrangements, creating a sound that feels both decadent and dirty.

Skepta – The Fork and Knife Out now Seven years after his last album, the rapper and producer returns with a record rooted in the sounds of modern Britain. Absorbing everything from grime to house to jungle, its lyrics explore identity and strength via tracks such as the dark-hued Pandora’s Box, while the Fred Again-produced Victory Lap is pure party.

La Roux – Old Flames Out now Never one to be rushed, 00s electropop survivor Elly Jackson, AKA La Roux, follows up 2020’s occasionally brittle Supervision with this warmer album. The minimalist throb of Babyline stands out on a record focused on fresh starts. MC

Talking Common Podcast This engaging new series from author Josh Connolly departs from the usual self-help format and looks for answers to personal problems in community solutions. Guests include the musician Sonny Green on breaking the generational cycle of addiction issues.

International Intrigue Online This daily newsletter briefing from former diplomats is one of the most concise and thorough rundowns of complex geopolitical issues available. Recent topics feature the race for a new UN chief and the EU’s Arctic Strategy.

The Life Scientific BBC World Service, Monday, 8.32pm Associate professor of chemistry Asel Sartbaeva reveals how her research into silica materials has the potential to free lifesaving vaccines from needing to be constantly refrigerated and therefore reducing their risk of becoming spoiled in transit. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: What now for Trump, a cruise from hell, and manhood enhancements

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:06:45 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert and Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

We went big this week. In this selection of reads from across the Guardian, big wins are dissected, big questions are asked, big bowls are taste-tested and dreams of being bigger are realised. Enjoy.

A blue wave has swept through the US. In what appears a remarkable repudiation of Trumpism, voters handed Democrats control over the House of Representatives and the Senate. Our Washington DC bureau chief, David Smith, called it an “extinction-level event” and one famous Democrat proclaimed it was “morning again in America”.

But how will Trump and the Republican party respond to having his power diminished to a veto pen? Will it eat away at his “cult-like” control over the GOP, and will conservatives conclude Trump is now a creature of the political past?

​What happens next? Come January, Democrats will have the power to significantly impede Trump’s agenda. Progressive lawmakers will be “a bulwark against Trump’s expansion of executive power”, with the ability to block legislation in Congress as well as launch investigations into Trump’s family business and the Epstein files.

​Notable quote: “A wounded Trump who feels he has nothing to lose over the next two years might turn out to be the most reckless and dangerous of all.” – David Smith

​How long will it take to read: Two minutes.

​Further reading: Why Democrats turned towards the politics of affordability, and the Republicans hopeful of succeeding Trump read through the tea leaves.

The recent rise in diagnoses of autism has brought with it a heated debate. From supposed “overdiagnosis” to whether some people are prioritised over others, the controversy has become a new front in the culture wars. But what do the experts make of it all? John Harris sat down with some key figures to find out.

Different conclusions: Dame Uta Frith, who helped come up with the accepted understanding of autism, once agreed with the idea of a broad autistic spectrum; now she has come to the conclusion that many people diagnosed as adults are different from those whose condition was obvious in their early years. “Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells Harris. Another expert, Simon Baron-Cohen, now thinks the catch-all term “autistic spectrum disorder” – or “autistic spectrum condition” – is proving increasingly problematic.

But there is strong disagreement: One is from Mary Doherty, an Irish anaesthetist and one of the founders of Autistic Doctors International, who believes there is potential harm done by “invalidating people’s life experience”. “If you are autistic, understanding your autistic nature is life-changing,” she says. “It’s so damaging to deny that to people, particularly people who are already at risk of mental health problems.”

How long will it take to read: 10 to 11 minutes.

Further reading: How the Beatles heped my autistic son find his voice.

It’s the epic story of the Odyssey – but not that one. In 2024, the owners of the MV Odyssey cruise ship made a tempting (but not cheap) offer: a four-year voyage at sea, in which one could escape the troubles of a land-based world in which Donald Trump had just been elected president. But things did not go to plan.

From haven to hellhole: Even with the best planning and even the best prices, it turned out there was no escaping the US president and his knock-on effects on fuel prices amid his disastrous war in Iran. Instead of being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil, leading to passengers being “unceremoniously” dropped in Cambodia.

Notable quote: “People were shellshocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger. “People were angry. They were hysterical.”

How long will it take to read: Four minutes

Further reading: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean.

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Interest in penile-enhancement is on the rise, and it is now a booming industry. Manhood, a new documentary from film-maker Daniel Lombroso (formerly of The Atlantic and The New Yorker), investigates the latest phenomenon tied to men’s obsession with their members.

While the subject matter may invite humour, Lombroso centres the film on the male self-esteem issues driving the enhancement trend, highlights the patience and tender attention afforded to the fragile men seeking treatment and portrays it as another form of gender affirming care: “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment,” Lombroso says.

​The economics of enhancement: one penis practitioner featured heavily in the documentary, Bill Moore, wants enlargement procedures to be “as common as Botox”. Moore’s company, which advertises its offerings as “girth enhancement”, now has 32 locations across the country. Moore offers “career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing” procedures for up to $20,000 out of his office in a Dallas strip mall.

​Notable quote: “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer” – Penis enlargement patient

​How long will it take to read: A modest three minutes (no need to extend it).

​Further reading: How toxic masculinity is reshaping young men’s faces, and a look back at the “original looksmaxxer”.

Max Veenhuyzen says the people of Darwin take their laksa seriously. He must be right, because the city in Australia’s far north hosts the Darwin international laksa festival – a celebration of multiculturalism and food that brings together chefs and foodies from across the country. More than 50 different vendors entered the competition, with only one walking away the winner.

The Golden Bowl: Vendors compete for the top prize – a gaudy laksa dish-shaped trophy – as chosen by a panel of judges who secretly visit the restaurants and blind taste the dish on stage.

Notable quote: “Can I get some tissues on stage, please?” – Golden Bowl judge and self-taught chef Junda Khoo as he struggles to taste-test finalists in the Darwin heat.

Who went home the winner? Angkor Takeaway walked away champions, with the judges unanimously awarding Cheata Ouch’s bowl the accolades on account of its seasoning and diverse body.

How long will it take to read? Just under two minutes, leaving you plenty of time to make and enjoy your own bowl of laksa.

Further reading: How to cook the perfect laksa.

Nations Championship, Rugby League World Cup and NFL action – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 20:33:58 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

There will be plenty to talk about in the world of football on Saturday morning. As well as building up to Saturday’s four Premier League games, David Tindall will be looking at the fallout from Frank Lampard’s return to Everton with Coventry on Friday night and reaction to Thomas Tuchel’s last England squad of the year. But it’s also FA Cup first round proper day, when League One and League Two sides find themselves pitched against other lower-division sides or at risk of being giantkilled by non-league clubs. There’s also a Savage occasion on Saturday night at London Road, when Robbie’s Peterborough take on the Reading side for whom his son Charlie plays. Send your thoughts on all the issues to matchday. live@theguardian. com, and let us know if you are off to one of those Cup ties.

It’s very tight in the Premier League’s mid-table, with three teams on 12 points and four on 11 occupying the places between eighth and 14th before this round of matches. One of the latter category host one of the former on Saturday, with Daniel Farke and Roberto De Zerbi fairly happy with their positions right now but aware that Leeds and Tottenham both need to push on if they are to stay properly clear of relegation talk and instead push claims for places in Europe. Scott Murray is your live host, while Aaron Bower reports from Elland Road.

North and south/east are meeting all this weekend as the second half of the inaugural Nations Championship builds towards its climax at Twickenham on the last weekend of the month, and the All Blacks’ trip to Murrayfield is the pick of the day’s matches. Scotland have still never beaten New Zealand, and the worry for Gregor Townsend’s team is that after some severe stumbles the visitors are back on firm footing. Daniel Gallan is your guide minute by minute, while Michael Aylwin is in Edinburgh.

There are two 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, with Arsenal hosting Hull and Newcastle at Fulham, and Barry Glendenning will have all the news from the leaders’ meeting with the playoff winners and a meeting of the dissatisfied at Craven Cottage. In the FA Cup first round, we will be on the lookout for shocks. Perhaps there will be one at Boreham Wood, where the runaway leaders of the National League are at home to the 2013 winners, Wigan. There are also some all non-league ties, including the phoenix club Salisbury FC of National League South at home to Sholing of the Southern League Premier and Dover, another National League South side, hosting Wealdstone, one step higher. If you are at any of the ties, let Barry know what’s going on.

Oliver Glasner’s move to Forest has not gone smoothly, as evidenced by his anguished comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford that “I don’t need to be liked. I’m not here to be liked. I’m here to bring success to this club.” Manchester City aren’t winning popularity contests at present, either, and have lost a couple of football matches, too, after their steamroller start – if Arsenal have beaten Hull in their afternoon game, then the visitors to the City Ground will kick off six points off the top. Tom Bassam will follow events live, while Jonathan Wilson reports.

After sealing the title in Mexico City last weekend to become the youngest ever F1 champion, Kimi Antonelli aged 20 and (almost) a quarter is back in action, as Mercedes seek to close out a first constructors’ title since 2021 and the rest of the grid try to maximise their finishing places over the next four rounds. Estimates say each place in the team standings is worth about £7m. Ferrari should take second place, holding a 122-point advantage over Red Bull, but the squabbles between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc aren’t helping, while it is still fairly close between Red Bull and McLaren in the battle for third. Join Philip Cornwall for qualifying live, while Giles Richards reports.

It’s a double-header in Sydney, as the Jillaroos take on Fiji in the women’s tournament before the Kangaroos face Samoa, as the World Cup hosts aim for places in the following Sunday’s Brisbane finals. Angus Fontaine is on minute-by-minute for the women’s match, while Jonathan Howcroft looks after the men’s, and Jack Snape reports on both.

It’s another bumper Sunday of Premier League action and Emillia Hawkins, Simon Burnton and Tim de Lisle will have all the buildup to the games as well as picking over Saturday’s action. Depending on results, a manager or two could be brushing up his CV. Talking of which, there will be news in advance of the match at Old Trafford, pitting Manchester United’s current manager, Michael Carrick, against someone tipped to be his successor, Unai Emery of Aston Villa. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your views

A week after the men’s team won at Anfield, Arsenal’s women arrive badly in need of victory: the once all-conquering Gunners are only in the top half on goal difference, thanks to Alessia Russo’s late equaliser against Aston Villa last Sunday. Liverpool are in 11th but with the same goal difference (minus one) and only two points fewer, but after last week’s 4-1 defeat at West Ham they have won only one of their last seven. Emillia Hawkins has the live blog while Tom Garry reports.

Before that game at Old Trafford, the Europa/Conference League rearrangements mean Brighton v Brentford, Crystal Palace v Liverpool, Sunderland v Chelsea and Ipswich v Bournemouth are all at 2pm. Simon Burnton will be going around the grounds, seeing if Brighton can hang on to the leaders’ coattails; if one of Liverpool and Palace can manage a win after three defeats and a draw between them across four matches in the previous week; if struggling Sunderland can get a much-needed win against Chelsea; and if Ipswich can maintain their mid-table status against the Europa League’s all-conquering Bournemouth.

With finals weekend of the inaugural Nations Championship coming up at the end of the month, England would love to be back at Twickenham on the Sunday, you would imagine, when the top team in the north plays the top team from the south. What, though, if Steve Borthwick’s side lose to Australia? They might still get a Sunday match – but in the fourth v fourth warm-up against, say, France or South Africa. England need a clean sweep and South Africa to beat France next weekend in order to make the grand finale, and Daniel Gallan will take you through their efforts live while Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher report from south-west London.

It’s the last Premier League game before an international break that could open up the managerial merry-go-round, despite being the old-style two-weeker rather than the three-week one that straddled September and October. Michael Carrick will be trying to build on Manchester United’s thrilling comeback against Roma, while Unai Emery will hope Aston Villa can respond to his latest defeat at the Camp Nou. Tim de Lisle will have all the live updates, while Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin report from Old Trafford.

It’s so nice they named it thrice: the grand prix venue can be referred to as the city of São Paulo; as the Autódromo José Carlos Pace; or perhaps most famously by the neighbourhood it sits in, Interlagos. If it wasn’t for that pesky kid, then this could be a title race for the ages: Max Verstappen is two points ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who is nine ahead of George Russell, with Charles Leclerc five more back. And even Lando Norris is within a win of Leclerc, and has twice as many race victories as the Monégasque and Hamilton. Daniel Harris is on the live blog, while Giles Richards reports.

It’s week nine, no one can go unbeaten now, and Graham Searles will have news of the crop of 1pm eastern, 6pm GMT kick-offs. They include the meeting of two table-toppers, though it’s fair to say the AFC West’s 6-and-2 Broncos are in better shape than the NFC South’s 3-and-4 Panthers, who are hosts. Other matches include the Jets at the Chiefs and the Lions at the Dolphins. Graham will also have news of the 9.30am eastern/2.30pm game between Atlanta and Cincinnati, the NFL’s first visit to Madrid.

Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The secretary of state’s role in drafting a secret memo highlights how top officials were concerned by this past spring about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence.

By Maggie HabermanJonathan SwanJulian E. Barnes and Tripp Mickle

The reporters have been covering China’s spying on Nvidia and America’s artificial intelligence industry.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy, multiple people briefed on the matter said.

The document was based on classified intelligence from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who was a senior executive at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips and being investigated for illegally smuggling them into China. U. S. officials had concluded that Ms. Huang was in a close relationship with the Nvidia chief, who is no relation, and that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security.

Mr. Rubio’s involvement in warning administration officials about the situation has not been previously reported. It highlights how concerns about the relationship and the spying were known to senior officials even as Mr. Huang, a pivotal figure in the explosive growth of A. I., remained an influential voice with Mr. Trump over policy on the issue.

Mr. Huang has opposed calls for more tightly regulating the export of the most advanced A. I. chips and has pushed to be able to sell all but the most recently developed technology to China, the main competitor to the United States in the global rush for A. I. supremacy.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it was opening an investigation into Mr. Huang after he acknowledged that he had been intimate with Ms. Huang, though the company said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

In a message to the company, Mr. Huang apologized.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

A State Department spokesman and a White House spokeswoman declined to comment.

Mr. Rubio’s memo was circulated to administration officials with high-level security clearances ahead of a trip Mr. Trump took to China in May, the people briefed on the matter said. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive material.

Despite his status as an A. I. pioneer and head of one of the world’s most valuable companies, Mr. Huang was initially left off the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr. Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the president’s policy of only lightly regulating A. I., people briefed on the matter said.

After Mr. Trump saw media coverage about Mr. Huang being absent from the delegation, the president asked him to join the trip by meeting Air Force One during a layover in Alaska. The president drafted a social media post saying that it was an honor to have “the Great Jensen Huang,” and other business leaders “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.”

The New York Times reported last month that Mr. Trump was briefed roughly a year ago that the U. S. intelligence community had electronic surveillance of Ms. Huang, and believed that she was an operative working for China’s intelligence services. The surveillance revealed a close relationship between Ms. Huang and a U. S. citizen. When officials asked for the name of the U. S. citizen to be “unmasked” — given Americans’ identities are routinely protected from foreign surveillance — it was revealed to be the Nvidia CEO.

The president chose at that point not to take any action. He has viewed Nvidia’s chips as integral to America’s competition with China in A. I. He sees Nvidia’s success as crucial to maintaining a robust stock market.

Ms. Huang speaks English well and has relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A. I. chip industry, including with Mr. Huang and the leaders of Gigabyte, one of the top assemblers of Nvidia supercomputers, people who have met her said.

It is unclear when Ms. Huang first met Nvidia’s leader. In 2024, around the time the two of them were photographed together with other industry executives at a bar in Taipei, her company, Megaspeed, began a multibillion-dollar purchase of advanced A. I. microchips.

Nvidia officials have said that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were “not unusual or unexpected” and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers. The company has also said customers like Megaspeed do not receive classified business information.

In recent years, Megaspeed, despite having essentially a storefront office and little local footprint, purchased $2 billion worth of Nvidia’s products. Megaspeed builds data centers in Southeast Asia that rent out their computing power to Alibaba, the giant Chinese internet company. U. S. officials suspect Megaspeed has been helping smuggle restricted advanced Nvidia chips into China.

Ms. Huang has not responded to attempts to reach her.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Chinese Spy

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Huang, the company’s chief executive, acknowledged on Sunday that he was intimate with a business executive who U. S. officials had determined was working for Chinese intelligence.

By Tripp Mickle

Reporting from San Francisco

Nvidia said on Sunday that it was opening an investigation into Jensen Huang, its chief executive and co-founder, after he acknowledged to the company’s board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U. S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman, who is named Alice Huang, became a U. S. government concern after surveillance revealed that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The revelation raised troubling possibilities because Mr. Huang is one of the most powerful figures in the A. I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump.

In a message to the company, Mr. Huang apologized. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that “the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” It said Mr. Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.”

Mr. Huang, 63, will continue to lead the company during the investigation, the board said. As a co-founder, he has set up a unique structure at Nvidia where he dictates all aspects of its business while overseeing some 60 people who directly report to him.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” said John Rizzo, a company spokesman. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C. E. O. without interruption.”

The New York Times reported last month that American intelligence agencies had discovered that Mr. Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, who U. S. officials concluded was gathering intelligence for Beijing.

The chip buyer was Ms. Huang or Huang Le, whose biography said she worked in China as a TV reporter before becoming a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company that had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. It bought more than $4.8 billion in chips over the past two years.

Nvidia has continued doing business with Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, even after The Times reported last year that the Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping China smuggle restricted A. I. chips. (Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are not related.)

Nvidia and Mr. Huang initially said there was nothing problematic or unusual about his relationship with Ms. Huang. In an interview with Bloomberg News last month, he said that his interactions with Ms. Huang had been “related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

What Talarico’s Win Reveals About Christianity in Texas

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Senator-elect James Talarico’s progressive Christianity seemed to resonate for many in a state whose politics and culture have been dominated by conservative evangelicalism.

By Ruth Graham

Reporting from Dallas

James Talarico, a onetime Sunday school teacher, opened his acceptance speech on Tuesday night with a Bible story.

“I’m reminded of that story from Scripture of a shepherd boy who goes up against a giant,” he told an ebullient crowd in Austin, Texas. In the end, of course, the shepherd boy defeats the well-armed Goliath with only a slingshot.

Mr. Talarico slew his own giant this week, ending decades of Republican control in Texas with a decisive win that carried multiple other Democrats in the state to victory. He did it in part by speaking easily and openly about how his Christian beliefs inform his politics, starting with the biblical command to love God and “love thy neighbor,” as the sign on his lectern read on Tuesday night.

He was one of many successful Democrats across the country who framed their politics in terms of their Christian faith. The Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton pulled off a similar upset in Kansas. Two ordained ministers, Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James, flipped House seats for Democrats in Iowa.

In Texas, Mr. Talarico was an underdog not just because of his party, but because of the type of Christianity he practices. He is a progressive mainline Protestant — a Presbyterian, specifically — in a state defined culturally and politically by conservative evangelicalism. Texas has seven of the 20 largest churches in the country, all of which can be characterized as evangelical. Sprawling big-box-style campuses line the highways, and steeples dot the back roads. In cities, Bible study gatherings often require microphones.

In recent years, an increasingly combative Christian conservatism came to feel like a kind of official state language of faith. This summer, Texas became the first state to mandate Bible readings in public schools, after a successful push to post the Ten Commandments in classrooms there. Republican lawmakers also turned the power of the state against some Muslim groups, often framing the cause as a spiritual battle.

More than a quarter of adult Texans are self-described evangelicals. But the state is also home to progressive Protestants like Mr. Talarico, millions of Catholics, and politically active Black congregations, including one in Dallas whose pastor was elected to Congress as a Democrat this week.

Mr. Talarico, an eighth-generation Texan and onetime seminarian, understood all that. His own grandfather, once a Baptist preacher, found himself on the “moderate” side when conservatives took over the Southern Baptist Convention in the 1970s and ’80s, a move masterminded in Texas. Mr. Talarico was raised in a church that has been known locally for its progressive activism for decades.

In a town hall hosted by CNN in October, a voter from his hometown of Round Rock, Texas, pressed him “Christian to Christian” about provocative past statements like “God is nonbinary.”

“Do you believe that the Bible is the absolute source of truth and God’s final authoritative word, even when our culture says otherwise?” she asked.

“Yes,” Mr. Talarico answered.

For many, his rise was a reminder of the capacious borders of Christianity in the state.

“The loudest voices that people hear are these megachurches, and they think that’s what we’re all doing,” said the Rev. Janet Maykus. She was raised in a progressive church in then-rural Lancaster, Texas, where she was taught that “faith is something particular to every person,” rooted in justice and kindness rather than doctrine.

Ms. Maykus, 64, now leads the United Christian Church of Austin, a small mainline Protestant congregation in the capital.

When her congregation recites the Lord’s Prayer, it’s a “train wreck,” she said fondly. Some people recite a version with gender-inclusive language; others tack on a few extra words here and there. In every service, Ms. Maykus also prays aloud for “our siblings in Christ who have lost their way to the lure of white Christian nationalism.”

In recent months, she said, she has talked with multiple visitors to the church who said they had been inspired by Mr. Talarico to seek out a church like hers. She is baptizing a baby on Sunday.

The growth of progressive congregations like hers is exactly why Robert Jeffress, pastor of the politically influential church First Baptist Dallas, watched Mr. Talarico’s ascent with alarm, he said in an interview this week.

“What James Talarico believes about the Bible and about Jesus, those beliefs don’t disqualify him from being a senator, but they do disqualify him from being a Christian pastor, or even a Christian,” Mr. Jeffress said, referring in part to Mr. Talarico’s suggestion that Christianity is not the only religion that points to the truth.

Last Sunday, Mr. Jeffress said, he alluded to Mr. Talarico as he preached about the tower of Babel, warning how “false religion always mixes truth with error.”

Mr. Jeffress’s church, established in the 1860s, is one of many institutions that have long made Texas a major exporter of politically conservative Christianity.

Texas is where the folksy fundamentalist radio host W. Lee O’Daniel became governor in 1938, with a platform based on the Ten Commandments and low taxes. It’s where W. A. Criswell, a predecessor of Mr. Jeffress, called the separation of church and state “the figment of some infidel’s imagination” in 1984. And it’s where Dan Patrick, the state’s current lieutenant governor, described his socially conservative agenda as an expression of his Christian faith.

In the run-up to the Senate race, pastors of some of the largest evangelical congregations in the state worked overtime to make the case against Mr. Talarico, even as they nodded at the scandal-ridden reputation of his opponent, Ken Paxton.

“Wise Christians can differentiate between a FALLEN candidate and an EVIL candidate,” Josh Howerton, the pastor of a large church in North Texas, wrote on X last week, without mentioning Mr. Paxton or Mr. Talarico by name.

A so-called fallen candidate has “personal sin” in his or her own life, the pastor wrote. An evil candidate, by contrast, “leads entire communities, states, and nations to sin.”

Mr. Paxton made his own pitch to conservative Christians. One ad used artificial intelligence to depict Mr. Talarico defacing a Bible and reciting quotes taken out of context from his sermons and speeches.

“If Christians don’t vote,” Mr. Paxton told the right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson on Election Day, “we’re going to have trouble sustaining Christianity in this country.”

But Mr. Paxton didn’t speak as easily about his own religious life. It was never clear during the campaign whether he still belongs to a church. His former pastor, Jack Graham, the longtime leader of a politically influential megachurch near Dallas, joined the faith council of his opponent in the primary, John Cornyn.

This week, some in the state wondered if they were seeing the end of one era of Texas Christianity, and the beginning of another.

“If that form of conservative Christianity was going to die out, this is what it would look like,” said Joseph Locke, an historian at the University of North Texas and the author of a recent book about religion in the state.

“It would start with these isolated victories, and you could see the cracks forming,” he said.

As a Texan, it's been fascinating to watch the way James Talarico's way of talking about his Christian faith has resonated with some people in the state, and infuriated others. Texas is dominated politically and culturally by conservative evangelicalism, so it has really shaken things up for a vocally progressive mainline Protestant to have a platform like Talarico's.

Ruth Graham is a national reporter, based in Dallas, covering religion, faith and values for The Times.

Jeffries Backs Impeaching Hegseth as Democrats Push for Accountability

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats have begun laying the groundwork for an aggressive oversight agenda aimed at the Trump administration. But a political reckoning could come before the new Congress begins.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from Washington

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader poised to become the next speaker of the House, said on Sunday that he would support impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, joining the growing calls to remove one of President Trump’s top cabinet secretaries after overwhelming Republican defeats in last week’s elections.

Mr. Jeffries said that he was a “hard yes” on a resolution to impeach Mr. Hegseth that was expected to come to the House floor this week — the first time the top Democrat has publicly expressed support for the idea.

“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Mr. Jeffries said during an interview on the ABC morning program “This Week,” adding, “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Democrats, emboldened by their decisive victories in the House and the Senate last week, have begun laying the groundwork for an aggressive oversight agenda aimed at Mr. Trump and his administration. But increased bipartisan pressure, especially on Mr. Hegseth, since the election suggests that a political reckoning could come before the new Congress begins.

Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican who is retiring at the end of his term after losing a primary to a challenger backed by Mr. Trump, is expected to force a vote in the House this week on impeaching Mr. Hegseth.

Mr. Massie first moved to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterms. That prompted Speaker Mike Johnson to call an early recess to avoid voting on the measure. Impeachment resolutions are privileged motions in the House and when introduced must be taken up within two days.

Because that effort expired, Mr. Massie must renew his notice to force action on the measure, which he is expected to do when the House returns this week, again setting off a two-day clock to take up the resolution.

Even if the House were to vote to impeach Mr. Hegseth, however, it would be unlikely to lead to his removal from office, which requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Only two cabinet officials have been impeached in U. S. history, and neither was removed from office by the Senate.

Mr. Jeffries predicted “incredibly strong support” among Democrats for the resolution on Sunday and said they would discuss the issue when they return to Washington this week.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said on the CNN talk show “State of the Union” on Sunday that the Justice Department would defend members of the administration like Mr. Hegseth from investigations or impeachment efforts. “Department of Justice represents members of the executive,” he said, adding that he “would be very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump wrote on social media that the calls for impeachment amounted to “extortion at the highest level” and ordered the Justice Department to investigate those making the push.

Some Republican lawmakers are also signaling openness to the case against Mr. Hegseth, even as they have stopped short of endorsing impeachment.

“I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment,” Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas, said during an interview on the CBS program “Face the Nation.”

Mr. Hill, who won re-election on Tuesday by fewer than 4,500 votes, expressed dissatisfaction with the administration’s handling of the war with Iran but cautioned that poor performance did not necessarily rise to the level of impeachment.

“If you don’t think he’s done a good job conducting his job, that doesn’t mean per se that he has committed an impeachable offense,” he said. He added that if Mr. Hegseth was not carrying out his mission properly, “the president ought to make a change there.”

Representative James R. Comer, Republican of Kentucky, has also raised questions about Mr. Hegseth’s leadership and future, warning that it was “very possible” that enough lawmakers would vote to impeach him.

In a NewsNation interview on Friday, Mr. Comer did not explicitly express support for removing Mr. Hegseth, instead saying, “That’s going to be a decision that President Trump’s going to have to make.”

Beyond the Pentagon, lawmakers have expressed varying levels of support for personnel changes across the administration.

Representative Marlin Stutzman, Republican of Indiana, criticized the appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, calling it a “bad mistake.”

And Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who is likely to lead the Senate’s health committee in January, said on Sunday that he was open to impeachment efforts against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

News Analysis

As Americans absorb a stunning new political reality, they face a gap between the time they effectively decided to be done with the president and the time he is actually done.

Credit... Alex Kent/The New York Times

Supported by

By Peter Baker

Peter Baker, the chief White House correspondent, has covered five presidents whose parties lost midterm elections.

In the days since his defeat, he has sounded like a man in denial.

With his party still picking through the wreckage of a political earthquake, a seemingly oblivious President Trump signed a steel beam for his new White House ballroom and flew to Florida to give a speech on the space program. He seems flat these days, maybe a little dazed.

If Donald Trump is still processing the election that swept his party from power in Congress last week, so too is Donald Trump’s America. Both parties are still absorbing the stunning reality of sweeping Democratic victories in states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina that were long G. O. P. strongholds — and possibly even Mississippi.

But as clear as the midterm verdict was, the future is cloudier. After a decade in which Mr. Trump has dominated national politics, the country now faces a period of profound uncertainty, an interregnum between the time that Americans effectively decided that they were done with Mr. Trump and the time when he is actually done.

How does an unpopular, lame-duck president spurned by the electorate govern in his final two years in office? How does a shattered Republican Party rebuild itself for a post-Trump era while Mr. Trump himself is still around and unwilling to cede the stage? How do newly empowered Democrats use their new majorities in Congress and define themselves beyond simply being the anti-Trump party?

To those who wondered whether Mr. Trump would choose conciliation or confrontation in response to his party’s defeat, his decision on Friday to install Stephen Miller, his top ideological warrior, as the next White House chief of staff provided an answer — and it was not conciliation. In case the message was not received, on Saturday he posted an offer on social media for Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, to be his press secretary. Mr. Trump may be wounded, but a wounded animal can thrash around powerfully.

Yet those in his circle wasted no time looking past him. Two senior members of his team, Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, quickly went public with sharply divergent views of the Iran war and the wisdom of prosecuting it. In effect, they began to set the parameters for a debate that will consume their party for the next year.

On Capitol Hill, Speaker Mike Johnson promptly indicated that he would step down, opening a leadership contest for the vanquished Republicans. And Democrats began mapping a path forward balancing the desire to investigate and hold Mr. Trump’s team accountable with the imperative of passing legislation addressing voter concerns about the cost of living.

“People are conveying: ‘Yes, we feel joy, we feel relief,’” said Representative Hillary Scholten, Democrat of Michigan. “But also: ‘Get to work, Congress. We do not want political theater, we don’t want drama, we don’t want infighting.’”

One thing seems certain — the days of virtual one-man rule are over. In the nearly 22 months since Mr. Trump took office again, he has sought to impose his will not just over the executive branch but also over big business, the tech industry, major universities, law firms, the central bank, private banks, entertainment, sports, museums, the news media, national parks, the financial sector, the energy sector, the military and nonprofit foundations.

He has turned the prosecutorial power of the F. B. I. and Justice Department against his adversaries and, while he has been blocked at times by judges and grand juries, the Supreme Court has validated many of his assertions of authority. He has sent the National Guard into the streets of Washington and other cities, while turning ICE into a paramilitary force to haul away not just criminals but also otherwise law-abiding undocumented immigrants with deep roots in their communities.

He has even sought to remake the face of Washington, tearing down the East Wing of the White House to make room for his new ballroom-qua-drone-launcher, building a helipad on the South Lawn, proposing a new triumphal arch, renovating the Reflecting Pool, overhauling Lafayette Square and replacing the East Potomac golf course. By his own count the other day, he has created or restored 83 statues, fountains and monuments in the city.

He can still be expected in these final two years to exert power in ways that previous presidents did not, but he will now face pushback from an opposition Congress armed with subpoenas and the power of the purse. Moreover, the fear that consumed private institutions in the early part of his second term and prompted them to buckle under to demands for money, policy changes and personnel decisions has certainly eased. If anything, some of them will now worry about offending the ascendant Democrats by appearing too deferential to Mr. Trump.

“The spell is broken, and the veil of invincibility pierced,” said Daniel M. Price, a former international economic adviser to President George W. Bush. “The genuflection is likely to cease, and those who paid tribute — whether for ballrooms or meme coins or to settle frivolous lawsuits or to make ‘documentaries’ or to secure regulatory favors or government contracts — may well be called to account.”

Michael Beschloss, a presidential historian, said that no other commander in chief in the past 80 years had touched so many sectors of society, leaving many nervous about what would come next. “It’s hard to find any precedent for that kind of sweeping, unpredictable change in any other post-World War II administration,” he said. “As a result, you could see apprehension on more than a few faces in this capital.”

This might be the most overwhelming moment of whiplash in an era that has been defined by sharp swings: Mr. Trump came out of nowhere in 2016 and shocked the world by winning the presidency, then crashed in defeat four years later and spread lies in an effort to overturn the election and hold onto power. He was indicted, put on trial and convicted, then staged an audacious comeback to reclaim the White House and now has endured what by some measures is the most devastating midterm repudiation of a president in half a century or more.

Through it all the country has been through a plethora of ordeals — the worst pandemic in a century, the biggest economic upheaval in generations, the most widespread racial unrest in decades, the first sacking of the Capitol since the British invasion of the early 19th century, the disastrous end of one overseas war and the rash start of another. All of which might still not eclipse the impact on society of artificial intelligence in the next few years.

This has certainly been a drama for the ages, one that would have been hard to imagine not long ago.

“We’ve just been through the looking glass, and Wonderland wasn’t Wonderland,” said Max Stier, president of the Partnership for Public Service, a nonprofit group that aims to make government work more effectively. “It was craziness and destruction.”

Tevi Troy, a presidential historian who previously worked for Mr. Bush, said all the disorder finally got to the public. “Now we’re looking at the tumult,” he said. “People aren’t happy. I think they wanted normal, and they’re not getting normal from either party.”

No president since Franklin D. Roosevelt has dominated the national conversation for as long as Mr. Trump has. Even while President Joseph R. Biden Jr. occupied the White House, Mr. Trump was still a central focus of attention. He drove dinner-table conversations and drove wedges among families, friends and neighbors. But last week’s election suggested that the public has grown weary, even in places he won handily in the past in the South and Sunbelt.

Unlike other presidents who suffered midterm defeats, Mr. Trump has largely not acknowledged the setback. After Mr. Bush’s Republicans lost both houses in 2006, he admitted it was a “thumping.” After President Barack Obama’s Democrats lost the House in 2010, he admitted it was a “shellacking.” Mr. Trump, by contrast, has offered no expression of humility or much recognition of public discontent with him.

Like other presidents after midterm defeats, Mr. Trump now faces an inevitable erosion of influence. After President Bill Clinton’s Democrats were swamped in 1994, he was left to argue plaintively that “the Constitution gives me relevance.” There were echoes of that last week when the White House was reduced to posting an online message saying, “TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.”

Mr. Clinton came back to win re-election two years later, but Mr. Trump does not have that opportunity under the Constitution. Each of the five presidents who were elected twice and served two full terms since World War II — Dwight D. Eisenhower, Ronald Reagan, Mr. Bush, Mr. Clinton and Mr. Obama — had an opposition Congress in the final two years of his tenure.

Even so, presidents can still make a difference in that final stretch without Congress, especially in foreign policy, noted Mr. Troy. His old boss, Mr. Bush, after the 2006 midterm elections, surged more troops to Iraq and changing strategy there, helping to turn around the war. Mr. Clinton in his final two years successfully prosecuted the Kosovo war.

“They didn’t go away,” said Mr. Troy, who is now a senior fellow at the Ronald Reagan Institute. “They didn’t have huge legislative accomplishments — none of them had control of Congress. But they all did important things. Things can and do happen in the last two years.”

Indeed, Mr. Trump in his second term has not sought to govern through Congress even when his fellow Republicans were in charge, so in that sense he has less to lose. Other than his tax cut bill, he has pursued his priorities largely through executive action.

Still, time is short and with each passing day, the focus will turn relentlessly to the next presidential election. The first scheduled primary is just 441 days away. And it will be wide open, the first contest since 1976 without a Bush, Clinton, Obama or Trump on the ticket.

“I’m already getting outreach from 2028 contenders who are going to pass through Michigan,” marveled Ms. Scholten, the congresswoman. “It’s wild.”

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.
