Justice Dept. Mulled Naming The Times as Conspirator in Comey Leak Case

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

It remains unclear how the Justice Department might proceed. The move would be a major escalation of the Trump administration’s recent attacks against the news media.

By Alan Feuer

Federal prosecutors told a judge last month that they were considering treating The New York Times as a conspirator in a criminal case accusing James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director, of leaking sensitive national security information.

The assertion, which came during a closed-door hearing in Federal District Court in Washington, raised extraordinary First Amendment concerns and would, if pursued, mark a major escalation of the Trump administration’s recent attacks against news organizations. It also reflected the White House’s relentless efforts to go after Mr. Comey, who was removed as the F. B. I. director by President Trump in 2017.

During the sealed hearing on Oct. 9, a prosecutor working on the case, Dustin Farahnak, told Judge Trevor N. McFadden that the department had weighed treating The Times as a criminal co-conspirator with Mr. Comey in publishing an article concerning a novel use of a surveillance technique, according to a transcript of the proceeding made public this weekend.

The proceeding stemmed from a case filed against Mr. Comey on Oct. 5 in which prosecutors accused him of making an unauthorized disclosure to The Times of national security information for the article. The article appeared in The Times exactly a decade before the charges were brought in order to fall within the 10-year statute of limitations.

Mr. Comey’s lawyers have asked a judge to dismiss the charges in the leak case, arguing that prosecutors failed to bring it within the statute of limitations. In an unusual procedural move, prosecutors filed the charges without the approval of a judge or a grand jury through a document known as an information, hoping that doing so would comply with the statute of limitations.

The department’s consideration of treating The Times as a conspirator appeared to be an attempt to connect the Oct. 5, 2016, article with subsequent coverage by The Times involving Mr. Comey in a way that they contend could extend the statute of limitations. In conspiracy cases, the statute of limitations is based on the last purported act of the criminal scheme.

“Whether or not The New York Times acted in concert and was a conspirator, which would greatly expand the statute of limitations, is an issue that we had to decide over,” said Mr. Farahnak, the prosecutor, who was brought to Washington from a U. S. attorney’s office in Texas to work on the case.

“The real issue is, who is in the conspiracy and how long did it persist?” he added.

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

For now, Mr. Farahnak said, prosecutors have decided to charge only Mr. Comey. But remarks that prosecutors made at a subsequent hearing, on Oct. 30, suggest that the prospect of other people or entities being charged remains a possibility.

At that proceeding, prosecutors said that the Justice Department was considering asking a grand jury to bring an indictment not just involving The Times article from Oct. 5, 2016, which concerned surveillance of email traffic on the platform Yahoo, but also involving other coverage dating to April 2017.

The prosecutors appeared to be referring to an article The Times published that month about Mr. Comey’s handling of the investigation the previous year into Hillary Clinton’s emails. The Justice Department later scrutinized whether The Times received classified information from an adviser to Mr. Comey for the article.

If the department were to treat The Times as one of Mr. Comey’s conspirators, it could provide prosecutors with a basis — however tenuous — to link the October 2016 article and the April 2017 article as part of the same plot.

A Supreme Court ruling in 1946 makes it difficult for prosecutors to prove a conspiracy in a situation in which one person acts as a hub and has criminal interactions with two or more people who, like spokes, do not interact directly with each other. The October 2016 and April 2017 articles involved different reporters, but both were published by The Times.

Even this theory of the case, should the department choose to pursue it, could be difficult to prove in court.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, federal investigators scrutinized Mr. Comey’s role in the publication of both articles and ultimately found there was no evidence to support criminal charges. Still, in his second term, Mr. Trump has openly demanded that the Justice Department continue to pursue perceived enemies like Mr. Comey.

The leak case marked the third time in 13 months that the Trump administration has sought to prosecute Mr. Comey, whom Mr. Trump fired as F. B. I. director in 2017.

The Justice Department first charged Mr. Comey in September 2025, accusing him of lying over years-old testimony to Congress. Those charges were later thrown out by a judge.

A second case in North Carolina is set to go to trial next year. It centers on a photograph of seashells on a beach that Mr. Comey shared on social media last year. The shells were arranged to say “86 47,” which prosecutors deemed to be a threat against Mr. Trump.

The revelation that the administration was considering treating The Times as a conspirator in the leak case came one day after the high-profile resignation of John Eisenberg, who had been assistant attorney general for the national security division of the Justice Department.

Mr. Eisenberg, who served in Mr. Trump’s first administration, stepped down because of disagreements with Attorney General Todd Blanche over how aggressively to go after reporters in leak investigations, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The Justice Department under Mr. Trump has already acted aggressively to crack down on what it sees as illegal leaks of sensitive information.

In January, federal agents searched the home of Hannah Natanson, a reporter for The Washington Post, a remarkably aggressive step for an administration to take in investigating a government contractor’s handling of classified information.

Prosecutors have also issued grand jury subpoenas to The Washington Post, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. The department withdrew its subpoenas to The Post and The Journal over their reporting on military action in Iran and Venezuela. But it is still fighting over the one it issued to a freelance reporter who had worked with The Times on an article about a failed top secret mission in North Korea.

In July, federal agents served grand jury subpoenas on several Times reporters in an effort to track down leaks about the security concerns of the Air Force One jet donated to Mr. Trump by Qatar.

Prosecutors ultimately withdrew the subpoenas after a federal judge in Manhattan grilled them for nearly an hour over whether they had heeded the law and the department’s own regulations in issuing them in the first place.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

The American Brain Drain Claims Another Scientist

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Kelly Holley-Bockelmann in her new lab in Leiden, Netherlands.

Supported by

Kelly Holley-Bockelmann was one of the top astrophysicists in the country until President Trump’s policies affected every part of her work.

By Eli Saslow

Visuals by Hilary Swift

Kelly Holley-Bockelmann had always oriented herself by looking up at the sky, but now it was tilted and unfamiliar. The Milky Way sank toward the horizon line, and darkness never arrived quite the way it had in Tennessee, fast and enveloping. Instead, there was hazy dusk and then stubborn twilight before the sun rose again over her extended-stay hotel thousands of miles from home.

She took a tram, then a train, then a bus until she arrived at a glass-walled building in the Netherlands. There was a Dutch flag near the entryway and a replica of a spaceship in the lobby. She rode the elevator to her new office, a small room with whitewashed walls, empty drawers and a handwritten note taped to the desk. “We are thrilled to welcome one of America’s great scientists,” it read.

A new colleague stopped at the doorway to check in on her. “I know it might not look all that impressive,” he said, gesturing around the office.

“It’s perfect,” Holley-Bockelmann said. “After these last few years, I’m just so grateful to be here.”

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

She had never expected to be starting over halfway across the world at age 55, just as she reached the pinnacle of a career that was often celebrated as uniquely American. She’d grown up in Montana, lying in the grass beneath the night sky and trying to feel the Earth spin. She dreamed of becoming an astronomer before she knew the word for it. Nobody in her house growing up had finished college. She’d never met a scientist. But she made herself into a theoretical astrophysicist, a leading expert on gravitational waves, a top adviser to NASA, and a chaired professor at Vanderbilt. She helped begin a new graduate program for astronomers and raised millions in federal money to recruit American scientists with backgrounds as unlikely as her own, only to watch that pipeline be dismantled piece by piece.

Her research funding was threatened after President Trump took office in 2025. Graduate students were squeezed out of the field. The space observatory that had become her life’s work was marked for elimination in the federal budget, twice. One by one, the scientists around her did the math and chose to leave, until she decided to move to Europe with a husband who had just become an American citizen and two teenagers who had spent their childhoods in Tennessee. She had devoted her career to studying the most violent events in the universe as galaxies merged and black holes collided, sending gravitational waves rippling through space for billions of years. Now the disturbance was closer to home, and she was still measuring the damage.

She left her office and walked down the hall to meet with a few co-workers at the Netherlands Institute for Space Research. She was the most established scientist in the room, but she fetched everyone coffee and sat back from the table, trying to disappear into the group despite her dyed pink hair and a vocabulary shaped by years in Tennessee.

“OK, y’all, where are we right now with LISA?” she said.

It was the question she’d been asking for more than a decade. LISA was a space observatory scheduled to launch in 2035: three spacecraft linked across millions of miles, using lasers to listen for gravitational waves. Scientists hoped it could detect signals from the universe’s earliest moments, beyond the reach of any telescope. In work for similar missions, American scientists had invented technology behind the camera sensors, lasers and satellites the country and its military came to depend on. The project was meant to be a collaboration between the United States and Europe, but the United States had fallen behind because of staffing and budget shortfalls at NASA. Trump had repeatedly tried to eliminate funding for the program, and Europe was making contingency plans to save the mission rather than cede a new frontier of physics and a generation of scientific advances to a similar project from China.

“I hate to say it, but right now America can’t be counted on as a full partner,” one scientist said. She glanced over at Holley-Bockelmann and winced. “Sorry,” she said. “The trust just isn’t there at the moment.”

“Please,” Holley-Bockelmann said. “I know it’s a mess. That’s why I’m here.”

“Maybe the system will recover,” another scientist offered.

Holley-Bockelmann shrugged. “I don’t recognize the place anymore,” she said. “Every lever I knew how to pull was just gone. I’m still trying to understand it.”

It had taken almost two decades at Vanderbilt for her to help build a program that was a national model for training astronomers, with more than 20 students who’d come from tech jobs in California, historically Black colleges or graduate programs around the world. They gathered in their Nashville lab for daily meetings named after Einstein’s equations and a weekly happy hour called ringdown, named for the final tremors of two black holes becoming one. The students sometimes referred to their program as its own solar system, and Holley-Bockelmann was the sun. She gave a TEDx talk in a dress adorned with purple gravitational waveforms and often described the sky as “almost holy, like a religious experience.”

Then came the day after Trump’s election in 2024, when she flew to Washington for a meeting as the chair of NASA’s Astrophysics Advisory Committee. She brought along one of her graduate students, a black-hole researcher named Kamara Culbreath who dreamed of working for NASA. Holley-Bockelmann was leading the group through a review of Trump’s campaign promises to cut federal funding and roll back diversity programs when Culbreath pulled her aside during a break. He showed her a text message on his phone from an unknown number, one that had been sent anonymously to dozens of other Black students at Vanderbilt and other universities.

“Good afternoon, you have been selected to pick cotton at the nearest plantation,” it read. “Masters will pat you down before entry. Make sure you pack some sturdy shoes.”

Holley-Bockelmann walked away from the meeting and forwarded the message to Vanderbilt’s administration and then the police.

“Where do I go to report a racial attack?” she wrote. “Do we have a protocol for crisis response?”

Trump was sworn into office a few months later, and it seemed to Holley-Bockelmann that crisis response was her new job. The federal government froze active grant payments, which many of her students depended on for living expenses. She wrote to the National Science Foundation for advice, but her emails bounced back. A few of her international students stopped coming into work for fear of immigration enforcement, and Culbreath moved out of state to finish his research remotely. Another early-career researcher had a panic attack, booked an overnight flight and then called Vanderbilt the next morning to say he’d permanently returned home to Santo Domingo.

Every few days, Holley-Bockelmann opened another all-caps email from colleagues about “an EXTINCTION level scientific event.” The administration threatened to cut funding for NASA’s science programs by as much as 47 percent. It took over the National Science Foundation’s headquarters in Alexandria, Va., on one day’s notice and gave the building to another department. Holley-Bockelmann scrambled to comply with Trump’s executive orders against diversity programs, changing the name of one Vanderbilt program from “Inclusive Training” to “Interdisciplinary Training,” and scrubbing grant applications of flagged terms like “gender,” “barriers,” “race” and “historically.”

She made several trips to lobby in Washington and organized media campaigns with other scientists, but the footholds she once used for support were disappearing. NASA’s advisory committee on astrophysics was disbanded. Vanderbilt’s chancellor, one of the country’s leading advocates of “institutional neutrality,” largely avoided criticizing the administration, even as cuts reached his own campus. It was increasingly left to Holley-Bockelmann to email her students with a running log of the program’s deterioration.

“I’m flip-flopping between rage and despair, with a side of determination.”

“We haven’t been shut down (yet).”

“Anxiety, depression, stress, fatigue …”

“Please take care of yourselves and others.”

“I’m spending the morning deploying mental health crisis teams.”

She arranged free counseling sessions for students and reserved space in their building for yoga, crochet, puzzles and therapeutic art. For the first time in her life, she didn’t have energy for science. Instead, she found herself gravitating to diamond art, sticking hundreds of dots onto a piece of paper and following a mindless pattern until her brain went numb.

Several months into Trump’s term, a colleague asked Holley-Bockelmann to speak at a conference for young astronomers. There was no money to pay for the flight, so she agreed to appear onscreen. She had won national mentorship awards as one of the best recruiters in American astronomy, but now some of the top astronomy programs were cutting graduate slots and the federal government was eliminating tens of thousands of scientific jobs. She worried that she was becoming a huckster, luring students into six years of training for heartbreak and dead ends. She opened her presentation by showing a photograph of herself, head down, her hands on her temples.

“How can we stay afloat?” the caption read. “How can I lead our community when I’m so enraged? How can I continue to do the work that I love?”

Marcel Levi followed what was happening in the United States and called his team together at the Dutch Research Council in the winter of 2025. He had friends at the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who were losing their funding, their labs, their jobs.

“It’s a tragedy for them, but a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for us,” Levi said.

He’d gone to medical school in the Netherlands in the 1980s and then watched many of his classmates move across the Atlantic. No country at that time spent more than the United States on research and development, and Levi found it difficult to do serious work anywhere else. He flew to Atlanta and Washington several times every year to study cardiovascular disease and blood clots in labs that were better than his own.

But Europe and Asia had begun to catch up. A few months after Trump’s election, Levi saw a poll of 1,600 U. S.-based scientists published in the journal Nature in which 75 percent of respondents said they were considering leaving the country. As president of the Dutch Research Council, Levi proposed setting aside €50 million to recruit some of them. The Netherlands named the program the Tulip Fund, after a flower the Dutch had imported from the Ottoman Empire four centuries earlier and then made their own.

“The roles have been partially reversed,” Levi said when the program began in July 2025. “Some of the brain drain is now moving the other way.”

More than a dozen other countries landed on a similar idea, starting programs to poach American scientists. There was APART-USA (Austria), Safe Place for Science (France) and Canada Leads. The European Union set aside $560 million. South Korea promised a fast track to citizenship.

Arfa Momin/The New York Times

The Tulip Fund offered Dutch institutions up to €1 million per recruited scientist, paid out over five years. The first selections included 29 Americans from places like Yale, Stanford and the National Cancer Institute. They specialized in everything from Alzheimer’s to artificial intelligence, and soon there was a job posting circulating on the American Astronomical Society’s website.

Gravitational wave specialist. Forty-two days vacation. Supporting the LISA mission as part of an “inclusive work force” that valued “collaboration” and “diversity.”

“We are looking for you!” the posting read.

Holley-Bockelmann saw it in Tennessee and showed the ad to her husband, Andreas Bockelmann. The position would require a pay cut. Andreas would need to quit his job as an automotive engineer. They had a house they loved and two teenagers who didn’t want to move. Their daughter was starring on her basketball team. Their son had special needs and thrived on routine.

As they weighed the possibility, Andreas became a citizen decades after arriving from Germany with a green card. He stood with dozens of immigrants early in Trump’s term, listened to “The Star-Spangled Banner” and recited the Oath of Allegiance. An official handed out American flags and played a video message from Trump. “Today you receive one of the most precious gifts ever granted by human hands,” Trump said, as Andreas looked at his family and wondered about the country they were inheriting.

Trump’s tariffs had upended his automotive work. Their children were both adopted from Asia, and lately Andreas had heard reports of state troopers pulling over people based on how they looked. His wife was happiest when she was immersed in science, and she hadn’t run a simulation in weeks.

He told his wife he was ready to move late last year, but she spent weeks going back and forth. “It feels like giving up,” she said. She hated the thought of abandoning her students and leaving the hardest problem of her career unsolved.

“I’m going to have survivor’s guilt,” Holley-Bockelmann said. “Is it worth rearranging our whole lives?”

“It makes more sense than staying here,” Andreas said.

Two months into her new job, Holley-Bockelmann crowded around a computer screen with a few other scientists to watch a simulation of the LISA launch. The mission wasn’t scheduled until 2035, but one of her colleagues had spent the weekend making a digital re-creation. He clicked a button and they watched three spacecraft lift out of French Guiana, escaping Earth’s gravity and flying past the moon. The spacecraft settled into formation about 31 million miles from Earth and exchanged laser beams across the darkness as a ticker of theoretical discoveries accumulated onscreen.

The simulation picked up the steady hum of tens of thousands of burned-out stars, each about the size of Earth but so dense that every spoonful of matter weighed several tons. The lasers registered signals from black holes colliding billions of years in the past, and small black holes falling into giant ones, tracing a hundred thousand loops before they vanished. The simulation reached back to the first million years after the Big Bang, behind the wall of hot fog that had blocked every telescope ever built.

“God, can you imagine?” Holley-Bockelmann said. “I want to know how the first black holes were formed.”

“The first stars, the first galaxies,” said Nora Lützgendorf, the lead project scientist for LISA. “And then we can look forward to all the real discoveries — the stuff we don’t even know how to anticipate or predict yet.”

“How am I going to wait another 10 years?” Holley-Bockelmann said.

Lützgendorf, a 41-year-old German scientist, knew what it meant to wait. She’d spent seven years in the United States working on the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest telescope ever sent into space. NASA had hoped to launch it in 2007, but the mission endured years of manufacturing delays, budget fights, testing failures and finally Covid. It lifted off on Christmas Day in 2021, and Lützgendorf waited another six months for the first images. One revealed hundreds of new stars emerging behind towering cliffs of rust-colored gas in the Carina Nebula, 7,600 light-years from Earth. Lützgendorf tried to call over a colleague to look, and the words caught in her throat.

“I couldn’t breathe,” she said. “I’d spent 10 years imagining these amazing discoveries, and then they were so much better than I thought.”

“Like we could finally see,” Holley-Bockelmann said.

“Yes, exactly,” Lützgendorf said. “I had a little telescope as a kid, and it was like that magical first moment when I got the moon into focus.”

“The glow. The sharp edges,” Holley-Bockelmann said, because she also remembered the feeling of being transported into the sky. Her parents were busy looking straight ahead at the problems of the next day, the next bill, the next job that kept them moving from town to town across Wyoming and then Montana. Meanwhile, she was studying constellations, reading Carl Sagan and writing letters in high school to European observatories to ask for obscure coordinates of black holes.

Each new fact opened into something larger: that the Earth was part of a Milky Way galaxy of a few hundred billion stars; that beyond the Milky Way there were as many as two trillion more galaxies in the observable universe; that most of the atoms in her body were forged inside stars that had died billions of years before the sun came to life. She tried to understand the vastness of space-time by imagining the history of the universe laid out across a 100-yard field. The Earth was born at the 67-yard line. Complex multicellular life formed after 96 yards. Apes began to walk upright in the final two inches. And all of human civilization — the end of the ice age, the birth of agriculture, every war and every empire — had come in the last three thousandths of an inch.

And then she became an astronomer, and what astonished her wasn’t just the universe but the scientists around her, humans pressed against the goal line who had somehow learned to map most of the field.

“LISA will finally give us the whole sky,” Holley-Bockelmann said.

“There are so many secrets hiding out there,” Lützgendorf said. “But 10 years is a long time to wait. People get bored, distracted. That’s where some of our work comes in.”

Germany was building the spacecraft. France and Italy were developing telescopes in case the United States failed to deliver. Lützgendorf and Holley-Bockelmann were building a scientific community in the Netherlands that would be ready for the data. America’s participation was still uncertain, but Holley-Bockelmann had already decided where she would be in 2035. She hit a button on her computer and started to play the simulation again.

Late afternoon in the Netherlands was morning in Nashville, and her graduate students would be waiting. She was still advising more than a dozen of them, so every evening she went back to her hotel and logged in for a second shift. Her family would join her in a few weeks. For now, there was her suitcase in the corner and a single box of crackers in the kitchenette. She filled a wine glass with orange juice, opened her laptop and waved as the first face came onto the screen.

“How’s your crazy new life?” Riddhi Patel, 24, asked.

“Is it awful of me to admit that it’s amazing?” Holley-Bockelmann said. “It’s sunny. There’s science happening, and I’m finally getting to do some of it again. What’s new with you?”

“Mostly trying not to stress out,” Patel said. She was finishing a master’s through a partnership between Vanderbilt and Fisk University, the historically Black college in Nashville. For two decades, the program had placed 85 percent of its students into Ph. D. programs. But now funding was precarious and Ph. D. slots were disappearing. No astronomy student had bridged from Fisk to Vanderbilt in two years.

“I’m getting ready to apply to like 20 places, but maybe that’s pointless,” Patel said.

“What’s unfair is it’s not about you,” Holley-Bockelmann said. “It’s the whole situation. Sometimes, I wish I’d stayed to fight, but I just couldn’t anymore. I’m sorry.”

They workshopped one of Patel’s papers, and then Holley-Bockelmann refilled her orange juice and clicked over to her next meeting. One by one, the students she had helped recruit into astronomy appeared on her screen.

“Maybe I’m just meant to be a math teacher,” one said.

“Is there even a job market anymore?” another asked.

She listened to their questions and anxieties until dark and carried them with her into the next day as she drove west with a colleague toward the beach. The astronomical calendar called for a partial solar eclipse, an event that had inspired awe and terror across human history. Maybe a celestial dragon was eating the sun. Maybe a corrupt emperor had angered the gods. People played drums or shot fiery arrows into the sky to reignite the sun as generations of early scientists began tracking the pattern, calculating the numbers and finally solving the mystery. Now Holley-Bockelmann stepped onto the sand with thousands of other people, put on her cardboard eclipse glasses and looked up over the North Sea.

She watched the moon march across the sun, leaving just a sliver of orange in the sky. The temperature dropped. Light drained from the water. The crowd went silent. She waited as the Earth kept turning and the moon continued its course until light flooded back across the beach.

I trailed Kelly Holley-Bockelmann across the Atlantic as she began her next chapter. I expected her to be bitter about starting over after a career at the pinnacle of American science — but she spoke mostly of relief. And then there were her observations about the universe, which repeatedly blew my mind.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

Republicans Don’t Understand Men, Either

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

David French

By David French

Opinion Columnist

On Dec. 18, 2025, the British comedian and actor Russell Brand walked onto the stage of AmericaFest, the Turning Point USA summit. He talked about his faith in Jesus, speculated that Hunter Biden used Joe Biden’s autopen to smoke crack and delivered a screed against the Covid vaccine.

On Thursday, a London court found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Sexual assault allegations against Brand first surfaced in September 2023, after a joint investigation by The Sunday Times, The Times of London and Channel 4 Dispatches, a British current affairs program.

In other news, men age 18-44 shifted 32 points to the left in the U. S. House of Representatives vote. Nonwhite men age 18-29 shifted 40 points to the left, according to The New York Times’s voter trends analysis,

This was not supposed to happen. The Republican Party was supposed to be the party of men, especially young men. That’s where the manosphere lives and breathes. That’s the party that hosts U. F. C. fights on the South Lawn of the White House.

The Democrats? They’re nothing but a bunch of man-hating feminists and soy boys who think driving pickup trucks and eating red meat is proof of toxic masculinity.

Think back to the Republican National Convention in 2024. The final night was a veritable celebration of Republican manhood. Dana White, the president and chief executive of the U. F. C. (and apparently Trump’s dream press secretary), spoke. So did Hulk Hogan, the legendary professional wrestler. Kid Rock performed.

The capstone of the night was the avatar of Republican masculinity himself, Donald Trump.

And it worked, at least for a while. Trump won in part on the strength of a multiracial surge in male support. He won 63 percent of the white male vote, 50 percent of the Hispanic male vote, and a surprising 19 percent of Black men.

There was a lot of loose talk about a Republican realignment. It was never going to last.

Look back again at the list of headliners at the Republican Convention. As I wrote at the time, White was once caught on video slapping his wife. Hulk Hogan had a sexual relationship with the wife of one of his best friends, a radio host I mention because he went by the name Bubba the Love Sponge. And Kid Rock? He had his own sex tape scandal and once faced an assault charge related to a fight in a Nashville strip club.

And we can’t forget Trump’s own terrible character and horrific treatment of women.

How many fathers actually want their sons to grow up to be like Kid Rock or Donald Trump? Some men might admire their fame or their wealth, but how many want to imitate their character?

Let’s look at more of Turning Point’s lineup at last year’s AmericaFest. In addition to Brand, it included Tucker Carlson, a man who never met a conspiracy theory he didn’t like.

It included Jack Posobiec, a man who came to fame while spreading the lunatic “Pizzagate” conspiracy theory, which, you will recall, claimed that senior officials of the Democratic Party were engaged in a child trafficking ring centered around the Comet Ping Pong pizzeria.

In December 2016 an armed man attacked the pizzeria, firing several rounds with an AR-15 in an attempt to open a locked door. Fortunately, he didn’t harm anyone, but his purpose (at least in part) was to investigate the conspiracy for himself.

Posobiec, a naval officer, was stripped of his security clearance.

And who headlined Turning Point USA’s alternative to the Super Bowl halftime show? Kid Rock, of course.

Far-right men flocked to figures like Andrew Tate, a pornographer, former kickboxer and manosphere influencer who is now facing his own criminal charges, including for rape and sex trafficking.

Others flocked to Nick Fuentes, a grotesque anti-Semite who once kicked off a speech by telling his supporters, “I love you, and I love Hitler.”

Collectively, the new right created a masculine culture that felt almost like a parody of a far-left toxic masculinity fever dream. It was a culture that celebrated raw physical aggression, sexual dominance and exploitation and the naked pursuit of wealth and power.

When anyone raised an objection, he or she was immediately mocked, bullied and lectured. Trump, the manosphere, and groups like Turning Point were reaching Gen Z, we were told. Get out of the way, Boomers, they said. They’re building a youth movement.

Indeed they did. But on the left. Even before the backlash showed up in the polls, I could see it on the ground. The vast majority of young men looked at the masculinity of the new right and reacted with revulsion and horror.

I teach at a Christian college, and I speak at colleges across the country. Despite the crowds at T. P. U. S. A. events, there was no groundswell of support for bullying, for conspiracies or for the kind of performative peacocking that was on display from men like Pete Hegseth.

It’s as if an entire political movement watched a movie like “Back to the Future” and decided that Biff Tannen was the hero. Or they watched a holiday classic like “A Christmas Story” and cheered for Scut Farkus, the kid who terrorized Ralphie on his way to school.

Since I became a journalist, I’ve been writing about the challenges facing young men. One of the first columns I wrote at The Times was about that very topic — that men were falling behind women in school and that they were dying deaths of despair. The antidote wasn’t for young men to demand respect or assert their power but for them to find a purpose, a virtuous purpose in loving and serving others, that would provide deep meaning to their lives.

And no, I don’t think that the left has always approached young men with an open heart and an open mind. I appreciate what my friend Richard Reeves wrote in his invaluable book, “Of Boys and Men: Why the Modern Male Is Struggling, Why It Matters, and What to Do About It.” Phrases like toxic masculinity wrongly taught young men that there was “something toxic inside them that needs to be exorcised.”

As the MAGA right knows, it’s possible to motivate young men through rage and fear. In fact, it’s possible to motivate anyone through rage and fear, at least for a while. But if you really want to reach a young man’s heart, you need to inspire him, not enrage him. Give him an ideal to aspire to, not a person or group to hate.

At least once a year I feel compelled to mention Jeffrey Rosen’s book, “The Pursuit of Happiness.” That phrase, taken from the Declaration of Independence, is often misunderstood. It didn’t mean the pursuit of joy or success so much as it meant “the pursuit of virtue — being good rather than feeling good.”

As Rosen wrote, “The classical definition of the pursuit of happiness meant being a lifelong learner, with a commitment to practicing the daily habits that lead to character improvement, self-mastery, flourishing and growth.”

Does anyone on the right want to call the founders “soy boys”? Actually, don’t answer that question.

What it comes down to is that the MAGA right forgot who a young man truly wants to be.

In my experience (with precious few exceptions), young men want to be good men. They want to be people who grow to be successful, yes. But more than that they want not just to be admired, but to be admirable — to be worthy of any honor or praise they receive.

You can hear it when they talk about the people who are the most positive influences in their lives. They’ll refer to a football coach who taught them to be honest, respectful and brave. They’ll remember the sergeant who showed them what professional excellence looked like. And they’ll talk about the father or uncle or Sunday school teacher who showed them what it meant to be a good husband and a loving father.

And then, when they have children of their own, they won’t brag about their wealth, or glory in their physical strength, or mock the weak. Instead, with their words and deeds they’ll remind young men of Rudyard Kipling’s poem “If—”:

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,

Or walk with Kings — nor lose the common touch,`

If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,

If all men count with you, but none too much;

If you can fill the unforgiving minute

With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,

Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,

And — which is more — you’ll be a Man, my son!

A Stake Through the Heart of Trump’s Red Map

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ezra Klein

By Ezra Klein

Opinion Columnist

When Donald Trump called the 2024 election “a historic realignment,” he, or whoever wrote those words for him, was referring to something specific. The idea of a realignment comes from a paper by the political scientist V. O. Key Jr. Writing in the 1950s, Key sought to describe a kind of “critical election” that recurred across American politics, but only occasionally. These critical elections had three common features: high voter turnout, a “sharp alteration” of the normal voting patterns in the electorate and, most important, “new and durable” groupings of voters that persist for years to come.

Trump’s 2024 election seemed, to many, to fit the model. Voter turnout was high. Trump’s support among Hispanic voters, Asian voters, Black voters, young voters and working-class voters spiked. This was, for Republicans, a new kind of coalition, and it built on Trump’s 2020 coalition, in which he’d made unexpected gains with some of those same groups, albeit not, then, large enough gains to win.

Tuesday’s repudiation of the Republican Party did more than drive a stake through the heart of Trump’s realignment. It raised the possibility of a dizzying new era in American politics — not one in which the electoral groupings are clear and durable, but rather one in which they are fluid and malleable.

It wasn’t a realignment election; it was a dealignment election: an opportunity for “a generational remaking of the Senate map,” Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Senate Democrats, told me.

The House vote, so far, shows a 15-point swing toward the Democrats from 2024. But the swings are much larger among the groups that supposedly realigned rightward two years ago: a 33-point swing toward Democrats among voters age 18 to 29; a 29-point swing among Hispanic voters; a 19-point swing among voters who didn’t attend college; and an 18-point swing among Asian voters.

These swings, and others like them, were large enough to dissolve the colors on the political map. Democrats bested Republicans in Texas and Georgia, Ohio and Iowa. They won a Senate seat in South Carolina and look likely to pick up another in Mississippi. They have already won more than 250 House seats, which is the largest majority either party has held since 2009. A top House Democratic aide told me he learned the names of some of their winning candidates only on election night.

I don’t know any Democrats who are counting on these voting patterns to automatically persist. What the 2026 midterms offer, rather than durability, is possibility. The election demolished old certainties. Democrats can compete in places they thought they could not. If it is possible for them to win in Kansas and Iowa this year, well, why not in 2028, when those states will again see Senate elections — alongside Florida, Alaska, South Carolina, and many more?

“We need to show the people in these states that Democratic senators can actually help them,” Schumer said. “And that’s a two-way street. Those senators need to instruct us on what issues matter most in their states. So now we have an opportunity in these states to learn what might work — and see if what might work in Kansas might work in Nebraska, if what might work in Mississippi might work in Alabama. We have to pay very close attention to that.”

To Schumer, this moment is reminiscent of when the Democrats began to realize that the Southwest, once a Republican stronghold, was winnable: “When we started out, the big four states of Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico had six or seven Republicans, and now they have eight Democrats. We learned how to do that.”

A Democratic Party that won or came close in states where it hadn’t been competitive in decades will pursue them again and others like them — Democrats lost the U. S. Senate contest in Louisiana by less than two percentage points — with renewed force. Candidates who might not have considered running when victory seemed impossible may take another look.

It is hard to achieve what you don’t consider possible. “So many party leaders and donors told Gina it couldn’t happen,” Rebecca Katz, one of the founders of Fight Agency, whose clients included Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, told me. “We almost didn’t win Texas because a lot of people didn’t believe we could.”

But now they know they can. This is the promise of dealignment: a country in which the parties take fewer voters for granted and compete more seriously and creatively in more places. Democrats won this year running seminarians and pastors and pediatricians. They won running D. S. A. members and prosecutors, even a paralympian and a crooner. “To win in the future, we need to be curious,” Katz said.

Midterms often produce big swings, both because disillusioned voters switch sides and because disaffected or uninterested voters stay home. Presidential elections can bring out a differently shaped, or differently inclined, electorate. Republicans won wave midterms in 1994 and 2010 only to bobble the presidential contest two years later. Democrats would err if they interpreted the election as a fulsome endorsement of their party.

“Midterm voters viewed the Democratic Party more unfavorably than favorably, including even a significant share of people who voted for Democrats,” Frances Lee, a political scientist at Princeton, told me. “This looks like an election where the out party was the vehicle for repudiating the party in power. The exit polls point toward an election that was a verdict on the administration: on prices, tariffs, corruption and the war with Iran. Rejecting the party in power is not the same as endorsing the new majority’s program.”

But the Democratic Party emerging out of the 2026 midterms is fundamentally different from the Democratic Party that emerged out of the 2018 midterms. In 2018, there was still a sense that Trump was an aberration or a fluke; that he’d gotten lucky in 2016 and Democrats could double down on who they were already and end MAGA without changing much themselves.

Democrats won power in 2018 and 2020 and wielded it so unconvincingly and alienatingly that Trump and his movement roared back, stronger and more dangerous, than ever. The Democratic Party that emerged from that bruising is chastened in a way its predecessor wasn’t. Democrats know they need to appeal to voters who mistrust them. They are not as liable to mistake Trump’s unpopularity for their popularity. All they have won is a chance to prove themselves. And so they may be more willing to learn lessons that this election had to teach.

“One of the major findings of my research is that geographic polarization is primarily driven by cultural battles,” David Hopkins, a political scientist at Boston College, told me. “Voters in red and blue America differ more on cultural views than on economics. And the 2026 election was overwhelmingly fought on economic grounds. In part, this was because of the affordability crisis putting financial concerns at the top of voters’ minds, but it was also because every faction of the Democratic Party and the larger liberal media/political sphere started talking less about controversial cultural topics and more about economic fairness after 2024.”

I asked Schumer about the tensions Democrats are going to face balancing bills that might lower costs with the manifold other priorities that Democrats hold. “If affordability doesn’t prevail, we’re in trouble,” Schumer told me. “We cannot impose on people what we think is important. We have to listen to what’s important to them and then deliver. The fact that we’ve had such success helps us sell this message. But these senators like Turek and Hamilton and Peltola will help us balance our caucus.”

And Democrats will now be thinking about what it might mean to win another Senate seat in Kansas or rebuild strength in Indiana, where Beau Bayh, a Democrat, just won the election for secretary of state, or break the Republican hammerlock on Florida. That is the gift of a dealignment election, one in which the seemingly durable electoral groupings reveal that they, too, are products of a political moment, and they will be broken in time, and that time may be now, if you are wise enough and creative enough to both lead and listen.

“Texas being competitive is overdue given its demographic composition,” Hopkins said. “The Texas Democratic Party has been basically moribund since the 1990s, and now it has not only a U. S. senator but also a whole cadre of state-level officials to build the party’s governing and organizational strength. Even if Texas Democrats can’t sustain the kind of success they had this week, it’s hard to believe that the state will easily snap back to unchallenged Republican rule in the years ahead.”

The electoral map may be somewhat fixed from year to year, but it is not fixed from generation to generation. Texas was once a Democratic stronghold. California was the political home of both Ronald Reagan and Richard Nixon. Sometimes stasis is less a function of the world around us than of our outdated perceptions.

And this may not be the bottom of Trump’s popularity nor the boundaries of the chaos he might cause. Trump is in his 80s, and his speech and behavior seem ever more discursive and erratic. The true state of his health is opaque. His response to an election in which Republicans hemorrhaged support among Hispanic voters was to … appoint Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. The extent of his family and his administration’s Brobdingnagian corruption will come into clearer view over the next two years. The war with Iran could worsen, as could Russia’s assault on Ukraine, as could the consequences of A. I. to the economy or national security or human flourishing. None of us knew, days after the 2018 election, that much of the 2020 election would happen amid lockdowns and face masks.

Democrats will have more chances to prove who they are, or who they are becoming. Schumer, for one, is counting on it. “We have an opportunity in these red areas to change what they think a Democrat is,” he told me. “Talarico is a Texas Democrat, not a national Democrat. Turek is an Iowa Democrat, not a national Democrat. Most of what people see as a Democrat is a Fox News caricature. Now we have an opportunity to actually show people in these states that a Democrat is different than what they thought.”

Democrats Now Have a Path to Sidestep the Electoral College. Would It Work?

The New York Times November 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Midterm victories have given states the opportunity to elevate the national popular vote, but obstacles like legal challenges would loom.

By Ben Blatt

Twice since 2000 — with George W. Bush and then Donald J. Trump — Republicans have lost the national popular vote but won the Electoral College. That has left many Democrats furious with the system.

Eliminating the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment, a highly unlikely prospect in a polarized nation. But after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats will soon have enough power in statehouses across the country to try to circumvent it without an amendment.

Since 2007, 18 Democratic-run states and the District of Columbia have joined a legal framework that would pledge their Electoral College votes to the nationwide popular vote winner, rather than the winner in their state. The effect of the pact, if enacted and enforced, would be the same as replacing the Electoral College with the popular vote. The pledge would activate only if the states in the pact accounted for at least 270 electoral votes, the majority needed to win.

The states already in the pact represent 222 electoral votes. On Tuesday, Democrats in Arizona, Nevada, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin achieved a “trifecta,” winning control of both chambers in their state legislatures and governor’s offices. If these states all joined the pact, they would represent a total of 283 electoral votes. That would be enough for the agreement, called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, to go into effect:

270 Pact goes into effect

Those states would need to pass laws to join the effort, and a trifecta does not ensure they will. In 2019, for example, the Nevada State Assembly and Senate voted to join the pact, but Gov. Steve Sisolak, a Democrat, vetoed the bill, saying it could “diminish the role of smaller states like Nevada in national electoral contests.”

All five states were swing states in the 2024 election, receiving outsize attention from the presidential campaigns — the kind of attention that the pact’s supporters say is unfairly focused on just a handful of battleground states. They say the agreement would bring the idea of “one person, one vote” to the presidential contest nationwide.

On a more partisan level, Democratic lawmakers may see an incentive to join the pact if they think a future Democrat might win the national popular vote but lose their state.

Lawmakers in all five states have introduced legislation to join the pact in recent years. Among them, Robert Wirch, a state senator in Wisconsin, said he had redrafted his bill. And Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told The New York Times that “the time is right.”

There is some room to spare. Pennsylvania and Michigan would have to join, but just two of Wisconsin, Arizona or Nevada would also need to join to reach 270 electoral votes.

Would it be as simple as that? Here are some possible obstacles:

Such a compact would face a variety of legal challenges.

The pact most likely violates a part of the Constitution known as the compact clause, said William G. Ross, a professor of law and ethics at Samford University.

The Supreme Court has ruled that the compact clause prohibits agreements between states that “interfere with the just supremacy of the United States” without consent from Congress, Professor Ross said. The circumvention of the Electoral College would qualify as interfering with the supremacy of the federal government because it changes the outcome of the presidential election, he said.

Michael Morley, a law professor at Florida State University, said the agreement would probably survive compact clause objections but would run afoul of state constitutions requiring voters in statewide elections to be residents of the state. If the national popular vote were used as the deciding factor for a state’s Electoral College votes, he said, it would essentially be granting voter eligibility to citizens of other states.

Additionally, Professor Morley and others have questioned whether the compact would be enforceable. Imagine a scenario where Republicans win the popular vote but Democrats win the traditional Electoral College. If there were concerns, legitimate or not, that the vote had been suppressed in other states, would Democratic officials still go through with selecting electors for the Republican Party?

Although the compact has language forbidding states to leave in the six-month period before a president’s term ends, states that had once willingly entered into the compact could try to challenge it in court.

“I don’t know that a federal court would order a state to appoint electors against the will of both its executive as well as the will of its own voters,” Professor Morley said.

Many Democratic states are either losing population or failing to grow and, as a result, are in line to lose Electoral College votes after the 2030 census.

According to a Times analysis, the current states in the pact and the five new trifecta states could have a total of 275 Electoral College votes in 2032 instead of the 283 they currently have. That means the pact would need all five new trifecta states to stay afloat. If it went into effect in 2028 with just four of them, it would fall apart in the next election cycle.

How the pact could shrink by 2032

270 Pact goes into effect

And although unlikely, if the population shifts are more severe, the pact could drop below 270 even if all five new trifecta states joined. (Of course, it is possible other states could join.)

The compact’s language says it would not go into effect if the number of electors were under 270 for a given presidential election.

If states can vote to join the pact, they can also vote to leave. As long as they do it six months before a presidential inauguration, it would just require passing a new law.

Right now, the states in the pact and the other trifecta states are under robust Democratic control. But this could always change after the next election. Arizona had a Republican trifecta as recently as 2022. Michigan and Wisconsin had a Republican trifecta in 2018.

Patrick Rosenstiel, who has been pushing for the compact as part of the National Popular Vote group since 2007, says it would be politically difficult for lawmakers to remove it once in place. He pointed to a Pew Research poll from 2024 in which 63 percent of Americans said they would prefer a national popular vote.

“After the first use, this is going to be a far more popular system than the current system,” he said.

It’s not a given that the pact would help Democrats in 2028, let alone in perpetuity. If the pact backfired, there could be a pact-member revolt.

It’s not far-fetched. Although changes in voting patterns tend to affect multiple states, in 2004, if John Kerry had flipped just 1.1 percent of Mr. Bush’s voters in Ohio alone, he would have lost the popular vote and won the Electoral College.

Democrats could have won the Electoral College but lost the popular vote ...

... if in 2004 Democrats had flipped 1.1 percent of the vote in Ohio

... if in 2024 Democrats had flipped 1 percent of the vote in Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania

Note: Popular vote percentages based on shifting just the vote in states with a hypothetical flip. Electoral college votes based on historical electoral map assuming no faithless electors.

The electoral math favors winning sparsely populated states: No matter how small, these states are guaranteed three electoral votes. A bigger factor is that the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College favors parties that can maintain a small lead in large states.

It’s hard to predict future trends, but if Democrats were to eke out a win in Texas, for example, while losing some of their winning margins in New York and California, they could become beneficiaries of the Electoral College.

Ben Blatt is a reporter for The Upshot specializing in data-driven journalism.

In her first interview with The New York Times since her victory, the governor-elect talked about tackling data centers, abortion restrictions and Elon Musk.

Credit... Christopher Lee for The New York Times

Supported by

By J. David Goodman and Edgar Sandoval

Reporting from the grounds of the Texas Capitol in Austin

Gina Hinojosa helped break the Republican grip on Texas in a single election, but the Democratic governor-elect made it clear in an interview with The New York Times on Friday that changing how the state was governed would not happen overnight.

“Legislators, and all of us, are trying to figure out, ‘What does this new world mean?’” she said, standing near the steps of the State Capitol in Austin. “This is an opportunity for all of us to take a moment to ground ourselves.”

Still, Ms. Hinojosa promised changes across a range of issues important to Texans — data centers, immigration, the cost of living, the influence of corporations and Elon Musk.

On data centers, she said, “I don’t think I have the power just to halt them all.”

On abortion, she said she would seek a compromise with Republicans who still have a majority in the State Senate.

On immigration, she said she would seek to work “in a collaborative way with Donald Trump.”

“We need to be partners in making sure that we keep our border secure,” she said.

Ms. Hinojosa’s win was part of a dramatic sweep that placed a Democrat in every statewide office that was up for a vote in Tuesday’s election. The Democratic Party now controls the Texas House. A Democrat is the chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court.

Texas Democrats have waited more than 30 years for any sort of statewide control, and many spent last week entertaining thoughts of what a newly blue Texas could look like.

Kendall Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democratic Party, said he hoped for anti-corruption legislation and a roll back of Gov. Greg Abbott’s private school vouchers program. Beto O’Rourke, the former El Paso congressman, said an effective early agenda could include raising the minimum wage and expanding Medicaid.

“The clock is already ticking,” Mr. O’Rourke said in a phone interview. “Sky high expectations have been set.”

Ms. Hinojosa has been careful to not over-promise or overreach. On Thursday, she named a Republican state legislator to be part of her transition team and praised Mr. Abbott for being “gracious” in defeat and willing to work with her.

In the Times interview on Friday, she said she would urge the legislature to help her fulfill her promise to send $1,500 checks to every Texas household, drawing on the state’s roughly $27 billion surplus.

“It is a very popular position,” she said. “I have yet to hear of a Republican legislator who’s against it.”

Her vision of what a blue Texas looks like, she said, is “a Texas that’s delivering for the people,” and not about partisan politics. She described her agenda as bipartisan and post-partisan.

It’s “not a Democratic agenda,” she said.

Tuesday’s election made clear that Ms. Hinojosa, along with other Democrats across Texas, had benefited from Latino voters shifting away from the Republican Party. She attributed the change to the rising cost of living and the federal immigration crackdown.

While Ms. Hinojosa said she would work with President Trump on some aspects of immigration enforcement, she added that the harsh tactics employed by some Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and their close collaboration with Texas state police, “cannot continue the way it is now.” She said she plans to tell President Trump that the current approach was “making a lot of people angry, afraid, and unsafe.” (The two have not yet spoken, she said.)

Ms. Hinojosa also vowed to review the budget for Mr. Abbott’s signature border security program, Operation Lone Star, to ensure it was “not political theater.” Under the program, Texas has spent billions of dollars on National Guard deployments and state police patrols to catch and deter unauthorized migration and to construct border barriers.

Also on the topic of immigration, Ms. Hinojosa said she would use the state’s licensing power to stop private prison companies from holding children in detention facilities in Texas.

“Locking up little kids like that, even with their parents, that is child abuse,” she said.

On a variety of fronts, Ms. Hinojosa said she was still determining what the limits of her new power will be starting in January, and how much she and her fellow Democrats would be able to achieve, given the power of Republicans to block legislation and thwart nominations in the legislature.

“We still have a Republican Senate,” she said in response to a question about the state’s strict abortion ban. She said she would “prioritize making sure that doctors are no longer prosecuted” for providing abortions in cases of medical emergencies. “Too many women are dying in Texas,” she said.

“I am just feeling pretty confident that we can come together in the name of saving women’s lives,” she said of her administration and Republican lawmakers.

During her campaign, Ms. Hinojosa harnessed discontent over data centers and garnered support from conservative rural communities as she promised to impose a moratorium on new facilities until new regulations can be adopted. In the interview, she said she would look to stop those that have already begun construction but still need certain permits.

“I will use my power to make sure those permits are held until we can protect Texans,” she said.

At the same time, she sought to reassure businesses leaders in the state, including Mr. Musk, its richest resident, that she was “pro-business” — provided the businesses were pro-Texas.

“I welcome him to be here," she said of Mr. Musk. “But it needs to be about what a relationship can provide for Texas.”

During the interview, conducted on the path leading to the State Capitol, a crowd gathered and watched in silence. Nearby a box truck with a digital screen displayed a series of messages bidding farewell to Mr. Abbott and celebrating the election of Ms. Hinojosa.

“Happiness is a new governor,” one message read.

As she finished the interview, the crowd erupted into cheers.

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

Edgar Sandoval covers Texas for The Times, with a focus on the Latino community and the border with Mexico. He is based in San Antonio.

When the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inducts Collins as a solo artist this month, it will recognize a hitmaker whose popularity often overshadowed his intensity.

Credit...

Supported by

By Jon Pareles

Visuals by Dana Scruggs

Phil Collins considers himself “lucky.” The English drummer, songwriter and frontman has been a child actor, a versatile sideman, a progressive-rock innovator with Genesis, a skillful producer and a prolific pop hitmaker. He has also gotten divorced three times, been mocked as uncool, struggled with alcoholism, and been rediscovered through sampling and nostalgia. Like all long rock careers, his has been complicated.

On Nov. 14, Collins, 75, will be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for the second time. The first, in 2010, was as a member of Genesis. Now he’s being recognized for his extensive, and hugely popular, solo work. With the renewed recognition, Collins has re-emerged to burnish and reassess his musical legacy, even though his performing years may well be over.

“I’d gotten quite used to being overlooked,” he said in an interview at his Manhattan apartment. Photographs of his five children filled a coffee table. On the windowsill sat a Diamond Award trophy, presented by the Recording Industry Association of America when his 1985 album, “No Jacket Required,” surpassed 10 million sales. Alongside it, an electric keyboard faced a view of Central Park.

“I didn’t go looking to see who was nominated this year, so I was quite surprised when I heard I was up for induction,” he continued. “It’s just a pat on the back, you know. If it wasn’t there, I wouldn’t be craving it. But it is there, and I’m very, very pleased.”

By the late 1980s, Collins was nearly ubiquitous, his music was such a radio staple that some began to dismiss him as anodyne easy listening, ignoring the emotional and rhythmic intensity of the songs themselves.

Collins’s career reached spectacular heights. He sold more than 100 million solo albums worldwide, and another 100 million as a member of Genesis. In 2022, he and the band sold their catalogs for a reported $300 million. Through the decades, Collins has won eight Grammy Awards, including album of the year for “No Jacket Required” and record of the year for his 1989 song “Another Day in Paradise,” which has lately been revived as the theme for the Hulu show “Paradise.” He won an Oscar for “You’ll Be in My Heart” from the Disney musical “Tarzan.”

Yet Collins’s most striking songs grew out of dark moments in a life that often pitted career against family. “I’ve always been — I won’t say a sensitive soul, but I’ve always worn my heart on my sleeve,” Collins said. “Each album categorizes a certain period in my life.” His first two solo albums, “Face Value” and “Hello, I Must Be Going!,” were written in the wake of his first divorce. His 1993 album, “Both Sides,” delved into the conflicting impulses around the collapse of his second marriage, which was damaged by an affair that briefly reunited him with a high-school girlfriend. “My love life is a cauldron of conflictions of which I am far from proud,” Collins wrote in his 2016 autobiography, “Not Dead Yet.”

Decades of intensely physical stage performances as a frontman and drummer left his back and legs damaged. In his autobiography, Collins wrote that frequent injections of prednisone, a corticosteroid he used to bolster his voice through long tours, made his bones brittle. He now gets around, stiffly and slowly, with a walker. “Everything that could go wrong, did,” he said, “all at the wrong time.”

He has rarely appeared in public in recent years and, after severe medical problems, Collins is unlikely to perform again. “I’m not match-fit,” he said.

COLLINS GREW UP making music. When he was 5 years old, family friends built him a mini drum kit with biscuit tins and a tambourine. He took a few piano and drum lessons, but never learned to read music. “Being self-taught as a drummer and a keyboard player, I would come up with things that were unusual,” he said. “Sometimes if you don’t know the rules, you don’t know if you’re breaking them.”

At 13 he was a child actor playing the Artful Dodger in the West End production of “Oliver!” He worked a journeyman’s assortment of gigs as a teenage drummer in London before joining Genesis in 1970. At the vanguard of early progressive rock, Genesis flaunted multipart song structures and complex rhythms, propelled by Collins’s nimble, microscopically subdivided beats and underlying swing.

Brann Dailor, the drummer in the progressive metal band Mastodon, is a vocal Collins admirer. “He really perfected the ability to camouflage odd time signatures and interesting high-hat work and rhythms where you’re like, “Oh, there’s more than meets the eye,’” Dailor said via video interview. “The layman can still shake their ass to it. But if you’re a schooled musician, or if you pay attention and you’re a player, you can hear that he’s doing lots under the surface.”

Peter Gabriel left Genesis in 1975, and after extensive auditions yielded no lead singer to replace him, Collins reluctantly stepped forward. He left behind “the security blanket of the drum kit,” he said. “No one was really looking, because they were looking at the singer. Suddenly I became the singer and that was very intimidating at first. But I got used to it.”

With Collins as frontman, the band’s songwriting evolved from expansive progressive rock to more concise — yet still intricate — material. Its audience scaled up to stadiums.

But Collins stayed even busier than the band. Between Genesis commitments, he also took on side projects that he couldn’t resist, moonlighting in a jazz-fusion band, Brand X, and playing recording sessions and tour dates with Gabriel, Robert Fripp, Brian Eno and others.

His constant gigging strained and then broke Collins’s first marriage. As 1978 ended, his wife moved to Canada with their two children. Living alone in the English countryside, Collins turned his master bedroom into a recording studio and started writing the songs that would fill his 1981 solo debut, “Face Value.”

“It wasn’t even an album,” he said. “It was just me trying to get the equipment to work and basically having a bit of fun improvising.”

“It’s so raw,” Hugh Padgham, who co-produced “Face Value,” recalled in a phone interview. “He hadn’t become a pop star yet — he didn’t even think he was going to be. So we didn’t have any inhibitions.”

Instead of the filigreed counterpoint and fantasy scenarios of Genesis songs, Collins found himself using space, silences and blunt emotional declarations that would soon reach mass audiences. What makes his songs so durable, he said, is that “I’m pretty normal, pretty ordinary, like everybody else is. And I write about things that have either happened to me, or I’m feeling, or situations I’ve been in. People relate to that.

“I have, over the years, thought about it — not too hard, because sometimes it’s better not to know what it is. And wow, this is great. I’m doing something that’s totally natural to me. And people are slapping me on the back saying, ‘That’s good, I like that.’ That’s really all it is.”

“Face Value” opened with “In the Air Tonight,” a song that would become a talisman of 1980s rock. The lyrics are at once foreboding and furious: “If you told me you were drowning / I would not lend a hand.” The track has a sparse drum-machine pulse, minor chords, phantom vocal harmonies and huge reverberant hollows. Suddenly, more than three minutes in, booming live drums make a volcanic entrance. They’re recorded with a gated-reverb sound — explosive, and then silent — that Padgham and Collins had discovered while recording Peter Gabriel’s track “Intruder.” Those drums would be sampled and imitated for years to come, including by Mike Tyson in a standout scene from the 2009 film “The Hangover.”

Through the 1980s, Collins kept racking up No. 1 hits, including “Against All Odds,” “Sussudio,” “One More Night,” “Two Hearts” and “Another Day in Paradise” on his own; and “Invisible Touch” with Genesis. He was a drummer and producer for Eric Clapton and Robert Plant, both musicians Collins had idolized as a teenager and wouldn’t think of turning down. “I just kept getting asked to do things,” he said.

Collins courted overexposure at the Live Aid concerts on July 13, 1985. In London, he sang two songs of his own and played piano with Sting. Then he crossed the Atlantic via Concorde to sing again, back up Clapton on drums and join a reunited, sloppy Led Zeppelin in Philadelphia. He had been invited to play with friends; he ended up overcommitted and under-rehearsed, accused of showboating.

COLLINS STAYED BUSY through the 1990s and early 2000s with solo albums, including “Both Sides,” a solitary project with songs about crumbling relationships, in which he sang and played all the parts himself. In his book, he describes it as “the innermost thoughts and feelings of this haunted, guilty man,” and — along with “Face Value” — a favorite among his albums.

It didn’t sell as spectacularly as his 1980s blockbusters, but he could still fill stadiums worldwide. On tour in Europe, he met a 21-year-old Swiss woman who would become his third wife. They settled in Switzerland, were married in 1999, had two sons and divorced in 2008. He still spends most of his time there.

The 1980s backlash receded as hip-hop producers rediscovered his drum sounds and melodic hooks; Lil’ Kim covered “In the Air Tonight,” and Bone Thugs-N-Harmony built their song “Home” on Collins’s “Take Me Home.”

Collins announced his retirement in 2004 with the First Final Farewell Tour, which continued into 2005. But he rejoined Genesis to tour in 2007 and 2021, and he followed the publication of his book with the “Not Dead Yet” arena tour, handing over the drumming to his son Nicholas.

By then, Collins’s body was beginning to fail. A viral infection left him with severe hearing loss in his left ear. During the 2007 Genesis tour, he found it increasingly difficult to hold his drumsticks. And faced with leisure time after decades on the road and in the studio, he took to drinking, at times so heavily he was near death.

In retrospect, would he have changed his work-life balance? “I wouldn’t,” he replied. “Because that would mean that I would have missed out on a lot of things that I learned from and I really enjoyed doing.”

Collins hasn’t made music for some time, but the Hall of Fame induction news has brought a new round of media interviews and questions about whether he will again someday. His home in Switzerland, he said, has a full studio setup waiting for him.

“At one point, if I went down there, it meant work,” he said. “When I was trying to retire, I used to go the longest way around to avoid being in it, you know? But I will get down there.”

Jon Pareles, a culture correspondent for The Times, served as chief pop music critic for 37 years. He studied music, played in rock, jazz and classical groups and was a college-radio disc jockey. He was previously an editor at Rolling Stone and The Village Voice.
